makkah.programmesIntro: Four programmes account for nearly every enquiry a Makkah family makes: the IB Diploma Programme, the Middle Years Programme that feeds it, the Primary Years Programme underneath, and Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel IGCSE, which many families in this city reach through a British-curriculum school rather than an IB one. Each is assessed differently, so each needs a different kind of tutor.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Final grades combine written papers sat in the May session with internally assessed work marked at school and moderated by the board. The core contributes bonus points through a matrix that pairs the Theory of Knowledge grade with the Extended Essay grade. The arithmetic matters: a student can lose a university offer on the core while every subject grade holds, which is why Extended Essay drift in DP1 is worth catching early.
programmes.countryNote: Makkah families reach the Diploma mostly through schools on or beyond the Jeddah corridor, so the weekly rhythm is set by travel as much as by timetable. A DP2 student who returns home only at the end of the school week often does better with two longer weekend sessions than four short weekday ones, and that is a scheduling decision to make in the autumn term rather than in the spring.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against published criteria rather than against a single examination paper, with each criterion carrying its own strands and its own descriptors. The Personal Project in the final year is the piece most families underestimate: it is assessed on process and reflection, not on the finished artefact. Criterion-referenced marking rewards a different habit from content recall, and students who have come from a national-curriculum or CBSE background usually need that habit taught explicitly rather than absorbed.
programmes.countryNote: In Makkah the Middle Years Programme is often where a family first discovers that the school cannot run a particular subject at the depth they expected. Catching that in Year 9 leaves room to build the missing foundation before Diploma subject choices lock. Catching it in Year 11 does not, and the catch-up then competes with Personal Project deadlines.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses assessed almost entirely by external written papers, with tiering in several subjects: Cambridge offers Core and Extended routes in Mathematics and the sciences, and the tier a student is entered for caps the grade available. Candidates in the Kingdom sit the June series as the main sitting and the November series for resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge also runs a February and March series, but that series is sat only in India, so a Makkah family should plan for June and November.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools around Makkah and along the Jeddah corridon set their own term dates, which means two children in the same district can face mock examinations a fortnight apart. Always work from your own school's published calendar and from the examinations officer's entry deadlines rather than from a date quoted by a tutoring company.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: An inquiry-led curriculum organised around transdisciplinary themes rather than discrete subjects, ending in the Exhibition. There are no external examinations, so support at this stage is about the things that surface later: fluency in number bonds and fractions, reading stamina, and writing in English at the length a secondary school will expect. Weak place-value work in Year 5 reappears as algebra failure in Year 9, and algebra failure in Year 9 reappears as a Mathematics Higher Level problem in DP1.
programmes.countryNote: Primary support for Makkah families is usually short and specific rather than open-ended: a term of weekly number work, or a block on written English before a transfer application to a school on the Jeddah corridor. Entry assessments at those schools are set at the receiving school's own standard, so ask them what they test before buying lessons.

makkah.subjectsIntro: The subjects below are the ones Makkah families most often cannot cover locally, and the notes say what each one actually assesses and where the marks go missing. Higher Level and Standard Level are not the same course with a different amount of homework; the Higher Level extension usually changes how the shared content is examined, not just how much of it there is.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: The algebraic route, and the one most engineering and physics courses expect. Higher Level adds proof, complex numbers and deeper calculus, and Paper 3 asks for extended investigative work that no amount of formula recall covers. Marks are lost in unjustified steps rather than wrong answers: the mark scheme pays for reasoning, so a correct result with no visible method still drops method marks.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The modelling and statistics route, assessed with the graphic display calculator assumed throughout. Students who choose it expecting an easier course often meet trouble in the statistics strands, where the difficulty is interpretation rather than computation. Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and more demanding modelling, and Paper 3 rewards students who can explain what a model fails to capture.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Mechanics, waves, fields and energy, with Higher Level extending into rotational dynamics and quantum topics. The most common failure is mathematical rather than conceptual: a student who cannot rearrange confidently loses marks on questions they understand. The internally assessed investigation needs a measurable, controllable variable, and a poor research question in the first fortnight limits the achievable mark however good the write-up.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Structure and reactivity, taught through the organising framework the current syllabus uses. Energetics, equilibrium and organic mechanisms are where outside teaching is asked for most. Higher Level questions routinely combine two topics in one item, so a student who has revised topic by topic can still stall. Precision in definitions is examined strictly, and loose wording costs marks that content knowledge cannot recover.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: A content-heavy course whose marks turn on command terms. The gap between what a student knows and what the mark scheme pays for is wider here than in any other science: outline, explain, distinguish and evaluate each demand a different shape of answer. Data-based questions in Paper 2 need practice against real mark schemes, and statistical reasoning is assessed more directly than most students expect.

subjects.name: Chemistry and Physics for the Extended Essay
subjects.description: An Extended Essay in a science subject fails most often on scope rather than on knowledge: a research question that cannot be answered in four thousand words, or an investigation with no measurable outcome. A tutor may discuss the question, point at the assessment criteria and give feedback on the student's own draft. The essay itself must be written by the student, and the school supervisor remains the formal supervisor.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram discipline decides the grade. Most lost marks come from axes without labels, curves without shift arrows, and evaluation that restates the argument instead of weighing it. Higher Level adds quantitative questions and a separate paper, and the internally assessed commentaries must each use a genuinely recent news article and apply a different section of the syllabus.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Assessed through tools, theories and techniques applied to real organisations, with a case study released in advance for one paper. Students lose marks by describing a business rather than applying a framework to it. Higher Level extensions include more demanding quantitative content, and the internally assessed project must rest on the student's own primary or secondary research.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided textual analysis, a comparative essay, the individual oral and, at Higher Level, an additional essay. Students arriving from a curriculum that rewarded summary have to be retaught to argue from the text. The individual oral needs a global issue and two extracts chosen early; left to the last term it becomes the weakest component on the transcript.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Systems fundamentals, algorithmic thinking and the internally assessed solution, with Higher Level adding abstract data structures and resource management. Marks go missing in the documentation rather than the code: the criteria pay for a defined client, a planned design and evidence of testing. A working program with no record of how it was designed scores poorly.

makkah.igcseSubjectsIntro: Many Makkah families follow a British-curriculum route rather than an IB one, so the IGCSE grid below sits alongside the Diploma subjects. Tier choice, calculator discipline and the difference between the Cambridge and Edexcel versions of the same subject are the three things worth checking before lessons start.

igcseSubjects.name: IGCSE Mathematics
igcseSubjects.description: The tier decision caps the grade, so it has to be made on evidence rather than on comfort. Extended papers assume fluent algebraic manipulation, and most lost marks sit in multi-step problems where a single early slip propagates. Edexcel and Cambridge differ in paper structure and in how much is calculator-free, which changes how a student should practise.

igcseSubjects.name: IGCSE Physics
igcseSubjects.description: Formula recall is the smaller half of the task; unit conversion and significant figures quietly remove marks across every paper. The practical paper, where a school enters for it, rewards students who have drawn and criticised real graphs rather than read about them. Extended questions often ask for an explanation where students supply a description.

igcseSubjects.name: IGCSE Chemistry
igcseSubjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and organic families are the three topics outside teaching is asked for most. Equation balancing and state symbols are marked strictly, and a correct product with a missing symbol still drops the mark. Students who learn reactions as lists rather than as patterns stall on unfamiliar examples in the Extended paper.

igcseSubjects.name: IGCSE Biology
igcseSubjects.description: A memory-heavy subject examined through precise language. Definitions of diffusion, osmosis and active transport are among the most strictly marked in the specification, and diagrams must be labelled with the terms the mark scheme uses. Extended-response questions reward structure, so a plan written in thirty seconds usually beats a longer unplanned answer.

igcseSubjects.name: IGCSE English
igcseSubjects.description: Two different qualifications that families regularly confuse. First Language English assesses reading response and directed writing with a tight register; English as a Second Language assesses comprehension, summary and controlled writing. Choosing the wrong one wastes a year, so check what the school has actually entered the student for before booking support.

igcseSubjects.name: IGCSE Economics and Business Studies
igcseSubjects.description: Both reward application over recall. Economics marks turn on diagram accuracy and on the chain of reasoning between cause and effect; Business Studies marks turn on using the right tool for the right question and on justifying a recommendation. Data-response questions in both are where students who have only revised definitions come unstuck.

makkah.regionsTitle: Makkah districts, and the slot each one can realistically hold
makkah.regionsIntro: Makkah is not one travel market. The expressway runs west towards Jeddah, the Taif road climbs south-east, and the central districts around the Haram slow down markedly in Umrah season. The notes below are about the school run and the lesson slot it leaves, because that is the practical constraint on weekly tuition in this city.

regions.name: Al Aziziyah
regions.note: A large residential district with good access to the Third Ring Road and onwards to the Jeddah corridor. Families here usually clear the school run earlier than those in the central districts, which makes a half past five start workable on most school nights.

regions.name: Al Awali
regions.note: South-east of the city towards the Taif road, with longer runs to schools on the western side. Six o'clock is a more honest starting point here, and a single longer session usually beats two short ones squeezed either side of the journey home.

regions.name: Al Rusaifah
regions.note: West of the centre and close to the Haramain high-speed railway station, which makes a Jeddah-corridor school reachable by rail for older students. Families using the train often prefer a fixed weekday evening slot over weekend blocks, because the return is predictable.

regions.name: Al Shawqiyah
regions.note: North-west, towards the expressway exits. Convenient for travel out of the city and less so for schools in the south-east, so evenings run late in term time. Weekend sessions are common here for students who stay nearer their school during the week.

regions.name: Al Nuzha
regions.note: Central-north residential streets with short local runs but heavy through-traffic in peak seasons. The pattern that works is a slot agreed for the whole term and moved deliberately during busy weeks, rather than renegotiated lesson by lesson.

regions.name: Al Umrah Al Jadidah
regions.note: West of the centre on the Jeddah side, with reasonable access out of the city. Families here frequently have one child at a local school and another on the corridor, which usually means two different slots on two different evenings rather than one shared session.

regions.name: Al Khalidiyah
regions.note: Dense central-west housing where the journey time depends almost entirely on the season rather than on the distance. Build the weekly plan around the slowest weeks, not the fastest, and the slot survives the whole term.

regions.name: Al Zahir
regions.note: Close to the central area, so school runs are short but the surrounding roads carry the heaviest pilgrim traffic in the city. A later start and a longer session is the arrangement most families here settle on after the first month.

schoolClusters.city: The Jeddah corridor, 80km west
schoolClusters.note: Most Makkah families following an international curriculum look along the expressway towards Jeddah, where the IB Diploma and Cambridge provision is concentrated. Jeddah itself runs as a long coastal spine from the historic centre north to Obhur, so two schools described as being in Jeddah can be forty minutes apart. Ask about subject availability at Higher Level before enrolling, not after.

schoolClusters.city: Thuwal and the coast north of Jeddah
schoolClusters.note: The KAUST School serves the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology campus community north of Jeddah on the coast. Campus and compound schools run a different weekly rhythm from city schools, with activities built into the day, and that compresses where a tuition slot can sit. Students we support attend schools of this kind.

schoolClusters.city: Riyadh and the Eastern Province, for families weighing a move
schoolClusters.note: Families who expect to relocate inside the Kingdom usually want to know whether the subject their child needs at Higher Level exists at the destination. Riyadh carries the widest IB provision; the Dammam, Khobar and Dhahran cluster behaves as a single school market, with families living in one city and attending school in another.

makkah.schoolDisclaimer: Schools are named here only as context for the curriculum map around Makkah and the wider Kingdom; IB Gram has no affiliation with any of them and claims none.
makkah.modesIntro: Four patterns cover almost every Makkah arrangement. The right one depends on the travel week rather than on the subject: a student who comes home on a Thursday and a student who is home by five every day need completely different timetables, even when they are sitting the same papers.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one on a fixed slot
modes.description: The default, and the pattern that produces the steadiest movement. One subject, one tutor, the same evening each week, pinned to Arabia Standard Time so it does not drift when a tutor's own country changes its clocks. Sessions usually run sixty or ninety minutes; ninety suits a Higher Level science where a full past-paper question plus feedback will not fit into an hour.
bullets: Same tutor, same slot, agreed for the whole term
Sixty or ninety minutes depending on subject and level
Written notes to the parent after each session
Slot pinned to Makkah's clock, not the tutor's

modes.title: Two subjects across the week
modes.description: Common from the spring term of DP1 onwards, when two Higher Level subjects are both losing marks. Two different specialists on two different evenings beats one generalist covering both, and the two tutors work to a shared written plan so the student is not asked to prioritise twice. Keeping them on separate evenings matters more than families expect; two hours back to back produces one good hour.
bullets: A specialist per subject rather than one tutor for both
Separate evenings, not a double session
One shared plan so targets do not conflict
Reviewed together at the end of each term

modes.title: Weekend blocks for weekly boarders and long commutes
modes.description: For students who stay nearer their school on the Jeddah corridor during the week and return home at the end of it. Friday and Saturday are the weekend here, so a longer block on one of those days is often the only arrangement that holds through a term. Two ninety-minute sessions across the weekend give more usable teaching than four rushed weeknight half-hours.
bullets: Friday or Saturday sessions, timed to the return journey
Longer blocks with a break rather than one continuous stretch
Work set for the week ahead, marked before the next block
Useful during Hajj and Umrah seasons, when weekday travel slows

modes.title: Intensive run-up to a series
modes.description: A short, dense block in the final weeks before the June or November series, built around past papers by component rather than around topics. The first session diagnoses which paper is losing the most marks; the rest attack that paper under timing. This is the one pattern where more hours a week genuinely helps, and it works only if content teaching happened earlier.
bullets: Diagnostic first session against a real mark scheme
Papers sat under exam timing, then marked line by line
Component-by-component targets rather than topic revision
Booked early, because specialist availability thins before a series

sections.heading: The school year, counted forward from where you are standing
paragraphs: Every decision about tuition in Makkah is really a decision about timing. The same subject, the same tutor and the same hourly rate produce completely different value depending on which part of the year you buy them in. Support bought in the autumn term of DP1 is cheap in effect, because it is fixing foundations while there is still room to fix them. The same spend eight weeks before a series buys technique, not knowledge, and technique only converts marks a student has already earned the content for.

The practical sequence runs like this. In the first half of the autumn term, diagnose. Find out what the previous course left missing, which is almost always algebraic fluency in the sciences and command-term discipline in the essay subjects. In the second half, when the first Internal Assessment briefs land and Extended Essay conversations begin, shift from content to mark schemes. Through the midyear break and the spring term, work on the student's own drafts and on timed practice. In the final eight weeks, narrow to the single component losing the most marks and stop teaching anything else.

After results the year does not stop, and this is where Makkah families lose the most time. A student retaking a subject in the November series has a short, awkward window and needs the entry confirmed by the school's examinations officer early. A student heading to a Saudi university needs the Ministry of Education equivalency route started well before the application opens, and needs Qiyas test preparation planned alongside school work rather than after it. Neither of those is a results-day job.

Entry deadlines, mock weeks and internal deadlines all differ school by school, including between two British-curriculum schools in the same district. Work from your own school's published calendar and from the examinations officer's dates. Any tutoring company that quotes you a single Kingdom-wide deadline is quoting something it cannot know.
bullets: Autumn term: diagnose the gap from the previous course, before Higher Level content stacks on it
Spring term: move from content to mark schemes and the student's own drafts
Final eight weeks: one component at a time, under exam timing
After results: resit entries, equivalency paperwork and Qiyas preparation

sections.heading: The Makkah school run, and the hours it actually leaves free
paragraphs: This is the part of a Makkah tuition plan that decides whether it survives a term. The city sits roughly 80km east of Jeddah, with the expressway running west, the Taif road climbing south-east, and the Third Ring Road carrying local traffic around the centre. International-curriculum schools are concentrated along the Jeddah corridor rather than inside Makkah, so a large share of families here are travelling further for school than a family in Riyadh or Al Khobar would. That travel comes out of the same evening a tuition slot wants to occupy.

The mistake we see most often is a family agreeing to a four o'clock slot in the first week of term because that is when the tutor was free, then cancelling it three weeks running because the car is still on the road at four. A slot that survives is one built around the slowest realistic journey, not the fastest. If the school run from Al Awali takes forty minutes on a good day and an hour on a busy one, the honest start time is six o'clock, and a six o'clock slot kept every week beats a half past four slot kept two weeks in three.

Central districts near the Haram behave differently again. Distances there are short, but pilgrim traffic in Umrah season and around Hajj can turn a fifteen-minute run into three times that, and the variation is seasonal rather than daily. Families in Al Khalidiyah or Al Zahir generally settle on a later start and a longer session, which also reduces the number of journeys the week has to accommodate.

For students who stay nearer their school during the week and come home at the end of it, the whole question changes. Friday and Saturday are the weekend in the Kingdom, so the workable pattern is one or two longer blocks across those two days with marked work set for the week in between. That arrangement is less convenient for the tutor and far more durable for the family, which is the right trade to make.

sections.heading: A Sunday-to-Thursday week against your tutor's own working week
paragraphs: The Kingdom's school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. Almost every piece of tutoring copy written for this market was adapted from British or Indian material and quietly assumes a Monday-to-Friday week, which is why so many arrangements fall apart in the second month. A tutor based in India or the United Kingdom is working on their own Monday-to-Friday timetable, so your Sunday evening is their weekend and your Thursday evening is their working night.

Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not observe daylight saving. That single fact causes more disruption than the offset itself. A slot agreed with a tutor in the United Kingdom will move by an hour twice a year from their side unless it is pinned to Makkah local time in writing at the start. Pin it to Makkah, and the family never has to think about it again; pin it to the tutor's clock, and a six o'clock lesson quietly becomes a seven o'clock one in the middle of a term.

The practical consequence is that a tutor's base matters almost as much as their subject. A specialist whose own evening lines up with yours will hold a weekly slot for a year. One whose evening does not will cancel, reschedule, or simply be tired, and a tired tutor at nine o'clock at night is worth less than a fresh one at six. We would rather tell a Makkah family that a particular Physics Higher Level specialist is wrong for their slot than book a lesson that will not last.

The table below takes a six o'clock Makkah slot and shows what it is in six common tutor bases, along with the tutor's own weekend. Read the last column first: it is the one that predicts whether the arrangement holds.

sections.heading: What tuition is advertised at around Makkah, and who publishes those numbers
paragraphs: Rates in this market are published by the people selling the lessons, which is worth saying out loud before any number appears. The figures below are advertised rates taken from tutoring platforms, tutor marketplaces and tutoring companies operating in the Kingdom. They are not a market average, they are not audited, and they are not IB Gram's price. They are useful as a band, because a family that knows the band can tell when a quote is out of line in either direction.

What moves a number, in rough order of weight: subject scarcity, then examiner or marking experience, then level, then whether the tutor travels, then package length. Scarcity dominates. A Mathematics Applications and Interpretation Standard Level tutor can be found in most cities; a Physics Higher Level specialist who has marked for the board is scarce everywhere, and the price reflects the queue rather than the hour. Travel loading is the reason in-home rates in Saudi cities sit above online ones for the same tutor, and it is quietly the largest line in an in-home quote outside the tutor's own fee.

Two patterns are worth watching. International providers quoting in dollars, commonly around USD 60 an hour, leave a Makkah family carrying the exchange rate as well as the fee, and the quoted figure often excludes materials and reports. And rates advertised as starting points rarely apply to the subject a Diploma family actually needs: the headline number is usually for a generalist at the lowest level on offer.

Group classes are genuinely cheaper per hour and sometimes the right choice, particularly for content catch-up in a subject where the student is simply behind rather than confused. They are the wrong choice for Internal Assessment feedback, for the individual oral, or for a student whose problem is specific and diagnosable. One hour spent on this student's own last paper is worth more than three spent on a shared revision sequence.

sections.heading: Hajj and Umrah seasons, and building a study week that survives them
paragraphs: Makkah is the one city in the Kingdom where the academic calendar bends around pilgrimage seasons, and treating that as a practical planning fact rather than a footnote is what separates a workable plan from an optimistic one. Traffic management around the central area, road closures, school adjustments and the simple density of visitors all change how long a journey takes and how much of an evening is left. None of this is unusual to families who live here. It is routinely missing from tutoring copy written elsewhere.

Two things follow. First, pick the slot that works in the busiest weeks rather than the quietest, because a slot chosen for an easy week has to be renegotiated when the hard week arrives, and renegotiated slots tend to be lost slots. Second, decide in advance which weeks of the term will be light and say so when the plan is agreed. A tutor who knows in the autumn term that a particular fortnight will be thin can front-load content and leave review work for that period, instead of discovering the gap on the day.

Ramadan deserves the same treatment. School days shorten, the household's rhythm changes, and the productive hour moves later in the evening for many families. Ramadan also moves roughly eleven days earlier each year against the Gregorian calendar, so it drifts across the academic year and lands in a different part of the course each time. We do not publish a date for it, and neither should anyone else: it is confirmed by moon sighting and differs by a day between countries. Plan it from your own school's announced timings.

The practical arrangement that works through all of this is a longer session less often, plus marked written work in between. A ninety-minute session once a week with two pieces of marked work carries a student through a disrupted fortnight better than three half-hour sessions that all depend on the road being clear.
bullets: Choose the slot that works in the busiest weeks, not the quietest
Flag light weeks when the term plan is agreed, not when they arrive
Longer, less frequent sessions plus marked work survive disruption best
Take Ramadan and Eid timings from your school, since both are confirmed by moon sighting

sections.heading: What schools around Makkah generally cannot staff, and why that is the real reason to look outside
paragraphs: Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, and school evaluation and accreditation run through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission. Those bodies set standards for the school. Neither of them staffs a particular Higher Level subject in a particular building, and that is where a family's problem usually sits. A school can be well run, well evaluated and still unable to offer Physics at Higher Level because one teacher left in the summer.

The shortages are predictable. Mathematics Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level, Physics at Higher Level, Chemistry at Higher Level and Computer Science are the four that thin out first, because the pool of teachers who can deliver them is small in every market and smaller in a city where international provision is thin to begin with. Economics and Business Management are usually covered, but often by a teacher carrying both. Languages beyond English and Arabic are frequently offered only through a self-taught or online route, with the school supervising rather than teaching.

Around Makkah this bites harder than it would in Riyadh. A family in Riyadh whose school drops a subject can sometimes find a second school that offers it. A family here is choosing between a longer commute down the corridor, an online arrangement, or dropping the subject, and dropping a Higher Level science closes university doors that the student may want open. Before enrolling anywhere, ask the school three questions: which Higher Level subjects ran last intake, who teaches them, and what happens if that teacher leaves.

This is the honest argument for online teaching in this city, and it is not about convenience. One-to-one lessons over live video give a Makkah family a choice from a national pool of subject specialists instead of a choice from whoever lives within driving distance. The student gets a Chemistry Higher Level teacher who has taught the current syllabus repeatedly, rather than a capable generalist reading ahead of the lesson.
bullets: Mathematics AA HL, Physics HL, Chemistry HL and Computer Science thin out first
Ask any school which Higher Level subjects actually ran, and who taught them
Dropping a Higher Level science narrows university options later
Online one-to-one widens the tutor pool from local to national

sections.heading: Equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili: the university endgame most pages skip
paragraphs: A foreign or international school certificate is not automatically accepted by a Saudi university. It needs an equivalency decision, mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before it is treated as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. This applies to the IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. Families routinely discover this in the final school year, when the paperwork has to compete with examinations, and that is the avoidable part.

Alongside it sit the two Qiyas tests. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment, and tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content; it can be sat in Arabic or in English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers the science-stream subjects: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English. The critical point for a Makkah family on an international curriculum is that Tahsili content follows the Saudi national curriculum. The material overlaps with the IB and IGCSE syllabuses, but the framing, the sequencing and the expected methods do not, which is why strong international-curriculum students frequently find it harder than their own examinations.

Universities publish their own admission criteria combining school grades with the two Qiyas results, and the weightings differ by university and by programme, with competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes leaning hardest on Tahsili. We do not publish any threshold or weighting formula on this page, because those numbers differ by institution and by intake and third-party sites disagree with each other. Take them from the university's own published criteria. Some universities also set a maximum age for the secondary certificate they will accept, which matters to a student taking a gap year.

Practically, treat equivalency and Qiyas preparation as a thread running from DP1 rather than a task for the final term. Tahsili preparation in particular works best as a separate strand alongside school work, taught against the national-curriculum framing rather than squeezed into subject lessons, because the two are answering different questions about the same physics.

sections.heading: What a tutor may do with an Internal Assessment, and what no tutor may ever do
paragraphs: This section exists because the Saudi tutoring market contains companies that will offer to produce assessed work, and a family that accepts the offer is risking the whole Diploma. The rule is simple and it is the student's rule, not ours: assessed work must be the student's own. A tutor who does not keep that line is not a cheaper option, they are a liability, and a school that suspects malpractice is obliged to investigate it.

What a good tutor does with an Internal Assessment is substantial. They explain the assessment criteria in the language of the subject, show the student what a strand actually asks for, discuss whether a research question is answerable within the limits, point out where a method will not produce usable data, and give written feedback on a draft the student has written. They teach the student to read the criteria themselves, which is the skill that transfers to every other component. None of that touches the student's authorship.

What no tutor does is write, redraft or dictate the work. We will not draft an Extended Essay, and we will never produce a Theory of Knowledge essay, a Personal Project or any coursework for a student. We do not supply model answers to be adapted, and we do not rewrite a paragraph for the student to paste in. The school supervisor remains the formal supervisor of an Extended Essay, and the number of drafts a school will formally review is set by the school, not by a tutor.

Keeping the boundary visible also protects the family. Date-stamped drafts, the student's own notes, and a record of feedback given rather than text supplied are what demonstrate authorship if it is ever questioned. Ask any prospective tutor directly what they will and will not do with a draft. The answer separates a teacher from an essay mill faster than any credential check.
bullets: A tutor explains criteria, questions a method and comments on the student's own draft
A tutor does not write, redraft or dictate any part of assessed work
The school supervisor stays the formal Extended Essay supervisor
Keep dated drafts and feedback records; they are what evidence authorship

process.title: Tell us the syllabus, not just the subject
process.description: Board, level, paper and school matter more than the subject name. Chemistry at Higher Level in the Diploma and Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry Extended need different teachers. Send the last marked paper or report if you have one; it usually tells us more in thirty seconds than a phone call does in twenty minutes.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the actual specialist
process.description: Not a sales call. Your child works with the tutor who would teach them, on a real question from their current topic, and you get a written note afterwards saying what the tutor found and what they would do first. If the match is wrong, say so and we change it before any payment.

process.title: A written plan that names the components
process.description: The plan says which paper or criterion the work targets, in what order, and roughly how long each stage should take. Plans that name components can be checked against results; plans that promise improvement cannot. Yours should be short enough to read in two minutes and specific enough to argue with.

process.title: A weekly slot pinned to Makkah's clock
process.description: The slot is agreed for the term and recorded in Arabia Standard Time, so it does not move when a tutor's own country changes its clocks. We build it around the slowest realistic school run from your district rather than the fastest, because a slot that survives the busy weeks survives the term.

process.title: Marked work between lessons, and a short note after each one
process.description: Written work set, marked against the real mark scheme, and returned before the next session. After each lesson you get a few lines: what was covered, what the student can now do, and what is still weak. No scores, no projections, just what happened.

process.title: A review at the end of each term
process.description: We look at what has moved, what has not, and whether to continue, change tutor, change frequency or stop. Stopping is a legitimate outcome and we will say so when the work is done. A tutor who cannot describe what is left to fix is a tutor who should be finishing.

whyPoints.title: The specialist pool is national, not local
whyPoints.description: A Makkah family choosing locally is choosing from whoever is within driving distance. Choosing online means choosing from subject teachers across the country, which is the difference between a Physics Higher Level specialist and a capable generalist reading the chapter the night before the lesson.

whyPoints.title: Built around the Sunday-to-Thursday week
whyPoints.description: Slots are agreed on Arabia Standard Time and matched to tutors whose own working week fits yours. Friday and Saturday blocks are available for students who stay nearer their school on the Jeddah corridor during the week and travel home at the end of it.

whyPoints.title: Rates discussed in SAR, with the bands named
whyPoints.description: We publish what the Saudi market advertises and who advertises it, so you can tell a reasonable quote from an unreasonable one. What we charge depends on subject, level and frequency, and we tell you the figure before a lesson is booked rather than after a trial.

whyPoints.title: The academic honesty line is stated, not implied
whyPoints.description: Tutors explain criteria, question a method and give feedback on a student's own draft. They do not write assessed work, supply model answers to adapt, or redraft a paragraph. This is written down because parts of this market do the opposite and do not say so.

whyPoints.title: The university route is covered from DP1
whyPoints.description: Ministry of Education equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili are part of the plan from the first Diploma year, with Tahsili treated as its own strand because its content follows the national curriculum rather than the IB syllabus. No thresholds are published here; those come from the university.

whyPoints.title: No numbers we cannot stand behind
whyPoints.description: No success percentages, no star ratings, no tutor headcounts, no grade promises. Everything quoted on this page is either a published market rate attributed to the kind of source that published it, or a verifiable fact about the system you are working inside.

faqs.question: What does an hour of one-to-one IB tuition cost for a Makkah family, and what moves that figure?
faqs.answer: Advertised rates across the Saudi market put IB subject tutoring from roughly SAR 180 an hour, with Higher Level and Advanced Placement tracks commonly listed around SAR 200 to 220. Those are figures tutoring companies publish about themselves, not a market average. What actually moves the number is subject scarcity first, then examiner or marking experience, then level, then package length. A Mathematics Applications and Interpretation Standard Level tutor sits near the bottom of the band; a Physics Higher Level specialist who has marked for the board sits near the top, because the queue for them is long. Ask what the figure includes before comparing two quotes.

faqs.question: Why is an in-home tutor around Makkah quoted higher than the same level of teaching delivered online?
faqs.answer: Travel loading. An in-home quote has to pay for the journey as well as the hour, and in this city the journey is long: international-curriculum schools cluster along the Jeddah corridor roughly 80km west, so a tutor attending in person is often buying back two hours of road to sell one hour of teaching. That cost appears in the rate. It also narrows the choice to tutors who live near you, which usually means paying more for a less specialised teacher. Online delivery removes the travel line from the quote and widens the pool at the same time.

faqs.question: Does the hourly rate for a Makkah candidate change in the weeks before the June series?
faqs.answer: Published rates do not usually rise, but availability collapses, which has the same practical effect. The specialists worth booking are full by the start of the term before a series, so a family looking eight weeks out is choosing from whoever is left rather than from whoever is best. Intensive blocks also cost more in total than weekly lessons simply because they contain more hours. The sensible move is to book the slot in the autumn term at a normal weekly rate and add intensity later, rather than buying a dense block under time pressure at the end.

faqs.question: Is a small group class better value than one-to-one for a Makkah student taking Physics at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: Sometimes, and it depends on the problem. If the student is simply behind on content and the gap is the same as the rest of the group's, a group class covers ground at a lower cost per hour and works. If the student understands the physics but loses marks on extended-response questions, a group class cannot help, because the fix is specific to their own scripts. Internal Assessment feedback, individual orals and mark-scheme work are one-to-one tasks. One hour on this student's own last paper beats three on a shared revision sequence.

faqs.question: What happens in the free trial lesson for a Makkah family who has never used online tuition?
faqs.answer: Your child works with the tutor who would actually teach them, for a normal-length session, on a real question from their current topic rather than a demonstration exercise. The tutor is looking for where marks are going: a method gap, a command-term problem, an algebra weakness underneath a science. Afterwards you get a short written note saying what they found and what they would do in the first month. You also find out whether your child can work on screen with this particular person, which is the thing no description can tell you.

faqs.question: Can we pause lessons during the Hajj season without losing our weekly slot?
faqs.answer: Yes, and in Makkah it is worth planning rather than improvising. Tell us at the start of the term which weeks are likely to be thin, and the tutor front-loads content before them and sets marked written work to cover the gap. The slot is held through an agreed pause. What causes slots to be lost is repeated short-notice cancellation, because the tutor eventually fills the hour. A planned two-week pause recorded in the term plan costs nothing; three unannounced cancellations in a row usually cost the slot.

faqs.question: What am I actually paying extra for when I ask for a tutor with examiner experience?
faqs.answer: Familiarity with how the marks are awarded rather than how the subject is taught. A tutor who has marked for a board has read hundreds of scripts against a scheme and knows which phrasings earn credit, where candidates lose method marks, and what a six-mark answer has to contain. That is most valuable in the final year, on extended-response and data-based questions. It is worth less for a Year 10 student who still needs content taught. Pay for it when technique is the bottleneck, not when knowledge is.

faqs.question: Are there costs beyond the hourly rate, such as papers, materials or written reports?
faqs.answer: There should not be, and you should ask before booking anywhere. Past papers and mark schemes are available through the school's examinations officer and the boards' own channels, so no tutor needs to sell them to you. Written notes after each session and a termly review are part of the arrangement here rather than an extra. Watch two things in other quotes: registration or assessment fees charged before any teaching happens, and rates advertised in dollars, where the exchange rate and any excluded extras land on you.

faqs.question: What is Ministry of Education equivalency, and when should a Makkah family actually start it?
faqs.answer: Equivalency, mu'adalah, is the Ministry of Education decision that lets a Saudi university treat an international school certificate as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. It applies to the IB Diploma, A Levels and an American high school diploma alike. Start gathering what it needs in the first Diploma year rather than the last: transcripts, the certificate when it arrives, and whatever attestations the Ministry asks for, with names matching the passport exactly. Families who leave it until the final term end up doing paperwork during examinations, which is the one part of this that is entirely avoidable.

faqs.question: Why do Makkah students on an international curriculum find Tahsili harder than their own examinations?
faqs.answer: Because Tahsili content follows the Saudi national curriculum, while the student has spent two years inside an IB or Cambridge syllabus. The topics overlap substantially, so families assume preparation is unnecessary. The framing does not overlap: the sequencing, the expected methods and the style of question differ, and a student who can answer a Diploma physics question can still misread a Tahsili one. Treat it as a separate strand taught against the national-curriculum framing, started alongside school work rather than after examinations finish. That is the single most useful thing to know about it.

faqs.question: Does a Makkah student finishing IGCSE still have to think about Qudurat at that stage?
faqs.answer: Not as a test to sit yet, but as a reason to protect certain subjects. Qudurat, run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment, tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and it can be sat in Arabic or English. The quantitative reasoning it rewards is built on exactly the algebra and number work that IGCSE Mathematics covers. A student who leaves IGCSE with shaky algebra carries that weakness into Qudurat, into Tahsili and into Diploma mathematics at once.

faqs.question: How does a Makkah family apply to Saudi and overseas universities in the same final year?
faqs.answer: It is normal and it is manageable, but the two tracks need different things at different times. The Saudi track needs the equivalency decision and the Qiyas results, with timings taken from the Ministry and from each university's own published criteria. The overseas track needs predicted grades from the school, subject prerequisites checked at Higher Level, and references. The clash is usually workload rather than policy, so map both calendars in the autumn term of the final year and decide which weeks belong to applications rather than to revision.

faqs.question: What platform do the lessons run on, and does a Makkah family need to install anything?
faqs.answer: Lessons run over live video with a shared interactive whiteboard, in a browser, so there is nothing to install and no licence to buy. A laptop or desktop with a webcam is better than a tablet, because the student needs to write and see the whiteboard at the same time. Headphones help more than most families expect, both for concentration and for sound quality. A second device is useful for photographing handwritten working and sending it into the session, but it is not required.

faqs.question: How does a tutor share a chemistry mechanism or a graph with a student sitting in Al Aziziyah?
faqs.answer: On a shared whiteboard both people can write on at the same time. The tutor draws the mechanism or the axes, and the student completes the next step while the tutor watches the working appear rather than seeing only the answer. That is the part that matters: most marks in a science or mathematics paper are method marks, and a tutor who sees only a finished answer cannot find where the method broke. Students can also photograph handwritten pages and drop them straight into the session for marking.

faqs.question: Are the online lessons recorded, and who in the family can watch them back?
faqs.answer: Sessions can be recorded at the family's request, and the recording is shared with the parent and the student, not with anyone else. Recordings earn their place in three situations: revisiting a derivation the student half-followed, a parent who wants to see how a topic is being taught without sitting in the room, and catching up after a missed lesson. They are less useful as general revision, because rewatching an hour is slower than redoing the question. The default is to record only when there is a reason to.

faqs.question: What happens if the connection drops in the middle of a lesson in Makkah?
faqs.answer: The tutor waits and reconnects, the whiteboard keeps everything already written, and short interruptions are made up inside the same session. If the session cannot be recovered, it is rescheduled rather than charged. Two practical habits help: join from a wired connection or a strong signal where possible, and keep a phone available as a fallback so the tutor can at least talk the student through the remaining question. Written work set for the week is sent separately, so a lost lesson never means a lost week.

faqs.question: What does a parent in Makkah actually see after each session without sitting in the room?
faqs.answer: A short written note: what was covered, what the student can now do that they could not last week, what is still weak, and what has been set before the next lesson. No score, no projected grade. Alongside that you get marked written work with the mark scheme's reasoning visible, and a termly review that says plainly whether to continue, change something or stop. If a note ever reads as encouragement rather than information, say so, because that is a reporting failure.

makkah.closingHeading: Tell us the week, and the subject, and we will tell you what is realistic
makkah.closingBody: The useful conversation starts with two facts: which week of the school year your child is in, and what the school run leaves of your evening. From those we can say which specialist fits the slot, what the first month would target, and what it costs, before anything is booked. Lessons are online, one-to-one, over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time so the slot holds through the term. Send the last marked paper or school report if you have one, and ask for the free trial lesson with the specialist rather than with a salesperson. If we do not have the right teacher free for your slot, we will say that instead of booking the wrong one.

najran.tutorsIntro: Below is the kind of specialist a Najran enquiry usually resolves to: a teacher who works on one syllabus at one level and marks written work between sessions. Because the pool is national rather than local, the limiting factor is the hour of the evening rather than the subject, so send the slot you need along with the subject.

intro.heading: Start with the marks the student is already losing
paragraphs: Almost every tutoring conversation that starts from Najran begins in the same place: a student is working, the school is doing what it can, and a grade is stuck two or three marks below where it should be in every paper. That pattern is diagnostic. A grade that moves around randomly usually means patchy content knowledge. A grade that sits consistently just below the student's apparent understanding almost always means marks are being lost in a repeatable, identifiable way, and repeatable faults are the cheapest thing in education to fix.

There are four faults that account for most of those lost marks, and they are not about ability. The first is answering the wrong command term: writing a description when the paper said explain, or listing when it said evaluate. The second is omitting the step that carries the method mark, which costs more in a calculation paper than a wrong final answer does. The third is imprecision in examined definitions, where a paraphrase scores nothing. The fourth is time, where a student who knows the whole paper runs out of minutes and leaves the last extended-response question half-answered.

What makes this matter more in Najran than in Riyadh or the Eastern Province is not the students and not the schools. It is the distance. International-curriculum provision in the south is thin, the nearest cities with a deep teaching market are several hours or a day's travel away, and the practical consequence is that a family here cannot solve a subject-specific problem by asking around locally. There is often no one within reach who has marked the paper in question, which means the fault goes unnamed and the student keeps making it.

Lessons through IB Gram are delivered one to one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time. We do not arrange in-home visits anywhere in the Kingdom; home visiting is a service we run only in India. For a Najran family, that is the whole argument rather than a caveat: a student here is matched to a specialist by syllabus and level, and the distance between that teacher and Najran stops being a factor the moment the lesson is a video call rather than a drive.

This page is organised around the faults first and the plan second. It names where the marks actually go in the subjects Najran students most often ask about, sets out what the school run here does to the hours a lesson can occupy, explains what an outside tutor may and may not do with an Internal Assessment or a Personal Project, and describes how to check a tutor's claim when there is no local parent network to ask. It also counts the year backwards from the examination series, which is the part most families leave too late.
bullets: A grade stuck just below a student's understanding is a technique fault, not a knowledge gap

najran.programmesIntro: Families in Najran arrive at IB and Cambridge courses by several different routes: a transfer from a school in another city, a move back from abroad, a boarding arrangement elsewhere in the Kingdom, or a school-delivered online course taken while living at home. These are the programmes those routes lead into, and what each one demands of a student working at a distance from the nearest specialist.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Two years of content examined by written paper, with a syllabus code printed on every past paper and a published mark scheme for each one. That combination is what makes the course so coachable at a distance: the student and the tutor can both see exactly what was rewarded. Cambridge splits some subjects into Core and Extended tiers, and the tier decision caps the grade available, so it deserves a deliberate decision rather than a default.
programmes.countryNote: Saudi candidates sit the June series as the main sitting, with the November series used for resits and November-entry candidates. Entries are made through a registered examination centre, and families outside the main cities need to confirm early where their entry will be made and where the papers will be sat. The school's examinations officer is the only reliable source for that, and the question is worth asking a full term before it becomes urgent.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups, each assessed against four published criteria marked out of 8, with the final year carrying the Personal Project. There is no terminal examination unless a school enters students for eAssessment, so the criteria are the whole of the grade. A student who writes well and never reads Criterion D is capped regardless of how good the writing is, which is the single most common and most fixable MYP fault.
programmes.countryNote: For a student in Najran taking the MYP through a school in another city or online, the Personal Project is the component that suffers most, because the supervisor is often not physically present. An outside tutor can help with planning, with the process journal discipline and with the criteria, while leaving the project itself entirely in the student's hands. The deadline discipline is usually what needs the support, not the idea.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Each subject carries an Internal Assessment worth a fifth to a quarter of its grade, and the core adds up to three points through the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix. The difficulty is less the content than the simultaneity: several independent pieces of assessed work fall due in the same stretch of the second year.
programmes.countryNote: A southern student taking the Diploma usually does so away from home or through a school-delivered online programme, and in both cases the weekly point of contact with a subject specialist is thinner than it would be in Jeddah or Riyadh. That makes the sequencing of the Internal Assessments the highest-value thing an outside tutor contributes, well before it makes content teaching the priority.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry-led and transdisciplinary, with no past papers and no mark schemes. Support at this age targets the mechanics the inquiry rests on: reading fluency and stamina, number facts, handwriting speed, and the habit of explaining a method out loud. Short sessions twice a week work far better than one long one, because attention rather than capability is the limiting factor at this age.
programmes.countryNote: Primary-age support in Najran is most often about English reading level, either because the family has moved between systems or because the child is being prepared for entry to a school in another city. A baseline against the receiving school's own reading benchmark is more useful than a general assessment, and it gives you something concrete to show at the admissions interview.

najran.subjectsIntro: The list below is written around where the marks go rather than what the syllabus covers, because that is the question a Najran family is usually trying to answer. These are the Diploma Programme subjects that come up most often in enquiries from the southern provinces.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The command term decides the mark here more than in any other science. Describe, explain, outline, suggest and evaluate each want a different shape of answer, and a student who writes everything they know about the topic scores below one who answers the verb in three lines. Higher Level adds whole topics with no Standard Level equivalent, and the internal investigation falls over at the design stage when the chosen variable cannot actually be controlled.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Marks are lost in two places with almost total consistency: calculation questions where the working is skipped, so no method marks can be awarded, and organic mechanisms where the curly-arrow convention was learned approximately and is then penalised in every question that uses it. The data booklet is a skill rather than a safety net, and students who have never practised finding a value under time pressure lose minutes they need later.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The recurring faults are units, significant figures and quoting a law instead of applying it. A graph question that produces a correct gradient and no statement of what the gradient means is a half-answered question. Higher Level extends several topics well beyond the Standard Level treatment, and those extensions tend to be taught late and quickly, which is where a student working away from a specialist falls behind first.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Assessed with the graphic display calculator in use throughout, which produces its own failure mode: students treat the calculator output as the answer and never interpret it in the context of the question, losing the marks that the context carries. Statistical tests are examined for the reasoning behind the choice of test, not only for the result, and that reasoning is what goes unpractised.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Paper 1 is sat without a calculator and exposes any weakness in algebraic manipulation within the first few questions. Proof is examined at Higher Level in ways that reward a learned structure, so students who have never written out an induction proof in full lose marks they could have banked. The exploration is marked against criteria that reward genuine personal engagement and honest reflection as much as the mathematics itself.

subjects.name: Arabic A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: A first-language course with the same analytical demands as any other Group 1 subject, and a common source of surprise for students who assume fluency carries the grade. It does not: the marks are for analysis of how a text produces its effects, for comparison, and for the individual oral. Students lose marks by summarising content rather than analysing technique, which is a teachable habit.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Reading, writing, listening and an individual oral, with marks awarded on task fulfilment and register as much as on range of language. A well-judged text type that answers every element of the prompt beats a more ambitious piece that drifts. Higher Level adds literary works. The commonest avoidable loss is choosing the wrong text type for the task and being capped before the writing is even read.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Case studies are the currency. An answer that argues well with no named, located, dated example scores in the lower bands, and one that names three examples without using them scores no better. The extended-response questions want a line of argument with evidence attached to it. The fieldwork component is where organisation rather than geography decides the mark.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Case-study driven, with a pre-released case for one paper and a research project built on real organisational information. Marks sit in application and evaluation, not in recall, so a student who can define every tool and apply none plateaus in the middle bands. Quantitative questions are straightforward and routinely dropped because they were never practised.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: An interdisciplinary course that students often choose expecting a lighter load and then meet a demanding synthesis of science and perspective. Marks are lost by answering with science alone where the question asks for a value perspective, or the reverse. The practical and investigative component needs the same design discipline as a full science Internal Assessment.

najran.igcseSubjectsIntro: At IGCSE the fault lines are narrower and easier to name, which is why this level responds so quickly to targeted work. The syllabus code is the first thing to establish, because two courses with the same subject name can be examined very differently.

igcseSubjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500)
igcseSubjects.description: Reading and directed writing, where the reading questions are the ones students underprepare. Marks go for selecting and using detail from the passage, not for writing well in general. The commonest loss is a response that is fluent, long and insufficiently anchored in the text it was supposed to be analysing.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
igcseSubjects.description: Extended is the tier any student heading towards Diploma Programme mathematics needs, and the tier choice is sometimes made for a student rather than with them. Most lost marks come from arithmetic slips under time pressure and from omitting the working, both of which respond to timed sets rather than to re-teaching.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610)
igcseSubjects.description: Definitions are examined strictly and a paraphrase scores nothing, so a student who understands osmosis perfectly can still lose the definition mark. The practical skills paper rewards students who have drawn and labelled their own diagrams rather than only looked at them, which is easy to practise on a shared whiteboard.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620)
igcseSubjects.description: Ionic equations, state symbols and mole calculations account for a disproportionate share of dropped marks. The qualitative analysis tables are a few hours of learning that convert reliably into marks, and they are the single highest-yield piece of memorisation in the course.

igcseSubjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0654)
igcseSubjects.description: A double award covering biology, chemistry and physics in one qualification, which suits a student who needs breadth without three separate courses. It covers less depth than the separate sciences, so a student intending to take a Higher Level science should understand what is being traded before the option is locked in.

igcseSubjects.name: Geography (Cambridge 0460)
igcseSubjects.description: Map skills and the interpretation of data carry marks that are available to every candidate and claimed by far fewer. Students lose them by reading a map scale carelessly or by describing a graph instead of explaining it. The case-study questions want specificity: a named place doing the thing being asked about.

igcseSubjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450)
igcseSubjects.description: Short structured questions and a case study. Application marks require the answer to be about the business in the extract rather than about business in general, which is the difference between the middle and the top bands. The calculations are reliable marks and are routinely left blank.

igcseSubjects.name: Arabic as a First Language (Cambridge 0508)
igcseSubjects.description: Comprehension, summary and directed writing, assessed on precision rather than on fluency. Students who speak the language at home sometimes prepare least for it and lose marks on the summary task, which has a strict word allowance and rewards selection over expression.

najran.regionsTitle: Najran, district by district, and what the school run costs
najran.regionsIntro: Najran is unusual among Saudi cities in that its problem is distance rather than congestion. The city runs along Wadi Najran as a low-density ribbon of neighbourhoods, farms and palm belts, so a school run here is measured in kilometres of open road rather than in minutes of traffic, and the province adds governorate towns hours further out.

regions.name: Aba As Saud and the old quarter
regions.note: The historic heart of the city by the wadi, with the mud-brick architecture Najran is known for. Schools are close for families here, which makes an early evening lesson slot genuinely available rather than theoretical, and leaves room for two subjects in one evening.

regions.name: Al Faisaliyah
regions.note: One of the more built-up districts, with shorter runs to the city's schools and reliable connectivity. For families here the limiting factor on lesson timing is dinner and family routine rather than the drive, so a slot after the evening meal often works better than one before it.

regions.name: Al Ukhdud
regions.note: The district around the archaeological site south-east of the centre. Housing is spread out and school runs cross open ground, so a parent collecting one child and dropping another makes the late afternoon unusable and the evening the only honest option.

regions.name: The Najran University side of the city
regions.note: The north-western approach, where university households concentrate. These families tend to be comfortable reading a lesson note rather than needing it explained, and often want a tutor who will set written work and mark it rather than fill the hour with teaching.

regions.name: Wadi Najran and the palm belt
regions.note: Agricultural land strung along the valley, with households many kilometres from the nearest school. The round trip can consume the whole late afternoon, which pushes lessons into the evening and makes a fixed weekly slot far more valuable than a flexible one.

regions.name: Al Nahdah and the newer northern districts
regions.note: Newer residential growth on the northern edge. Distances to school are longer than from the centre but the roads are clear, so the run is predictable; a parent can commit to the same time every week with some confidence, which is the main thing a tutor needs.

regions.name: Habuna, Yadamah and Badr Al Janub
regions.note: Governorate towns north and west of the city, well outside its school catchment. Families here either board a child in the city or accept a long daily drive, and in both cases an online specialist is the only realistic weekly academic support available.

regions.name: Sharurah
regions.note: Far to the east of the province across open desert, several hours from Najran city. Weekly travel for tuition is not a serious option from here at any price, which makes a stable video slot and a reliable connection the two things worth getting right.

regions.name: Khamis Mushait and Abha
regions.note: The nearest cities with larger school markets, in 'Asir at high altitude and roughly 25km apart from each other, sharing a catchment. They are still a long drive from Najran, which is why families compare boarding there against staying home with online specialist support.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah — the nearest large international-school market
schoolClusters.note: International-curriculum provision in Najran itself is limited, and families following the IB or a Cambridge pathway usually do so through a school in another city, a boarding arrangement or a school-delivered online programme. Jeddah is the closest market with real subject breadth, and the schools below appear in IB and Cambridge listings. It is a long way from Najran, which is exactly why online specialist support is worth comparing against relocation.

schoolClusters.city: Riyadh — the widest subject choice in the Kingdom
schoolClusters.note: Riyadh carries the deepest range of IB and Cambridge provision, including schools running the full IB continuum. For a Najran family it is a relocation or boarding decision rather than a commute, and the question worth asking any of these schools before committing is which Higher Level subjects they can actually run in a given year, because a small cohort decides that more than the prospectus does.

najran.modesIntro: Four formats cover what Najran families ask for. All are delivered live and one to one over video on Arabia Standard Time, and the choice between them depends on whether the fault is content, technique or coursework discipline.

modes.title: A fixed weekly slot after the school run
modes.description: The same hour every week, late enough that the drive home and the evening meal are done, with written work set and marked between sessions. A fixed slot matters more here than in a dense city because the alternative is a weekly negotiation around a long, variable school run, and a slot that moves every week is the one that quietly stops happening after half a term.
bullets: Pinned to Najran local time, not to the tutor's clock
Work set and marked between lessons, with the mark scheme attached
A short written note to the parent after each session
Ninety minutes for a Higher Level science, sixty for most else

modes.title: Two subjects in one evening
modes.description: Two shorter sessions back to back with a break between them, which suits families whose evening is already fragmented by distance and who would rather concentrate tuition into one night than spread it across three. It works best when the two subjects are genuinely different in kind, so the student is switching mode as well as topic rather than doing two hours of the same thinking.

A real break between sessions, not a handover

Each session still gets its own written note and its own work set

modes.title: Past-paper clinic before a series
modes.description: Timed papers sat under examination conditions, marked against the published scheme, and then worked through error by error. The agenda comes from the script rather than from the syllabus, which is why a clinic often finds faults a year of weekly teaching did not surface. Friday and Saturday mornings are available for these, when the school week is not competing for the time.
bullets: Papers sat to time, not as untimed homework
A running list of recurring errors that gets revisited, not mentioned once
Two or three sessions a week for a fixed block, then it ends

modes.title: Coursework and Personal Project review
modes.description: Scheduled sessions around the student's own Internal Assessment, exploration, Extended Essay or Personal Project. The tutor reads what the student has produced, maps it against the published criteria, and asks the questions the examiner will ask. They do not write, redraft or edit any part of it, and they do not supply data or analysis. Keeping the work the student's own is the point of the session, not a disclaimer at the end of it.

sections.heading: The four faults that cost Najran students the most marks
paragraphs: A student losing two or three marks per question across an entire paper is not short of knowledge. They are making the same mistake repeatedly, and because nobody has named it, they practise it every time they revise. Naming the fault is most of the work, and it takes one marked script and one mark scheme to do. The four faults below account for the large majority of avoidable losses in written examinations at both IGCSE and Diploma Programme level.

The command term is the first. Examination papers use a defined vocabulary — state, describe, explain, outline, suggest, compare, evaluate, justify — and each term licenses a different kind of answer with a different number of marks attached. A student who explains when asked to describe wastes time and gains nothing; one who describes when asked to explain loses the marks outright. This is the cheapest fault in education to fix, because it needs no new content at all, only a habit of reading the verb and answering it.

The second is the missing method step. In any calculation, marks are allocated to stages, and a student who writes the final answer alone forfeits every stage mark if the answer is wrong. Students skip steps because they are fast, and speed is rewarded nowhere in a mark scheme. The third is definitional imprecision: a number of definitions in biology, chemistry and economics are examined to the word, and a sound paraphrase earns nothing. These have to be learned as they are written, which students resist and then discover costs them a grade.

The fourth is time. A student who knows the whole paper and leaves the final extended-response question half-written has lost more marks than anyone's weakest topic ever cost them. It is fixed by timed practice with a watch and a hard stop, not by more revision. All four faults are visible in a single marked script, which is why the first session with a new tutor should be spent reading one rather than teaching anything.
