sections.heading: What to ask a tutor before agreeing to anything, and what a weak answer sounds like
paragraphs: In an established market a family can rely on reputation. In a new one they cannot, so the interview matters. Five questions do most of the work, and all of them are about specifics rather than credentials. Which board and specification have you taught, and for how many cohorts? What is the weighting of each paper at this level? Where do students most often lose marks in the component my child is struggling with? What will you do with an Internal Assessment draft, and what will you refuse to do? And what will you tell me after each lesson?

The answers sort people quickly. A specialist answers the weighting question without hesitating, because they have taught to it. They answer the lost-marks question with something diagnosable: a command-term failure, an uncertainty treatment, a missing justification step. A generalist answers in generalities about confidence and foundations. Neither answer is dishonest, but only one of them is what a Higher Level candidate eight months from a series needs.

Be equally careful with claims that cannot be checked. A tutor who offers a success percentage, a star rating or a promise about the final grade is offering something that cannot be verified and should never be claimed. Examiner experience is a real and valuable thing, but it is a specific claim about a specific board and subject, so ask which board, which subject and which component, and treat a vague answer as a no. The same applies to any provider claiming approval or accreditation from a board or a regulator.

Finally, ask what happens if the match is wrong. The answer should be straightforward: say so after a lesson or two and the tutor changes, without argument and without a penalty. A student who does not get on with a tutor will not do the written work, and a student who does not do the written work will not improve however good the teaching is. Fit is not a soft factor here; it is the mechanism.
bullets: Ask for paper weightings at the student's exact level; a specialist answers immediately
Ask where marks are lost in the specific component, and expect a diagnosable answer
Treat any percentage, rating or grade promise as a reason to walk away
Confirm how a wrong match is changed, before the first paid lesson

process.title: Send the board, the level and the last marked script
process.description: The subject name is the least useful part of an enquiry. We need the board, the specification, the level, the component in trouble and ideally a photograph of the last marked paper. That tells a specialist more in thirty seconds than a conversation does in twenty minutes, and it is what lets us say honestly whether we have the right person free.

process.title: An inventory session for anyone who arrived mid-course
process.description: For transferring students the first session is an audit rather than a lesson: what the previous course covered, what the new one assumes, which internally assessed work is salvageable and which needs restarting. You get that written down, including the parts a tutor cannot fix and the school has to.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the specialist who would teach
process.description: Not a consultation with a coordinator. Your child works with the actual tutor on a real question from their current topic, and you receive a short note afterwards saying what the tutor found and what they would attack first. If the fit is wrong, say so and we change the tutor before anything is paid.

process.title: A plan written in components, not in adjectives
process.description: The plan names the paper, criterion or skill each stage targets, the order, and roughly how long each stage takes. Plans written in components can be checked against results. Plans written as promises of improvement cannot. Yours should be short enough to read quickly and specific enough to disagree with.

process.title: A slot recorded in Arabia Standard Time
process.description: Agreed for the term and written down in Saudi local time, so it does not drift when a tutor's own country changes its clocks. Rotational and shift households tell us the pattern up front, and we match a tutor whose own working week fits yours rather than one who will be renegotiating by the second month.

process.title: Marked work, short notes, and a termly decision
process.description: Written work set and marked against the real scheme before the next session, a few factual lines to you after each lesson, and a review each term that says continue, change or stop. Stopping is a legitimate outcome and we will say so when the work is finished.

whyPoints.title: Specialism instead of proximity
whyPoints.description: In a new school market the local pool is small and rarely subject-specific. Matching online means choosing a teacher for the board, the subject and the level rather than for where they live, which is the only way a NEOM student reaches a Higher Level specialist at all.

whyPoints.title: Built around mid-course arrivals
whyPoints.description: Transfers are the normal case here, not the exception. Support starts with a written inventory of what carried over and what did not, including internally assessed work, and runs for a defined block aimed at the gap rather than rolling on indefinitely.

whyPoints.title: The tutor survives a relocation
whyPoints.description: Households in this region move between sites, cities and countries. An online arrangement follows the student, which matters most in the middle of a two-year course where continuity is worth more than any local convenience.

whyPoints.title: The weekly shape is designed, not assumed
whyPoints.description: Slots are set in Arabia Standard Time against a Sunday-to-Thursday week, with Friday and Saturday blocks available for shift households and students staying away during the week. A slot built for the hardest weeks survives the easy ones.

whyPoints.title: Prices discussed as bands, with the source named
whyPoints.description: We publish what this market advertises and who advertises it, so a quote can be judged. What we charge depends on subject, level and frequency, and you are told the figure before a lesson is booked rather than after a trial lesson has done its work.

whyPoints.title: Claims limited to what can be checked
whyPoints.description: No success percentages, no ratings, no tutor headcounts, no grade promises, and no claim of approval from any board or regulator. Everything stated here is either an attributed market rate or a verifiable fact about the system a Saudi family is working inside.

faqs.question: What should a NEOM family budget for a Higher Level science specialist, and why is that band above a Standard Level one?
faqs.answer: Advertised listings in the Saudi market put IB subject tutoring from roughly SAR 180 an hour, with Higher Level and Advanced Placement tracks commonly advertised around SAR 200 to 220. Those are figures companies publish about their own services rather than an audited average. The gap between Higher and Standard Level is a supply gap, not a loading applied for difficulty: far fewer teachers can deliver the Higher Level extension topics and the investigative paper confidently, so the queue for them is longer everywhere. Examiner or marking experience in that specific subject pushes a quote further up the same band.

faqs.question: Is flying a tutor in for a block of in-person lessons ever cheaper than teaching online across a whole term?
faqs.answer: Almost never, and the arithmetic is not close. Travel and accommodation for a short block in the Kingdom's north-west corner costs more than a term of weekly online lessons with the same teacher, and the block delivers its hours all at once, which is the wrong shape for most learning. Weekly contact with marked work in between produces more than an intensive week followed by nothing. IB Gram does not run home visits in the Kingdom in any case; in-home tutoring is a service we offer only in India, so this is a comparison rather than an option we sell.

faqs.question: Does a family in a new school community pay more because there are fewer tutors within reach?
faqs.answer: No, because the pool being matched from is national rather than local. That is the main practical benefit of online delivery in this region: the rate reflects the subject and the level, not the distance. Where geography does cost money is indirectly, through scarcity of the subject itself. If a student needs a second modern language the school cannot staff, the specialist pool for that language is small everywhere, and the rate reflects that. Ask what the quote is driven by, and a straight answer should name the subject and level rather than your address.

faqs.question: How many lessons a week does a student who joined DP1 part-way through need, and what does that cost over a term?
faqs.answer: Usually more at the start and fewer later, which is cheaper overall than a flat weekly arrangement. A typical shape is two sessions a week for four to six weeks while the inventory gap is closed, dropping to one once the student is level with the class. Over a term that is roughly a third more hours than steady weekly support, concentrated where they do most good. Multiply by whichever band the subject sits in and ask for the plan to state the number of weeks, so the intensive phase has a defined end rather than quietly becoming the norm.

faqs.question: What can a trial lesson tell a parent who has just relocated and has no school report yet?
faqs.answer: More than a report would. The tutor works through a real question from the student's current topic and watches the method rather than the answer, which surfaces the things reports describe vaguely: whether algebra is secure under pressure, whether command terms are understood, whether the student can structure an extended answer. You get a short written note of what was found and what the first month would target. For a family mid-relocation with paperwork still in transit, that note is often the first concrete account of where their child actually stands.

faqs.question: Can two siblings in NEOM share one session to halve the cost?
faqs.answer: Only if they are sitting the same specification at the same level and are at a similar stage, which is rarer than families hope. Two students a year apart in the same subject have different immediate problems, and a shared hour becomes half an hour each with the overhead of switching. Where siblings genuinely are aligned, a shared session can work for content coverage and does lower the cost per student. It does not work for Internal Assessment feedback, individual orals or component technique, because those are specific to one student's own scripts.

faqs.question: What should a family expect to pay for Internal Assessment feedback compared with weekly subject lessons?
faqs.answer: The hourly figure is the same, but the number of hours is far smaller and the timing matters more. Useful Internal Assessment support is typically three or four sessions spread across the drafting period: one on the research question and method before any data exists, one on the analysis, and one or two on feedback against the criteria for a draft the student has written. Buying ten hours of it is usually a sign the work started too late. Booking the first session before the method is fixed is where the value actually sits.

faqs.question: Does a student finishing the Diploma in the Kingdom need Ministry of Education equivalency if they are only applying overseas?
faqs.answer: Not for the overseas application itself, which runs on the Diploma transcript, predicted grades and the university's own requirements. It is still worth obtaining. Plans change, deferred entry happens, and a student who later applies to a Saudi university, or needs the certificate recognised for employment or further study in the Kingdom, will need the equivalency decision then, usually with less time and with documents harder to retrieve. The process is administrative rather than academic, so doing it while the school can still certify records is simply the easier moment.

faqs.question: Where does a student based in NEOM sit Qudurat and Tahsili, and how far ahead should that be planned?
faqs.answer: Both are administered by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment, and registration and available sittings are published by them rather than by schools or tutoring companies. For a family in the north-west the planning issue is travel: a sitting may mean a journey, so it belongs in the calendar early and should be placed away from school assessment weeks. Preparation, particularly for Tahsili, works best as a weekly strand started in the first Diploma year rather than a block attempted after final examinations finish.

faqs.question: Does Mathematics Analysis and Approaches or Applications and Interpretation matter more for an engineering application?
faqs.answer: Analysis and Approaches, in most cases, and usually at Higher Level. Engineering and physical science courses generally expect the algebraic and calculus content that route covers, and some state a Higher Level mathematics requirement explicitly in their published entry criteria. Applications and Interpretation is a serious course and the right choice for many degrees, but it is accepted less widely for engineering. The decision has to be made when subject choices are confirmed, because switching routes later in the Diploma is difficult. Check the published requirements of the actual universities on the student's list.

faqs.question: How do Diploma points translate into an overseas offer for a student schooled in NEOM?
faqs.answer: Offers are usually expressed as a total points figure plus specific Higher Level subject grades, and the subject conditions are the part students underestimate. A total that clears the headline figure still fails if a named Higher Level grade is missed. Different countries read the Diploma differently, and some systems weight the core or particular subjects. The practical approach is to collect the published entry requirements for each university on the list during the first Diploma year, then work backwards to which Higher Level grades the student has to protect.

faqs.question: What does a university mean when it asks for a subject prerequisite at Higher Level?
faqs.answer: It means the subject must be studied at Higher Level rather than Standard Level, usually at a stated grade, because the course assumes the depth the Higher Level extension provides. This is where a thin school timetable becomes a university problem: a student whose school could not run Chemistry at Higher Level cannot satisfy a prerequisite that names it, however good the Standard Level grade. That is the strongest practical argument for securing outside support in a scarce Higher Level subject early, rather than dropping it to Standard Level when the course gets hard.

faqs.question: Does a one-to-one video lesson work when the household connection is shared across several devices?
faqs.answer: It works, but it is worth preparing. A wired connection to the student's machine makes the biggest single difference, followed by headphones, which improve both sound quality and concentration. Agree a quiet hour with the household so streaming and large downloads are not competing with the lesson. If the connection does degrade, the tutor drops video and keeps audio and the shared whiteboard, which preserves nearly all of the teaching. Short interruptions are made up in the same session; a lesson that cannot be recovered is rescheduled rather than charged.

faqs.question: Can a parent sit in on an online lesson without changing how the session runs?
faqs.answer: Yes, and occasionally it is useful, particularly for a first session or where a parent wants to understand how a subject is being taught. Be aware that most teenagers work differently when a parent is visibly present, and the session you observe is not quite the session that happens otherwise. A better default for most families is a recording of a specific lesson, or the written note after each session. If something concerns you, ask for a short conversation with the tutor without the student, which is more productive than observing.

faqs.question: How does a tutor mark handwritten physics working between lessons?
faqs.answer: The student photographs the pages and sends them in, and the tutor marks them against the published mark scheme, annotating where method marks were earned and where they were lost. That annotation is the valuable part: most marks in a physics paper are method marks, and a student who only sees a score learns nothing about why. Marked work comes back before the next session so the lesson starts from the errors rather than from a cold topic. During a session, the same pages can be dropped straight onto the shared whiteboard and worked through live.

faqs.question: How is progress tracked across a term when nobody in the family ever meets the tutor?
faqs.answer: Through three things that are all written down. A short factual note after each lesson saying what was covered, what the student can now do, and what has been set. Marked written work with the mark scheme's reasoning visible, so improvement is legible rather than asserted. And a termly review that compares the plan's named targets against what actually moved, ending in a decision to continue, change something or stop. If a note ever reads as encouragement rather than information, say so, because that is a reporting failure and it is fixable.

faqs.question: Is a tablet enough for an online Chemistry Higher Level lesson, or does the student need a laptop?
faqs.answer: A laptop or desktop is better, and the reason is screen area rather than processing. A Higher Level chemistry session involves a mechanism or a graph on the shared whiteboard, the student's own working, and often a past-paper question at the same time. On a tablet those compete for the same space and the student ends up switching rather than thinking. A tablet with a stylus is genuinely good as a second device for handwritten working alongside a laptop. As the only device it works, but it costs the student attention every lesson.

neom.closingHeading: Tell us what the school cannot cover, and we will tell you whether we can
neom.closingBody: The most useful first message names the board, the level, the component in trouble, and whether your child arrived part-way through the course. From that a specialist can say what the first month would target, which weekly shape fits your household, and what it costs, before anything is booked. Lessons are online, one-to-one, over live video, recorded in Arabia Standard Time so the slot holds all term. Ask for the trial lesson with the subject teacher rather than a consultation with a coordinator, and ask them the paper-weighting question first. If we do not have the right specialist free for your slot, we will say so rather than book the nearest alternative.

qatif.heroSubtitle: IB and IGCSE tutors in Qatif are usually hired at a particular point in the year, and that point decides what can still be changed. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time and timed to the Sunday-to-Thursday week, which matters here because most Qatif families school their children in Dammam, Dhahran or Al Khobar and are rarely home before the late afternoon.

qatif.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed below are matched to a stage rather than a subject alone: an MYP 5 student in Safwa with a Personal Project due, a Year 11 candidate in Tarout rebuilding Physics 0625 before the June series, a DP2 student in Qatif centre whose internal assessments are all landing in the same fortnight.

intro.heading: The question that decides everything is which term you are in
paragraphs: Qatif is not one town. It is a coastal governorate north of Dammam made up of a dense run of settlements, with Safwa and Awamiyah to the north, Saihat to the south, Tarout Island across its causeway, and smaller communities such as Anak, Al Jarudiyah, Al Qudaih and Umm Al Hamam in between. Date agriculture shaped the geography, and the Dammam, Dhahran and Al Khobar conurbation shapes the school map, because that is where almost all of the province's international and British-curriculum provision sits.

So a Qatif family's first problem is a commute, and their second is a calendar. This page leads with the calendar, because it is the thing most tutoring decisions get wrong. A parent gets in touch in the autumn term asking for help with a subject, when the useful question is which series the child is entered for, which internal assessment deadlines have already passed, and what is still genuinely movable between now and the papers. The answer to that is different in MYP 4, in Year 11 and in DP2, and the support worth buying is different too.

Counting backwards is not a flourish. Entries close months ahead of a series, tier decisions in Cambridge subjects are made by the school and then cap the grade available, internal assessment work is submitted long before the written papers, and a predicted grade is produced from evidence collected earlier still. Each of those is a door that closes. A family who understands the order of the doors spends money on the things that are still open.

Delivery for Saudi families is online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Qatif address; home visits are a service we offer only in India. For families on this coast that is the practical arrangement anyway, because the number of specialist IB and IGCSE teachers living inside the governorate is small, and almost everyone who teaches these syllabuses in the province is already employed full time at a school in Dhahran, Dammam, Al Khobar or Jubail.

The sections below work through the year in order: where your child sits in it, what the run-up to a series looks like counted backwards, what each paper is worth, how predicted grades and boundaries behave, and then the university endgame that almost nobody writing about tutoring in the Kingdom covers properly, which is Ministry of Education equivalency and the two Qiyas tests. Rates are deliberately not the organising idea here, because the hourly figures advertised in this market tell a parent far less than the stage their child has reached. A family who knows which doors are still open can judge whether an hour is worth paying for at all, and a family who does not will pay a perfectly reasonable rate for support that was never going to change the outcome.
bullets: Lessons are one-to-one and online, pinned to Arabia Standard Time (UTC+3)
Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel candidates here sit the June and November series
The February and March Cambridge series is available only to candidates in India

qatif.programmesIntro: Four programmes cover almost every Qatif student: the IB continuum of Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma, and the Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel route taken in most of the province's British-curriculum schools. What follows is organised around when each programme makes its irreversible decisions, because that is what sets the deadline for useful support.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Inquiry units across six transdisciplinary themes, with no external papers and no grades in the familiar sense. The final year carries the PYP Exhibition, a collaborative piece of work that is the first time many students plan something over weeks rather than lessons. Progress is reported through portfolios, conferences and teacher judgement against learning outcomes.
programmes.countryNote: There is no examination clock here, which is why primary support in the Eastern Province is best bought early and in small amounts. The two things that pay off later are arithmetic fluency without a calculator and the habit of writing an explanation, because both are assumed by every Middle Years and IGCSE course the province offers.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Eight subject groups assessed against four published criteria, each marked out of eight and converted by the school to a grade from one to seven. The decisive year is MYP 5: the Personal Project runs through it, mathematics splits into standard and extended routes, and subject choices that shape the Diploma are made at its end.
programmes.countryNote: Families here see the MYP mainly in Dhahran and Jubail. The Personal Project is the item that catches a Qatif household by surprise, because the long commute leaves little weekday time for a piece of work that needs sustained independent planning rather than short bursts of homework.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three Higher and three Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Internal assessment sits inside nearly every subject and is marked at school then moderated. The written papers come at the end, but the internal components are produced across both years, and in DP2 they tend to land together.
programmes.countryNote: Qatif Diploma students are concentrated in the Dhahran and Jubail schools that run the programme. The pressure point is the DP2 autumn and spring, when internal assessment deadlines, the Extended Essay and mock examinations arrive in the same weeks, and a long daily drive leaves little slack to absorb any of it.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: Subject-by-subject courses examined at the end of Year 11, graded A* to G by Cambridge and 9 to 1 by Pearson Edexcel. Several Cambridge subjects are tiered, so the school enters a candidate for either Core or Extended papers, and the sciences choose between a practical test and an alternative written paper.
programmes.countryNote: This is the majority route in the Eastern Province, and the two decisions that matter most are made inside the school: the tier and the practical route. Both are usually settled during Year 10 or early Year 11, well before entries close for the June series, and a family who asks about them late has fewer options than one who asks early.

qatif.subjectsIntro: The subject notes below are written around components and timing: which parts of the grade are produced during the course, which are decided on the day of the paper, and therefore when outside teaching changes an outcome rather than merely adding hours to a week.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Two written papers at Standard Level and three at Higher, plus the exploration, which is produced during the course and submitted well before the session. Higher Level Paper 3 is extended problem solving in unfamiliar settings and cannot be prepared by revisiting notes; it needs timed practice on problems the student has not seen.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Statistics and modelling with the graphical calculator treated as a core tool. The exploration again sits inside the course rather than at the end. Students arrive at the papers able to run a calculator procedure and unable to state the model, its parameters or its limitations, which is where the commentary marks live.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Three papers at the end, plus an internal investigation produced during the course. The investigation is the component a family can still influence a year ahead; the papers reward precision in units, significant figures and the difference between describing a graph and accounting for its gradient or intercept.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Structure, reactivity and quantitative work across both levels, with the data booklet available in the examination. Organic mechanisms and equilibrium carry the Higher Level extension. The internal investigation needs a quantity that can actually be measured in a school laboratory, and choosing it badly costs marks no revision later recovers.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: A content-heavy course examined through command terms that separate outline, describe, explain and evaluate strictly. The internal investigation needs a controlled variable and a sample a student can defend under questioning. Diagram and data-handling questions are the most predictable marks on the paper.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Essay and data-response papers, with Higher Level adding quantitative questions and a policy paper. The internal assessment is a set of commentaries on published articles, written during the course at intervals the school sets, so it is the one part of the grade that is entirely in hand months before the session.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Guided textual analysis, a comparative essay, an internally assessed individual oral and, at Higher Level, the HL essay. The oral and the essay are produced during the course. Students lose marks by paraphrasing a text instead of analysing how a writer's choices build meaning for a particular audience.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Five prescribed themes examined through a productive writing paper and a listening and reading paper, with an internally assessed oral. Text type carries real marks: an answer written as a generic essay when the task asked for a blog, a speech or a formal letter loses them before the language is judged.

subjects.name: Arabic A and Arabic B
subjects.description: A frequent source of confusion for families in the Eastern Province, where a child speaks Arabic at home and has been schooled entirely in English. Arabic A is a literature-based first-language course; Arabic B is language acquisition. The level a school enters a student at affects both the Diploma grade and later equivalency paperwork.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: A pre-released case study for Paper 1 and an internally assessed research project. Because the case study is published in advance, the autumn term of DP2 is when work on it actually pays; once the paper is sat, the only remaining variable is how well the stimulus was applied rather than how much theory was recalled.

qatif.igcseSubjectsIntro: Eastern Province schools enter candidates with both Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel, and the same subject differs between them in tiering, paper structure and practical assessment. Confirm the board and the code on your child's statement of entry before buying support for any of these.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Edexcel 4MA1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Foundation and Higher
igcseSubjects.description: The revised Cambridge syllabus gives each tier a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper of equal weight, which exposes students who have practised only with a calculator in hand. Edexcel 4MA1 keeps two equally weighted calculator papers. The tier is chosen by the school and caps the grade available.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Edexcel 4PH1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Cambridge Extended candidates sit a multiple-choice paper worth thirty per cent, an extended theory paper worth half the grade, and a practical component worth the remaining fifth, taken either as a practical test or as the alternative-to-practical paper. Which one your child sits is a school decision made long before entries close.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620, Edexcel 4CH1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and organic chemistry decide most grades at the boundary. The practical fifth of the Cambridge grade is where preparation is thinnest, because the alternative paper asks for apparatus, precautions and sources of error that a student who has only watched demonstrations cannot supply.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610, Edexcel 4BI1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Definitions are marked against wording rather than approximation, and the genetics and transport topics that carry the Extended tier are the ones most often rushed at the end of Year 11. Planning the final two terms around those topics is more useful than a general revision course.

igcseSubjects.name: Economics and Business (Cambridge 0455 and 0450)
igcseSubjects.description: Both are examined through short structured questions and data response, and both reward a definition, a diagram where one applies, and then evaluation in that order. Students who write everything they know and never answer the command term lose marks consistently across every paper in these subjects.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
igcseSubjects.description: Reading and writing, listening, and speaking, with the two codes differing in how the speaking result is reported. Students at an English-medium Eastern Province school still lose marks here, because the examination tests exercise technique, register and summary writing rather than conversational fluency.

qatif.regionsTitle: Qatif towns, and the drive that sets the lesson hour
qatif.regionsIntro: Qatif is a run of towns rather than a single centre, so the school commute differs from one neighbourhood to the next even within the governorate. The detail that matters for a lesson slot is the direction of the drive and the time the student is back at a desk, which is later here than in any of the cities the schools are in.

regions.name: Qatif centre
regions.note: The administrative and commercial core of the governorate, with the oasis and the old town behind it. Families here face the standard southbound run to Dammam or Dhahran, which puts a realistic lesson start at around six in the evening on school days, and makes weekend mornings the better slot for long pieces of work.

regions.name: Tarout Island
regions.note: Reached by causeway, with Darin and Al Zour on its far side. The crossing adds a fixed amount to every journey in both directions, so students here are among the last home in the province. A single well-placed weekday lesson plus a Friday or Saturday session works far better than two weekday hours.

regions.name: Safwa
regions.note: North of Qatif centre and closer to Ras Tanura than to Dammam, which makes the southbound school run one of the longest in the governorate. Families in Safwa are the ones most likely to ask for a later evening slot, and the ones for whom a lost lesson cannot simply be made up the next day.

regions.name: Saihat
regions.note: The southern end of the governorate and the nearest point to Dammam, which gives students here the shortest run and the earliest workable lesson time. That extra half hour is worth planning around: it is often the difference between one subject an evening and two on separate days.

regions.name: Awamiyah
regions.note: North of Qatif centre within the oasis belt, with most secondary students travelling to schools in Dammam or Dhahran. The practical consequence for tutoring is a late start and a strong preference for a fixed recurring slot, because rearranging a lesson mid-week rarely survives the commute.

regions.name: Anak and Al Jarudiyah
regions.note: Western settlements closer to the Dammam highway than to the coast road, which can shorten the drive compared with the coastal towns. Families here often combine a weekday evening lesson with a weekend session for internal assessment or Personal Project work that needs uninterrupted time.

regions.name: Al Qudaih and Umm Al Hamam
regions.note: Northern Qatif communities where school choice is effectively the Dhahran and Dammam list, with a few families looking north to Jubail instead. The further north the household, the later the lesson, and the more valuable a slot that is held for the whole term rather than booked week by week.

regions.name: Ras Tanura side
regions.note: The northern edge of the Qatif catchment, where some families are inside camp communities with their own schools and their own calendars. A camp school year may not align with the international schools further south, which matters when planning the weeks before a series.

schoolClusters.city: Dhahran: where most of the province's Diploma enrolment sits
schoolClusters.note: The nearest cluster running the IB Diploma, and the destination for a large share of Qatif students who take it. British-curriculum provision sits alongside it, so two children from the same Qatif street can be following completely different assessment calendars in schools a few minutes apart.

schoolClusters.city: Dammam, Al Khobar and Jubail: the rest of the commute map
schoolClusters.note: Dammam is the shortest drive from Saihat and Qatif centre, Al Khobar extends the run by a further stretch of highway, and Jubail is the northern alternative for families in Safwa and Al Qudaih. Term dates and reporting cycles differ between all of them, so a family should take dates from their own school only.
schools: The Aramco camp schools at Dhahran and Ras Tanura

qatif.schoolDisclaimer: These schools are named only to describe the local picture a Qatif family is choosing from; no affiliation with, endorsement by or relationship to any of them is implied.
qatif.modesIntro: Which pattern suits a Qatif student depends on the term rather than the subject. A DP1 student in the autumn, a Year 11 candidate two terms from the June series and a November resit candidate need different things, and buying the wrong one is the most common way money is wasted here.

modes.title: A weekly slot held for the term
modes.description: The pattern that works with a long commute: one named hour a week, on a fixed evening, agreed in Arabia Standard Time and held for the whole term rather than rebooked each week. Work is set between sessions and marked before the next one, so the hour itself is spent teaching rather than reading through what was done.
bullets: Same tutor, same evening, held across the term
Late starts available for Safwa, Tarout and Al Qudaih families
Written work marked between lessons, not during them
Reviewed against marked papers at the end of each term

modes.title: Internal assessment support, timed to the deadline
modes.description: A short run of sessions placed around a school deadline for an exploration, an investigation, a commentary set or a Personal Project. The work is the student's own throughout; the sessions cover the criteria, the method, the statistics and the questions a moderator will ask. Scheduled backwards from the school's submission date.
bullets: Built around the criteria the school marks against
Method and data handling taught, never written for the student
Scheduled from the submission date backwards
Dated drafts kept so authorship is demonstrable

modes.title: A pre-series block
modes.description: Heavier, time-limited work in the weeks before a June or November series, built on past papers and mark schemes rather than new content. It suits a student whose content is broadly in place and who is losing marks on technique, timing and command terms. It is not a replacement for teaching that should have happened a year earlier.
bullets: Two or three sessions a week for a fixed number of weeks
Whole papers under timed conditions, then marked against the scheme
Weekend mornings used, since Friday and Saturday are free here
An honest answer first about whether a block will help at all

modes.title: Resit and November-series preparation
modes.description: For a candidate retaking a subject in the November series, or sitting it for the first time in November after a disrupted year. The plan starts from the component breakdown of the previous result, because a student who lost marks on a practical paper needs something entirely different from one who lost them on theory.
bullets: Starts from the statement of results, component by component
Entry timing confirmed with the school's examinations officer first
Separate plans for theory marks and practical or coursework marks
Runs through the summer where the series timing requires it

sections.heading: Start from where your child is in the year, not from the subject
paragraphs: Almost every useful decision about tutoring follows from the stage, not the subject. A parent who says their child is weak at chemistry has described a symptom. A parent who says their child is in Year 11, entered for Extended papers, with the alternative-to-practical route and two terms to the June series, has described a situation that can be planned. The same chemistry weakness in MYP 4 calls for a different purchase entirely, because there is time to rebuild foundations rather than triage technique.

The table sets out what each stage still controls. Read it as a list of doors: the ones still open are where outside teaching changes an outcome, and the ones already shut are where it cannot, however many hours are bought. The most expensive mistake families on this coast make is paying for intensive help in DP2 on a component that was finalised in DP1, when the same money in DP1 would have moved the grade.

Two practical notes. First, the dates that matter are your school's, not the province's: international and British-curriculum schools here set their own calendars and most run three terms, while Ministry of Education schools run two semesters, so neighbours can be in different parts of their year. Second, ask the school's examinations officer rather than guessing; the statement of entry is the only document that tells you which papers your child is actually sitting. Families who read it in the autumn term have options; families who read it after a mock result has alarmed them are usually reading a decision rather than a choice.
bullets: Ask which series and which papers your child is entered for, in writing
Identify what is already fixed before paying for anything
Earlier money buys more change than later money, at every stage
Term dates come from your own school, never from a city-wide calendar

sections.heading: The June series, counted backwards
paragraphs: Nobody in this market publishes the year in reverse, which is strange, because that is the order a family actually needs it in. The written papers are the last event, not the first. Before them come study leave, mock examinations, predicted grades, internal assessment submissions, final entries and tier decisions, and each of those has its own lead time. A plan that starts from the papers and works outwards arrives too late at every one of them.

The table below is the sequence rather than a set of dates, because dates belong to your school and to the board. Entries close several months ahead of a series and your school's examinations officer holds the exact deadline; internal assessment deadlines are set by the school and are usually earlier than students expect; results arrive in the weeks after the series, and a remark or an inquiry about results has a short window after that.

One fact to get right, because rival pages copied from Indian websites get it wrong: Cambridge's February and March series is available only to candidates in India. Candidates in the Kingdom sit the June series as their main one and the November series for resits or November entry. A family told to aim at a spring sitting has been given a timetable that does not exist for them, and will discover it after entries have closed. If a provider offers a plan built around that series, treat it as evidence that the plan was written for a different country and nobody checked.
bullets: Entries close months before the papers; the examinations officer holds the date
Internal assessment deadlines are school-set and come earlier than expected
The main series here is June, with November for resits and late entries
A results inquiry or remark has a short window after results arrive

sections.heading: What each component is worth, and why that changes the plan
paragraphs: A grade is a weighted sum, and families routinely spend their budget on the lightest component in it. An IGCSE science candidate who loses a fifth of the available marks on the practical component is not helped by more theory teaching, and a Diploma student whose written papers are solid but whose internal assessment is thin has a problem that revision cannot touch. Knowing the weightings turns a vague sense of weakness into a priority order.

The pattern is consistent enough to be useful. Cambridge Extended science candidates meet a multiple-choice paper worth roughly thirty per cent, an extended theory paper worth about half, and a practical component worth the remaining fifth. Cambridge mathematics now splits each tier into a non-calculator and a calculator paper of equal weight. In the Diploma, internal assessment is a meaningful share of every subject, and at Higher Level a third paper adds a distinct demand rather than more of the same content.

Ask the school for the component breakdown of your child's most recent mock, not just the grade. A single letter hides everything that matters: two students with the same overall mark can need opposite interventions. The breakdown also tells you whether the problem is content, technique or timing, and only the first of those is fixed by covering more syllabus. Timing problems in particular look exactly like knowledge gaps on a report and respond to nothing except whole papers against a clock, which is why a tutor who asks for the mock script before quoting a plan is worth more than one who does not.
bullets: Ask for the component breakdown of every mock, not only the grade
A fifth of a Cambridge science grade sits in the practical component
Higher Level third papers test a different skill, not extra content
Internal assessment cannot be recovered by revision at the end

sections.heading: Predicted grades and grade boundaries, and what neither one is
paragraphs: A predicted grade is a professional judgement made by the school about what a student is likely to achieve, based on the evidence it holds: classwork, internal assessment drafts, mock papers and the teacher's knowledge of the cohort. It is used in university applications, and it is not a promise, a negotiation or a target the school owes a family. Asking what evidence a prediction rests on is reasonable; asking for it to be raised because it is inconvenient is not.

Grade boundaries move between series, and that unsettles parents more than it should. They move because papers differ slightly in difficulty from one sitting to the next, and the boundary is adjusted so that the same standard of work earns the same grade. A paper where a boundary fell is not a paper where marking was generous; it is a paper that was harder. This is also why a mock marked against last series' boundaries gives only an approximate picture.

The practical use of all this is diagnostic. A mock three marks below a boundary is a different situation from a mock fifteen marks below one, and the first is often a timing or command-term problem rather than a knowledge gap. Ask for the marks, the boundary used and the component split, and the right intervention is usually obvious from the three together. It also tells a family when to stop buying help: a student consistently a little above a boundary across several components is being served well enough by their school, and the money is better held for the term before the series.
bullets: A prediction is evidence-based judgement, not an entitlement
Boundaries move to hold the standard steady across series
Three marks below a boundary is usually technique, not content
Mocks marked to an older boundary set give an approximate signal only

sections.heading: Ministry of Education equivalency, and the two Qiyas tests
paragraphs: This is the largest gap in everything written about tutoring in the Kingdom, and it matters most to exactly the families reading a page like this one. An IB Diploma, an A Level certificate and an American high school diploma are all foreign qualifications, and a Saudi university treats them as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate only after an equivalency decision, known as mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education. That is an administrative process, and it runs on its own timetable.

Alongside it sit the two tests run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment, Qiyas. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, assesses verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and is available in Arabic and in English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers the science-stream subjects: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English. Universities publish their own admission criteria combining school results with these tests, and the weightings differ by university and by programme.

Nothing on this page should be read as a threshold, a formula or an entitlement. Cut-offs and weightings differ between institutions and between programmes, and third-party sites disagree with each other about them, so the only reliable source is the university's own published admission criteria for the programme your child wants. What a family can do early is understand the sequence, start the paperwork in good time, and make sure a student who may sit Tahsili has met its content somewhere.
bullets: Equivalency is a Ministry of Education decision, not a school one
Qudurat tests reasoning; Tahsili tests science-stream subject content
Weightings and cut-offs differ by university and programme
Check the university's own published criteria, and nothing else

sections.heading: Why Tahsili is harder for an international-curriculum student
paragraphs: Tahsili follows the Saudi national curriculum. That single fact explains most of the difficulty an IB or IGCSE student has with it, and it is rarely explained to families until late. The material overlaps substantially with what a Diploma or IGCSE science student has studied, but the framing, the vocabulary, the expected order of topics and the question style belong to a different course. A strong Higher Level chemistry student can meet a Tahsili chemistry question and not recognise what is being asked.

The gaps cluster in predictable places. Terminology learned in English has to be recognised in Arabic for students taking the Arabic version. Topics the national curriculum treats at length may be a minor part of an international syllabus, and the reverse is also true, so an international student has both unfamiliar content and content they know far better than the test requires. Mathematics notation and conventions differ in small ways that cost time under pressure.

The practical approach is to treat it as a separate course rather than as revision. Work from the official published specification for the test, map it against what the student has actually studied, and teach the difference. Starting early matters more here than for anything else described on this page, because the overlap has to be found before the remainder can be taught, and both steps take longer than a family expects from a test that looks familiar on paper. A student who begins in the final weeks is usually reduced to guessing which half of the specification to read.
bullets: The content overlaps; the framing and vocabulary often do not
Students sitting the Arabic version need the terminology in Arabic
Map the published specification against what has actually been taught
Treat it as a separate course, not as revision of school work

sections.heading: Living in Qatif, schooling in Dhahran: the late-start problem
paragraphs: Qatif's school map is not inside Qatif. Almost all the province's international and British-curriculum provision sits in Dhahran, Dammam, Al Khobar and Jubail, which means a secondary student here spends a substantial part of every school day travelling. From Saihat the run south is short; from Safwa, Al Qudaih or across the Tarout causeway it is considerably longer, and the return journey lands in the heaviest part of the afternoon.

The consequence is a narrow usable window. For many families the first realistic lesson start is around six in the evening, which makes a single well-placed session far more durable than two stacked hours. It also makes the weekend genuinely valuable: Friday and Saturday are free here, and a weekend morning is the best time in the week for work that needs sustained thought, such as an exploration, an investigation write-up or a Personal Project review.

This is also the honest argument for teaching online rather than in person in this governorate. The number of specialist IB and IGCSE teachers living in Qatif is small, and most people in the province who know these syllabuses are already teaching them full time at a school to the south. A family insisting on someone who will drive to Safwa for a seven o'clock lesson is choosing from a very short list, and subject specialism is the first thing that gets traded away. The question worth asking is not who can reach the house, but who has taught this paper to this tier before.
bullets: Tell us the arrival-home time, not the school's finishing time
One durable weekday slot beats two that collapse by mid-term
Weekend mornings suit internal assessment and project work
Specialist supply in the governorate is thin; online widens the pool

sections.heading: The November series, resits and the student who missed a paper
paragraphs: The November series exists for resits and for candidates who enter in November rather than June, and it is used more often in the Eastern Province than families expect, partly because of mid-year relocations into and out of the province. The decision to resit should start from the statement of results rather than from disappointment: the component breakdown shows whether marks were lost on theory, on the practical component, or on coursework that cannot be retaken in the same form.

That distinction decides whether a resit is worth entering at all. A candidate who lost marks across a theory paper has something a term of teaching can address. A candidate whose coursework or practical mark is carried forward has a ceiling that no amount of theory work will lift, and the right answer may be a different subject, a different tier or a different route altogether. Ask the examinations officer what can be carried forward and what must be retaken before committing.

Where a paper was missed through illness or an emergency, schools have a formal process for it, and the board has provisions that depend on evidence and on timing. That is school and board territory, not a tutor's, and a family should go to the examinations officer the same week rather than waiting for results. What a tutor can do afterwards is rebuild for the next series, starting from whatever the previous attempt actually produced. Keep every document the school issues in the meantime, because the next series' entry decisions are made from them.
bullets: Start a resit decision from the component breakdown, not the grade
Ask what marks can be carried forward and what must be retaken
A missed paper is a school and board process, handled immediately
November entry timing is confirmed by the examinations officer

process.title: Tell us the stage before the subject
process.description: The first questions are the year group, the board, the series your child is entered for and the date of the next internal deadline. That tells us what is still movable. Subject and level follow, and so does the realistic lesson hour given where in Qatif you are driving back from.

process.title: Read the entry and the last mock
process.description: The statement of entry shows the codes, tiers and papers your child is actually sitting, and the mock breakdown shows which component is costing marks. Those two documents replace most of the guesswork, and they frequently change what we recommend buying from what a parent first asked for.

process.title: A diagnostic session against the real papers
process.description: A short first session using past questions from the exact syllabus and tier, so the gaps are evidence rather than impression. It produces a short written list ordered by what is assessed first, which is not usually the same order as what feels weakest to the student.

process.title: A free trial lesson, with the proposed tutor
process.description: The trial is taught by the specialist who would keep the slot, not by a different teacher or a salesperson. You see how they explain something your child has already failed to follow once. If the match is wrong, we propose another rather than asking anyone to persist with it.

process.title: A plan anchored to the calendar, reviewed each term
process.description: Lessons run to a fixed weekly slot in Arabia Standard Time, with intensity planned around the school's deadlines and the series. At the end of each term we report against marked work and say plainly whether to continue, change the pattern or stop.

whyPoints.title: Planned from the series, not from the enquiry date
whyPoints.description: Support is built backwards from entries, internal deadlines and the series your child is actually sitting. That changes what is worth buying: the same budget spent in DP1 moves a grade that the same spend in DP2 cannot reach, and we say so rather than selling the later package.

whyPoints.title: Correct on the series a Saudi candidate can sit
whyPoints.description: Cambridge candidates here sit the June and November series. The February and March series is available only to candidates in India, and several pages aimed at Gulf families say otherwise because they were written for an Indian audience. Acting on that mistake costs a year.

whyPoints.title: Late slots for a long commute
whyPoints.description: Lessons can start late enough to suit a family driving back to Safwa, Al Qudaih or Tarout after a school day in Dhahran, and the slot is held in Riyadh and Qatif local time so it does not drift when a tutor's own country changes its clocks.

whyPoints.title: The university pathway explained as mechanism
whyPoints.description: Equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili are described here as processes with owners and sequences. No thresholds, no weighting formulas and no admission promises, because those differ by university and programme and only the institution's own published criteria are reliable.

whyPoints.title: A fixed line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches the criteria, the method and the reasoning, and gives feedback on a draft the student has written. Nobody here produces an exploration, an investigation, a commentary or a Personal Project for a student, and we keep dated drafts so authorship can be shown.

faqs.question: When should an MYP 5 student at a Dhahran school start getting help with the Personal Project?
faqs.answer: Early in the year, and for planning rather than content. The project is assessed on planning, applying skills and reflecting, so the marks are won in how the student sets a goal, chooses criteria for success and evidences their process, not in how impressive the final product looks. A Qatif family's practical difficulty is the commute: this is work that needs unbroken stretches, so weekend mornings suit it far better than a weekday evening. A tutor can teach the criteria and question the plan, but the project must be the student's own throughout.

faqs.question: What should a Qatif family in Year 10 be doing differently from one in Year 11?
faqs.answer: Year 10 is for content and for the tier conversation. It is the year in which a family can still influence whether a child is entered for Core or Extended papers, and whether the science practical is taken as a test or as the alternative paper, because those decisions are usually settled before entries close. Year 11 is for technique, timing and the practical component, because the tier is fixed once entries are in. Spending Year 10 money on examination technique and Year 11 money on foundations is the wrong way round, and it is a common sequence.

faqs.question: Is it worth starting support in DP2 when the written papers are two terms away?
faqs.answer: Yes, with a narrower aim. By DP2 the subject and level combination is fixed and some internal components are submitted, so the work shifts to written-paper technique, command terms, timing and whatever internal assessment is still open. That can move a grade, particularly where mocks sit a few marks below a boundary. What it cannot do is rebuild two years of foundations in one subject while five others continue. The honest conversation at this stage is about which subjects to protect, and sometimes about which to let go.

faqs.question: How much notice does a November-series resit need for a candidate in Saihat?
faqs.answer: Start the term before, and begin with the statement of results rather than the overall grade. The component breakdown shows whether marks were lost on a theory paper, on the practical component or on coursework, and that determines whether a resit can realistically improve the outcome. Your school's examinations officer confirms the entry window and what, if anything, can be carried forward from the previous attempt. Entering late and preparing for the wrong component is the most common way a resit produces the same grade twice.

faqs.question: What does the final term before the June series need to achieve for an IGCSE candidate?
faqs.answer: Three things, and new content is not among them. Whole papers under timed conditions, marked against the published mark scheme rather than by impression. Command-term discipline, so a question asking for an explanation does not receive a description. And the practical component, which in Cambridge sciences is about a fifth of the grade and is usually the least rehearsed part of the course. If content gaps are still large in that final term, they should be triaged by weighting, not covered in full.

faqs.question: When are IGCSE tier decisions locked in, and who actually makes them?
faqs.answer: The school makes them, usually during Year 10 or early Year 11, and they are confirmed when entries are submitted several months ahead of the series. The tier caps the grade available, so it is worth asking early rather than discovering it on a statement of entry. A family can raise a case for a different tier with the subject teacher, supported by marked work, but the decision stays with the school. Ask for the statement of entry and check the code, tier and practical route for every subject on it.

faqs.question: Why do grade boundaries move between series, and what should a parent read into it?
faqs.answer: Papers vary slightly in difficulty from one sitting to the next, and boundaries are adjusted so that the same standard of work earns the same grade each time. A boundary that falls indicates a harder paper, not generous marking. For a parent the practical implication is modest: a mock marked against an older boundary set gives an approximate signal, so ask which series' boundaries were used. What matters more is the raw mark and the component split, because those point to whether the problem is content, technique or timing.

faqs.question: What is a predicted grade for a Diploma student, and what evidence is it based on?
faqs.answer: It is the school's professional judgement of the grade a student is likely to achieve, used in university applications. Schools build it from classwork, internal assessment drafts, mock papers and knowledge of how previous cohorts performed. It is not a promise, and it is not something a family can negotiate upwards because an offer requires it. Asking which evidence the prediction rests on is entirely reasonable, and the answer usually identifies the component that needs work. Treat a disappointing prediction as a diagnosis rather than a verdict.

faqs.question: What share of an IB science grade is produced before the written papers?
faqs.answer: A meaningful one. Each IB science subject includes an internal investigation, marked at school and moderated externally, and it is produced during the course rather than in the examination room. That has two consequences. A student who chooses an unmeasurable variable or an indefensible sample locks in a loss that no later revision recovers. And a family deciding when to buy support should weigh an investigation a year ahead against paper technique at the end, because only one of them is still open early. Ask the teacher for the criteria the investigation is marked against.

faqs.question: How do the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay grades add to a Diploma total?
faqs.answer: They are combined through a matrix that awards up to three additional points on top of the six subject grades. The practical effect is that the core is worth roughly half a subject grade at the margin, which is enough to decide a university offer. Families tend to treat both as administrative hurdles and then find the points missing at the end. A weak Extended Essay cannot be offset by a strong subject grade, because the matrix reads the two core components together. Both deserve real time in DP1 rather than panic in DP2.

faqs.question: What is Ministry of Education equivalency, and when should a Qatif family start it?
faqs.answer: Equivalency, or mu'adalah, is the Ministry of Education's decision that a foreign certificate is equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. Without it, a Saudi university does not treat an IB Diploma, an A Level certificate or an American high school diploma as a qualifying school leaving certificate. It is an administrative process with its own requirements and timelines, and families routinely discover it after results rather than before. Begin enquiring during the final school year, and take the current requirements from the Ministry itself rather than from a forum or an agent.

faqs.question: Does an IB Diploma student in the Eastern Province have to sit Qudurat and Tahsili?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on where the student applies. Saudi universities set their own admission criteria and most include the Qiyas tests for their programmes, while universities outside the Kingdom generally do not ask for them at all. A student applying in both directions may need to prepare for the tests and for an overseas application in the same year, which is a scheduling problem worth planning early. The reliable source is the published admission criteria of each university and programme on the student's list, read before final-year subject decisions are made.

faqs.question: Which subjects does Tahsili cover, and how do they line up with a Diploma student's six?
faqs.answer: Tahsili covers the science-stream subjects: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English. A Diploma student taking three Higher Level sciences will have met most of that content, but not in the same order, the same depth or the same vocabulary, because the test follows the Saudi national curriculum. A student who dropped biology or physics after MYP has a genuine content gap rather than a framing one. Map the official published specification against what the student has actually studied, and treat the difference as a separate course.

faqs.question: Is Qudurat sat in Arabic or English, and does that matter for a child schooled in English?
faqs.answer: It is available in both, and the choice matters more than families expect. Qudurat assesses verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, so the verbal section is heavily language-dependent: a student schooled entirely in English may reason comfortably in English and find the Arabic verbal section far harder, even as a native speaker, because academic and test register differ from everyday speech. Decide which version to sit early, then practise in that language specifically. Registration details and available sittings come from Qiyas rather than from a school.

faqs.question: Where should a Qatif family check a Saudi university's actual admission criteria?
faqs.answer: On the university's own admissions pages, for the specific programme and intake. Third-party sites, agents and forums disagree with each other about weightings and cut-offs, and those differ by university, by programme and over time, so anything quoted second-hand should be treated as unreliable. Competitive engineering, medicine and science programmes weight the Qiyas tests most heavily, which is a general pattern rather than a formula. Print or save what the university publishes at the time you apply, because requirements are revised and an old screenshot settles later arguments.

faqs.question: How recent does a secondary certificate have to be for a Saudi university application?
faqs.answer: Some universities set a limit on how old the certificate they will accept can be, and others do not, so it is a question for each institution rather than a single national rule. It matters most for a student considering a gap year, a late resit or a change of direction after results, because a plan that looks harmless can put the certificate outside a university's window. Check the published admission requirements before committing to a delay, and ask the admissions office directly where the wording is unclear.

qatif.closingHeading: Tell us which term you are in
qatif.closingBody: The useful first message is not the subject but the position: year group, board, the series your child is entered for, the date of the next internal deadline, and which town in Qatif the school run returns to. From that we can say what is still movable, what is already fixed, and whether a specialist is free in the hour that actually exists in your week. If nobody suitable is available we will say so rather than offering a generalist. Lessons are one-to-one, delivered online over live video, and pinned to Arabia Standard Time.

ras-tanura.tutorsIntro: The tutors listed below teach Cambridge IGCSE, the Middle Years Programme and the Diploma across the Eastern Province. Whether the match is an IGCSE tutor in Ras Tanura or an IB Diploma tutor in Ras Tanura, it is made to the component a student is losing marks on rather than to the subject as a whole, and every slot sits late enough for a commuting student.

intro.heading: The marks are not lost at random, and in Ras Tanura they are lost in the same four places
paragraphs: A student who is working hard and still dropping grades is almost never short of effort, and usually not short of content either. The marks are going somewhere specific. Across the enquiries that reach us from Ras Tanura and the northern Gulf coast, four places account for most of them. The extended-response question, where a student describes a phenomenon that the command term asked them to explain or derive. Paper 3 at Higher Level, where the question is lost in the first twenty seconds of setup rather than in the algebra. The alternative-to-practical paper at IGCSE, which is a written examination about experiments and gets revised as though it were theory. And the Internal Assessment, scoped too broadly in week one and capped from that moment regardless of how well the rest is executed.

Naming the place is the whole job, because each of those four has a different fix and none of them is 'more revision'. A student losing extended-response marks needs to rewrite answers against the published mark scheme until the ordering of steps is automatic. A student losing Paper 3 marks needs setup drills: state the model, name the variables, then touch the algebra. A student losing alternative-to-practical marks needs that component's own past papers, which look nothing like the theory papers from the same subject. A student with a badly scoped research question needs an hour on the question itself before any data exists. Generic tutoring buys none of those things; a matched specialist buys all four.

Ras Tanura adds a constraint that Riyadh and Jeddah do not have. It is a refinery town with its own residential camp and a small, self-contained community, which means a student's subject options are set by one school's staffing rather than by a city's worth of schools. In a larger market, a Higher Level option that does not run at one campus runs at another two districts away. Here, if the subject is not on the timetable it is not on the timetable, and families deal with it by travelling south, by changing schools, or by bringing in an outside specialist for that one subject.

The travelling matters more than the distance suggests. Senior-school provision for the community sits mostly down the coast road, around Dhahran, Al Khobar and Dammam, and that journey is the single largest item in a commuting student's day. By the time a coach or a parent's car gets back, a notional 5pm lesson has already gone. This is the practical reason every lesson for Ras Tanura families runs online: a tutor driving to the camp would arrive into the same gap and then drive back out of it. No tutor travels to a Ras Tanura address. In-home visiting is a service we run only in India, and the phrase a parent types into Google does not change what we actually sell.

What online delivery buys here is not convenience, it is access. The set of people who can teach Higher Level Chemistry to the current syllabus and have marked the Internal Assessment against its criteria is small in any country, and the subset of them living within reach of a Gulf coast refinery town is effectively nil. Over live video, that subset stops mattering. The remaining constraint is the clock, which is why the Sunday-to-Thursday week and Arabia Standard Time get a section of their own rather than a footnote.

The rest of this page works through the four failure points in order, then the staffing problem behind them, then the commute, then what a curriculum switch leaves missing, then the week, then the first month and how progress is reported, then the line we will not cross on assessed work, and finally what this costs in the Eastern Province and when to stop paying for it.
