ras-tanura.programmesIntro: Four programmes turn up in Ras Tanura enquiries, and each fails in its own way. Below is what each one is assessed on and the characteristic place a student in this community loses ground in it.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: No external papers, no grade boundaries: progress is judged through units of inquiry, teacher assessment and the Year 6 exhibition. The characteristic failure at this stage is invisible for years. A child who was taught a written method one way in a previous country, and a different way here, quietly stops trusting either, and the hesitation surfaces in Year 7 as slow arithmetic rather than as a gap anybody logged.
programmes.countryNote: Children in a refinery-camp community frequently change school systems with a parent's posting, sometimes twice before Year 5. The inquiry work travels well; the procedural layer underneath it does not. Short sessions of thirty to forty minutes, rebuilding one method at a time, fit this age and fit the window between the camp school day and dinner.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Each subject is assessed against four criteria, each marked out of eight, converted to a one-to-seven grade. The Personal Project runs in the final year. The characteristic failure is a correct answer that does not address the command term, and a Personal Project submitted with a good product and no evidence of the process behind it. Both are presentation failures rather than knowledge failures, and both respond fast to direct teaching.
programmes.countryNote: Students arriving from an American-curriculum camp school meet criterion marking for the first time in the Middle Years Programme and are routinely surprised by a lower grade on work they consider better than last year's. The content is not the problem. Reading the criterion and writing to it is a learnable skill, and it is usually two or three sessions of work rather than a term of it.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three Higher and three Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. The core contributes up to three further points through the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix. The characteristic failure is a Higher Level extension topic that was taught thinly because the group had very few students in it, and discovered in a mock paper rather than in a lesson.
programmes.countryNote: Diploma provision for this community is mostly down the coast, and option groups are small. A Higher Level subject may be taught by the nearest available member of a department rather than by its specialist, which is arithmetic rather than negligence. Ask the Diploma Programme coordinator how many students are in each Higher Level group before subject choices lock, and who teaches it.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE and Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Two boards, different paper structures, different tiering and different coursework options. Cambridge Mathematics 0580 splits into Core and Extended; the sciences at 0620, 0625 and 0610 each carry multiple-choice, theory and an alternative-to-practical or practical component. The characteristic failure is the practical component, prepared as though it were revision for the theory paper and examined as something else entirely.
programmes.countryNote: Candidates in the Eastern Province enter for the June series, with November available for resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge's February/March series is an India-only sitting, so nothing in a Ras Tanura student's year is planned around it. Entry windows close months ahead of the papers, and the examinations officer at the school holds the exact dates rather than any tutoring provider.

ras-tanura.subjectsIntro: These are the Diploma subjects Ras Tanura and northern Gulf coast families ask about most, described by where the marks actually leak rather than by what the course covers.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Energetics and organic mechanisms carry most of the lost marks, and the Internal Assessment is where strong candidates most often underscore. The usual leak is an uncertainty treatment that reports a value without justifying it. The Higher Level extension to equilibrium and acid-base chemistry is separate content, not harder revision, and it needs taught time. A tutor questions and reviews the student's own write-up; they never draft any part of it.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The extension topics at Higher Level assume the data booklet is a working tool rather than a reference sheet, and the extended-response items punish description where derivation was asked for. Students who can calculate confidently still lose marks explaining how an uncertainty was reduced. In a community with one senior school, this is the subject most often taught by a department's second physicist rather than its first.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Paper 3 at Higher Level is two extended problem-solving questions worth twenty per cent of the grade, with no scaffolding and a reading demand students consistently underestimate. The leak is in the setup: the wrong method chosen in the first twenty seconds, then executed perfectly. Proof and calculus applications account for most of the remainder, along with answers that never state what a variable represents.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Calculator-permitted throughout, with modelling, statistics and interpretation at its centre. Students who move across from Analysis and Approaches expecting an easier course lose marks for presenting a bare number where an interpretation in context was required. The Higher Level course adds matrices, graph theory and a statistics load heavier than the course title suggests.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Examined on precision rather than recall. A six-mark answer that lists accurate facts without linking structure to function scores poorly, and definitions are marked strictly. Data-based questions in Paper 2 reward graph reading more than biological knowledge. The Higher Level extension to genetics, plant biology and physiology cannot be absorbed in a final-term sprint and is routinely left too late.

subjects.name: Environmental Systems and Societies
subjects.description: Often chosen as a lighter option and then examined on systems thinking, which is not lighter at all. Candidates lose marks writing environmental opinion where the question asked for a model, a flow or a named value system. The Internal Assessment requires a genuine fieldwork or data investigation, and a question that cannot be answered with the data available is the most common early mistake.

subjects.name: Geography
subjects.description: Case-study specificity is what the mark scheme pays for: named place, named figure, named process. Generic answers about coastal or urban processes score at the bottom of a level regardless of how well written they are. Higher Level adds the global interactions extension, and candidates underprepare the fieldwork Internal Assessment because it feels finished once the data is collected.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: The pre-released case study for Paper 1 rewards work most candidates start too late. Paper 2 is quantitative tools plus data response, and Higher Level adds an extension paper. The leak is confident general commentary that never applies a named tool to the stimulus, which reads well to a student and scores poorly against the criteria.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The individual oral and the Higher Level essay are internally assessed before external moderation, and both decide more of the grade than students expect. Paper 1 is unseen textual analysis under time pressure, where a candidate trained to summarise rather than analyse runs out of things to say. A tutor builds that analytical move on texts the student is not being assessed on.

subjects.name: Design Technology
subjects.description: The design project is a sustained piece of documented work, and the marks sit in the justification of decisions rather than in the artefact. Candidates lose marks presenting a finished design with no evidence of iteration or testing. Higher Level adds a heavier materials and manufacturing load, and the written papers assume technical vocabulary that classroom project work does not always build.

ras-tanura.igcseSubjectsIntro: Cambridge dominates the British-curriculum provision in this part of the Eastern Province, and these are the papers that produce the most questions from Ras Tanura families.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
igcseSubjects.description: Extended is the tier that keeps the Diploma and A Level sciences open; Core caps the grade available. The marks leak on algebraic manipulation under time pressure, and on questions that ask for method to be shown where only an answer has been written. Marking their own paper against the scheme is what makes those method marks visible to a student.

igcseSubjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606)
igcseSubjects.description: Taken alongside 0580 by students heading for Higher Level mathematics, and a genuinely useful bridge into the Diploma. It introduces calculus, functions and trigonometric identities earlier than the main syllabus, and candidates who treat it as extra homework rather than as a second subject lose marks on the longer multi-step questions.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625)
igcseSubjects.description: The alternative-to-practical paper is the clearest example of a component that fails for the wrong reason. It is a written examination about experimental method, and candidates who prepare it as theory revision cannot describe how to reduce uncertainty in a measurement or read a printed instrument scale.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620)
igcseSubjects.description: Mole calculations, qualitative analysis and the organic unit separate the grades. Marks leak on state symbols, on unbalanced equations, and on answering with a conclusion where the question asked for the observation. The practical component follows the same pattern as physics and needs its own past papers.

igcseSubjects.name: Co-ordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0654)
igcseSubjects.description: Three sciences compressed into a double award, which is efficient on a timetable and demanding in a revision plan. Students are often strong in one of the three and carry the other two, and because the papers interleave the subjects, a weak biology section quietly pulls down a grade the student attributes to chemistry.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a First Language (Cambridge 0500)
igcseSubjects.description: Directed writing and the composition task reward register control and structure, not vocabulary range. Reading responses lose marks when a candidate retells the passage instead of analysing how the writer achieves an effect. This is a technique subject, and it improves faster than most students expect once the structure is explicit.

igcseSubjects.name: Information and Communication Technology (Cambridge 0417)
igcseSubjects.description: Two practical papers plus a theory paper, and the practical work is marked on exact outcomes rather than on competence. Candidates who use software daily still lose marks for not following a specification precisely, which is the single most common cause of a disappointing grade in this subject.

ras-tanura.regionsTitle: The Eastern Province places a Ras Tanura family's week actually runs through
ras-tanura.regionsIntro: A Ras Tanura week is not contained in Ras Tanura. School, medical appointments, weekend activities and often the senior-school campus itself sit elsewhere on the coast. These are the places that shape the timetable, listed by what each does to an evening.

regions.name: Ras Tanura camp
regions.note: The residential community beside the refinery and terminal, with its own school for the younger years. Students who are still schooled on the camp have the widest usable evening in the whole province, and a 4:30pm or 5pm lesson is realistic for them in a way it is not for a commuter.

regions.name: Rahima
regions.note: The town immediately adjacent, where much of the local and national-curriculum schooling sits. Families here often run a mix: a Ministry of Education school for one child and a Cambridge-curriculum school further down the coast for another, which makes a shared study hour hard to find before 6pm.

regions.name: Safwa and Tarout
regions.note: South along the coast towards Qatif, with established residential areas and a short hop onto the main road. Journeys from here to the Dhahran campuses are marginally shorter than from the camp, and families frequently share school transport along the same route.

regions.name: Qatif
regions.note: The main town between Ras Tanura and the Dammam conurbation, and the point where coast-road traffic starts to thicken in both directions. Anything scheduled in the hour either side of the school return from the south is unreliable, which is why we fix slots after it rather than inside it.

regions.name: Dhahran
regions.note: The usual senior-school destination for this community, holding several of the province's international campuses including the ones running the Diploma. The journey down and back is the largest single block in a commuting student's day, and it is the reason the standard Ras Tanura slot starts at 6:30pm.

regions.name: Al Khobar
regions.note: Beyond Dhahran, inside the Dammam, Khobar and Dhahran conurbation that behaves as one school and labour market. Families routinely live in one of the three and attend school in another. The King Fahd Causeway to Bahrain also puts weekend travel into the picture more than elsewhere in the Kingdom.

regions.name: Dammam
regions.note: The provincial capital, west of Khobar, with the broadest set of schools in the province and the heaviest city traffic at the end of the run. A Ras Tanura student attending here has a comparable journey to Dhahran plus the city streets at the far end of it.

regions.name: Jubail
regions.note: North along the coast rather than south, and against the main commuting flow, so often quicker than the map suggests. The industrial city holds international provision of its own, and a few Ras Tanura families travel north instead of south for exactly that reason.

regions.name: Abqaiq and Udhailiyah
regions.note: Inland company communities with the same shape of problem as Ras Tanura on a smaller scale: one school, a small cohort, and no second campus down the road. Online teaching is the only format that reaches them with a Higher Level specialist at a usable hour.

schoolClusters.city: Ras Tanura and the company communities
schoolClusters.note: The company school network serves the residential communities at Ras Tanura and inland, and provision is organised by community rather than by district. Senior-year provision for this population commonly means travelling, so confirm with each school directly what year groups it currently runs before planning two years ahead. Students we support attend schools including the following.
schools: Saudi Aramco Expatriate Schools, Ras Tanura

schoolClusters.city: Dhahran and Al Khobar, the senior-school destination
schoolClusters.note: This is where most Ras Tanura senior-school commuting ends up. The International Schools Group runs several campuses in the province, the Diploma is offered at some of them and not others, and the British-curriculum schools here follow Cambridge. Diploma option groups are small, which is the staffing fact behind most of the enquiries we get from this coast.

schoolClusters.city: Jubail and Dammam along the same road
schoolClusters.note: North and west of the Ras Tanura camp, both reachable on the same coastal and ring-road network. Jubail carries international provision including a Diploma campus, and Dammam has the widest school choice in the province. Families weighing a northward commute against a southward one usually decide it on traffic direction rather than on distance.
schools: Royal Commission Schools, Jubail Industrial City

ras-tanura.modesIntro: Three formats. Which one a family needs follows from the diagnosis rather than from a price list, and the cheapest of the three is often the right answer.

modes.title: Component clinic
modes.description: A short run of sessions aimed at one failing component and nothing else: the alternative-to-practical paper, Paper 3 setup, the extended-response ordering, the Internal Assessment research question. It has a defined end point, because a component either starts paying out or it does not, and that becomes visible within four or five sessions rather than over a term.
bullets: One named component, agreed in writing before the first session
Built from that component's own past papers, not from the textbook
A clear finish point rather than an open-ended weekly slot
Usually four to six sessions in total

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one after the coach gets back
modes.description: A fixed weekly hour for a student carrying a subject the school cannot staff deeply, held late enough to survive the commute down the coast. Sessions run sixty minutes at IGCSE and Middle Years level and seventy-five to ninety for Diploma candidates working whole papers, because a Higher Level paper cannot be attempted properly in less.
bullets: Slot held in Arabia Standard Time and not in the tutor's own time
Same tutor each week, so the work accumulates
Starts at 6:30pm or later for senior-school commuters
Written notes to the parent after each session

modes.title: Transfer catch-up
modes.description: For a student who has just moved into or out of the province mid-course. The first task is an audit of what actually transfers and what does not, which is rarely what the previous school's report implies. The plan that follows is time-boxed to a term and reviewed against marked work, not against a feeling that things are going better.

Separates genuine gaps from differences in assessment style

sections.heading: The four places marks go missing, and what each one actually needs
paragraphs: Start with the component, not the subject. A parent who says their child is weak at chemistry is describing a grade; a tutor needs to know whether the grade is being lost in the multiple-choice paper, in the extended-response items, in the practical component or in the Internal Assessment, because those four need four different interventions. The single most useful thing a family can do before any tuition begins is to lay out the last two marked papers and add up where the marks went. It takes twenty minutes and it changes what you buy.

The extended-response failure is the most common and the most fixable. Mark schemes pay for named steps in a defined order. A candidate who reaches a correct conclusion by a route the scheme does not recognise loses marks they are certain they earned, and no amount of additional content teaching helps. The fix is mechanical: rewrite answers against the published scheme, repeatedly, until the ordering is automatic and the student can predict what the examiner will pay for before writing a word.

The Paper 3 failure at Higher Level is a setup failure. Two extended questions, no scaffolding, and a reading demand that students treat as preamble. A candidate who starts the wrong method and executes it perfectly scores very little. The fix is to practise only the first ninety seconds of a question, over and over: state the model, name the variables, write the relationship, and only then begin. Students resist this because it does not feel like doing maths, and it moves grades faster than anything else available in the final term.

The practical and Internal Assessment failures are both planning failures rather than execution failures. The alternative-to-practical paper is examined on experimental method in writing and needs its own past papers. The Internal Assessment is capped by its research question, so the highest-value hour in the whole piece is the one spent narrowing that question before any data is collected. The table below lays all four out with the fix next to the failure.

sections.heading: In a camp town, one school's staffing decides a student's subject list
paragraphs: Every school builds its timetable from option blocks, and an option block needs enough students in it to justify a specialist. In a city, a Higher Level subject that does not run at one campus runs at another one a few districts away, and a determined family can change school. Ras Tanura does not work like that. The community is small and self-contained, senior provision for it is concentrated, and if a subject is not on the timetable there is no second timetable to consult. That is the structural difference between this coast and Riyadh or Jeddah, and it is the honest reason outside teaching is more common here per family than it is there.

The second-order effects are the ones that catch families out. A Higher Level group with very few students in it may be taught by the department's second specialist rather than its first, or combined with the Standard Level class for part of the week, or in rare cases offered as supervised self-study. None of that is a criticism of a school doing arithmetic with the staff it has. But it changes what a student needs: not revision at the end, but taught time on the extension topics during the course, before a mock paper reveals that a topic was covered thinly.

A student who is the only person in their year sitting a subject also loses something that has nothing to do with teaching. There is nobody to argue with about a mark scheme, no benchmark for what a good answer looks like, and no study group. Working alone is a measurable disadvantage in its own right. An outside specialist partly replaces that function, because they have seen many versions of the same answer and can say which version gets paid.

The practical move is to ask the school a precise question early, in the year before subject choices lock rather than after. How many students are in each Higher Level group this year. Who teaches each one, and what is that teacher's own degree subject. How is the practical component resourced. Schools answer questions phrased that way, and the answers tell a family whether they are buying support for two years, for one component, or not at all.

sections.heading: The coast road, and what the commute leaves of the evening
paragraphs: Ras Tanura's scheduling problem is not traffic inside a city, it is distance between towns. The camp sits on the Gulf coast north of the Dammam, Khobar and Dhahran conurbation, and the senior-school options for this community are mostly in that conurbation. The daily journey is therefore an intercity run on each side of the school day, and it is the largest single block in a commuting student's timetable. A family planning tuition around a 5pm start has not yet looked at the clock on the day it actually happens.

Compare that with a student still schooled on the camp. Their journey is minutes, their usable evening is the widest in the province, and a 4:30pm lesson is genuinely workable, which also means a second session for a sibling at six is possible. Two children in the same household, one on the camp and one commuting to Dhahran, need two completely different slots, and families routinely discover this three weeks into an arrangement rather than before it.

The table below sets out each destination against what the journey does to the evening and the lesson slot that survives it. The journey characterisations are the patterns families describe rather than measured data, and a closure on the coast road or roadworks around Qatif will beat any estimate. The point of the table is not precision; it is to get the right slot chosen on the first attempt instead of the third.

There is a consequence for the tutor side of the match. If the honest earliest start is 6:30pm Saudi time, the tutor has to be someone whose own day still has teaching in it at 6:30pm Arabia Standard Time. That rules out a large part of the world regardless of subject knowledge, and it is why the match process asks for the hour before it asks for anything else. A superb specialist for whom your slot falls at midnight is not a match, and saying so early is cheaper than discovering it in week two.

sections.heading: Command terms and mark schemes: teaching the thing that is actually being marked
paragraphs: A command term is an instruction with a defined meaning, and the examiner is paid to treat it as one. State, describe, explain, analyse, evaluate, derive, justify and compare are not stylistic variations on 'write about'. Each sets a different bar, and each has a mark allocation that reflects it. A student who writes an excellent description where an explanation was required has not misunderstood the chemistry; they have answered a different question from the one on the paper, and the mark scheme has no mechanism for giving them credit for it.

This is the highest-yield thing to teach a student in the Eastern Province or anywhere else, because almost nobody teaches it explicitly. The method is simple and unglamorous. Take a question. Before writing anything, say out loud what the command term requires and how many marks are available. Predict the scheme. Then write the answer, then compare it with the real scheme and count the difference. Students find this uncomfortable for about two weeks and then start doing it automatically in examinations.

The companion skill is reading mark allocation as structure. A four-mark question wants four distinct creditable points, not one point expressed four ways, and a two-mark question does not want a paragraph. Students who write at length because length feels like effort routinely score less than students who write exactly four things. Making that visible — counting the marks in their own answers against the scheme — converts a vague instruction to 'answer the question' into something checkable.

None of this replaces content. A student who does not know the chemistry cannot be taught to fake it, and anyone selling that is selling nothing. But in our experience of the enquiries that come in from this coast, the split is usually two-thirds technique and one-third content for a student stuck in the middle grades, and the technique two-thirds moves faster. That is why the diagnostic hour comes before the plan: we would rather sell four sessions on technique than twenty on content a student already has.

sections.heading: What a curriculum switch leaves missing, and how to find it before a mock paper does
paragraphs: Families move in and out of this community on postings, and mid-course transfers are normal rather than exceptional. The problem with a transfer is not that a student is behind. It is that the previous school's report describes achievement in a system with different content sequencing, different assessment style and different expectations about independent work, so the report cannot tell you where the gaps are. A strong grade from one system and a weak start in another is almost always a sequencing mismatch, not a sudden collapse in ability.

The practical answer is an audit rather than a judgement. Take the new syllabus, go through it topic by topic, and sort each one into three piles: covered properly, covered differently, and never met. The second pile is the dangerous one, because the student believes they know the topic and will not flag it. A student who studied electricity in an American-curriculum course and is now in Higher Level Physics has met the content and not the treatment, and that shows up as a sudden low mark on a topic they considered safe.

Assessment style transfers worst of all. A student arriving from a system that rewards a well-organised model answer has to learn to write against a mark scheme, which is a different activity. A student arriving from a Middle Years Programme into Cambridge IGCSE has excellent criterion-based writing habits and no experience of the past-paper volume the IGCSE year expects. Neither of those is a content gap, and neither is fixed by content teaching.

The table sets out the common moves in and out of this province with what transfers cleanly and what has to be built. The honest message in it is that one term recovers a great deal when the work is targeted and very little when it is general. The audit is what makes it targeted, and it is the first thing we do for a transferring student rather than the third.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week on Arabia Standard Time, in a shift-work town
paragraphs: The school week here runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend. That single fact invalidates most tutoring schedules designed elsewhere. A tutor whose own working week runs Monday to Friday has their quietest day on your weekend and their busiest on your Sunday, and an arrangement built without noticing it falls apart in the third week. We build the week the other way round, from the Saudi school calendar outwards, and ask tutors to fit it.

The Kingdom keeps Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, and does not observe daylight saving. Any slot agreed with a tutor in a country that does change its clocks will drift by an hour twice a year unless it is pinned to Saudi local time, and we pin it there. The tutor's stated hour moves; yours does not. A commuting student's evening has no slack in it, so an hour of drift is not a minor inconvenience, it is the difference between a lesson and a missed lesson.

A refinery town adds shift patterns on top of all of this. One parent may be on a rotation that does not line up with the school day, which affects who is at home when, who can read the session notes and who attends a review call. We handle that by making the written record the primary channel rather than the conversation: notes after every session, short enough to read on a phone, so a parent coming off shift is not relying on being told about it secondhand.

Ramadan shifts the whole pattern, and because the Islamic calendar moves against the Gregorian one by about eleven days each year it drifts across the academic year rather than sitting in one term. School days shorten and the productive study hours move later into the evening. We move slots later for that period rather than cancelling them, and families who would rather pause keep their slot. Nobody should be publishing dates for it, including us: the start is confirmed by moon sighting and differs by a day between countries.

sections.heading: The first month, and how progress gets reported rather than asserted
paragraphs: The first session is a free diagnostic. Bring two pieces of marked work, ideally a recent past paper and one piece of coursework or an Internal Assessment draft. The tutor spends the hour establishing where the marks are going, not demonstrating a teaching style. At the end you get a written view: which component is leaking, whether the cause is content, technique or pace, and what the shortest route to fixing it looks like. Sometimes that view is that no weekly tuition is needed, and we say so.

Weeks two to four are the targeted work, and they have something checkable at the end. The plan names components, not grades, because a target grade set by a tutor is a guess presented as a commitment. What it can promise is a measurable change in a specific thing: method marks recovered on an Extended-tier paper, a research question narrowed to something answerable, an alternative-to-practical past paper scored and reviewed. Those are things a parent can verify without taking anybody's word for it.

Reporting is written and comes after every session: what was covered, what the student got wrong, and one specific thing to do before the next lesson. At the end of the first month there is a review against the marked work rather than against impressions. If the component is paying out better, we continue or reduce to periodic review. If nothing has moved, that is information, and we act on it rather than selling a second month to see what happens.

What we do when it is not working is the part most providers leave vague. If the tutor is the wrong fit, we reassign at no cost and the new tutor reads the previous notes so the diagnostic is not repeated. If the problem is not academic — sleep, a timetable with no slack in it, a subject choice that was wrong from the start — we say that, even though it means fewer billable hours. A family on this coast has few local alternatives, which makes being straight with them more important rather than less.

sections.heading: Assessed work: the line we do not cross, and why we say so in writing
paragraphs: Several providers visible in Saudi search results are selling the completion of assessed work. We are not, and the boundary is worth stating precisely rather than gesturing at. A tutor may teach the skills an Internal Assessment demands. They may explain each assessment criterion and what it rewards. They may read a student's own draft and interrogate it: is this research question answerable with the data available, is this variable actually controlled, does this conclusion follow, is this uncertainty treatment defensible. They may teach referencing, and they may work a full example on a topic the student is not being assessed on.

A tutor may not write any of it. Not a paragraph, not a handed-over research question, not a rewritten conclusion, not a tidied methodology. We decline requests to produce or complete an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay, a Theory of Knowledge essay or a Middle Years Personal Project, and we decline them explicitly rather than quietly. The work must be the student's own, the school supervisor certifies that it is, and a student who submits work that is not theirs risks the whole Diploma rather than one subject grade.

The useful consequence of that boundary is that honest help is front-loaded. The most valuable hour on any Internal Assessment is spent on the research question before data exists, because a badly scoped question caps the achievable mark regardless of execution. The second most valuable is spent on the criterion the student has misread, which is almost always the evaluation one rather than the method one. Both are teaching, both are legitimate, and both are more effective than editing a finished draft.

Keep a family record. Dated drafts, notes from school supervision meetings, and a clear memory of where each idea came from. That is not defensive paperwork. It is what lets a student talk confidently about their own work in a supervision meeting, and it is the habit the Extended Essay reflection requirement exists to build in the first place.

sections.heading: What this costs in the Eastern Province, and when to stop buying it
paragraphs: Rates in the Kingdom are published by vendors rather than by any regulator, so every figure available is an advertised rate rather than a market average, and none of them is our price. The published range is wide. General online tutoring with no subject specialism is advertised from around SAR 55 an hour, and budget international platforms list Cambridge IGCSE one-to-one from about SAR 35. Tutor-marketplace guides put private tuition for primary years near SAR 50 and senior-school examination subjects above SAR 200. Companies listing IB work specifically advertise from about SAR 180, reaching SAR 200 to 220 for Higher Level tracks, and some international providers quote around sixty US dollars an hour.

What moves a number, in order: subject scarcity, then marking or examiner experience, then level, then travel, then package length. Scarcity dominates, and parents consistently under-weight it. A Standard Level Applications and Interpretation specialist is a common profile. Someone who can teach Higher Level Physics extension topics and has marked the Internal Assessment against its criteria is not, and the gap in price between them reflects supply rather than effort. In a province where the local pool for a given Higher Level subject may be nobody at all, that is the whole argument for buying the hour over video.

The question families here should ask is not what an hour costs but how many hours this needs. A component clinic of five sessions aimed at the alternative-to-practical paper is a smaller purchase than a year of weekly general tuition and frequently does more, because it targets a thing that was measurably broken. The diagnostic hour exists to make that judgement possible before any money changes hands.

Knowing when to stop is part of the service and almost nobody writes it down. A student whose method marks have come back, whose research question is sound and who can predict a mark scheme does not need a standing weekly appointment. At each review we say plainly whether the marked work justifies continuing. Periodic review every three or four weeks is often the right landing place, and it costs a fraction of weekly teaching. We would rather make that recommendation and keep the family than hold a slot nobody needs.

faqs.question: How does a lesson fit around a Ras Tanura student's coach ride back from a Dhahran school?
faqs.answer: By starting after it rather than inside it. The honest earliest start for a student commuting down the coast road is about 6:30pm, once they are home, fed and no longer a passenger. We fix the slot there and keep it, rather than booking 5pm and rescheduling it every other week. On a heavy homework night a shorter session that actually happens is worth more than a long one that gets cancelled, so the agreed slot includes a shorter fallback length.

faqs.question: Can a Ras Tanura student take a lesson on a Friday or Saturday instead of a weekday evening?
faqs.answer: Yes, and for some families it is the better pattern. Friday and Saturday are the weekend here, so a session then does not compete with the commute or with homework. It works well for students who board or weekly-board away in term time, and for intensive blocks before a series. The trade-off is that a weekend lesson is further from the school week, so homework set in it needs to be specific enough to survive five days before the next contact.

faqs.question: Our tutor is in the United Kingdom. What stops our Ras Tanura slot moving when their clocks change?
faqs.answer: The slot is recorded in Arabia Standard Time, which does not change, and the tutor absorbs the shift. A 6:30pm Saudi lesson is 3:30pm for them in their winter and 4:30pm in their summer; both sit inside a working afternoon, which is why British-based tutors suit this coast well. Without that discipline the lesson drifts by an hour twice a year, and in a household with no slack in the evening an hour of drift means a missed lesson rather than a late one.

faqs.question: How do lesson times change during Ramadan for a family living on the refinery camp?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and the productive study hours move later, so slots move later with them rather than being cancelled. Families who prefer to pause keep their slot and resume afterwards at no cost. Because the Islamic calendar moves against the Gregorian one by roughly eleven days a year, this lands in a different part of the academic year each time, which is why we agree it a few weeks ahead rather than assuming last year's arrangement. We do not publish dates for it; the start is confirmed by moon sighting.

faqs.question: What happens to a Ras Tanura student's weekly slot during the long summer break?
faqs.answer: It is held if you want it held. Many families on company postings travel for a long stretch of the break, so the usual pattern is to pause and resume with the same tutor and the same hour. Some students keep a reduced schedule through part of it, which is genuinely useful for a candidate entering the Diploma or moving into Year 11, because the summer before a two-year course is the cheapest time to close a gap. We do not charge to hold a paused slot.

faqs.question: How late can a session start if the school transport gets back after six?
faqs.answer: Seven o'clock works, and half past seven is the practical limit for a session that still achieves something on a school night. Beyond that a tired student absorbs very little and the hour is wasted money. If the commute regularly runs that late, the better answer is usually one longer weekend session plus short written tasks during the week, rather than forcing a weekday evening slot that neither the student nor the tutor can rely on.

faqs.question: Can a Diploma student in Ras Tanura take two different subjects in one evening?
faqs.answer: It is possible and rarely a good idea on a school night after an intercity commute. Two hours of one-to-one teaching demands sustained attention, and the second hour tends to deliver a fraction of the first. Where a student genuinely needs two subjects, we split them across two evenings, or put one on the weekend. The exception is an intensive block before a series, when the student is not also carrying a full school day and the pattern changes completely.

faqs.question: What transfers when a Ras Tanura student moves from an American-curriculum camp school into the IB Diploma?
faqs.answer: Breadth transfers well: a student used to six or seven subjects at once copes with the Diploma's shape better than a student arriving from three A Levels. Written stamina transfers. What does not transfer is depth at Higher Level, particularly in maths and the sciences, where the extension topics have no equivalent. The Internal Assessment is also a different kind of task from a graded lab report, closer to a small research project with its own criteria. An audit in the first weeks finds both gaps before a mock paper does.

faqs.question: A family relocating to Ras Tanura mid-Diploma: what is realistically recoverable in one term?
faqs.answer: A great deal if the work is targeted and very little if it is general. One term is enough to close two or three specific topic gaps, to rebuild examination technique against the new board's mark schemes, and to get an Internal Assessment properly scoped before the school deadline. It is not enough to re-teach a year of Higher Level content. The first task is the audit that separates those two categories, because the previous school's report cannot tell you which gaps exist in the new syllabus.

faqs.question: What does a Cambridge IGCSE student need to catch up before starting Higher Level sciences?
faqs.answer: Three things, in order. Mathematical fluency, because Higher Level physics and chemistry assume algebraic rearrangement happens without thought. Laboratory write-up discipline, since the Internal Assessment asks for uncertainty handling that IGCSE practical work only gestures at. And the habit of reading a question for its command term. The content jump is smaller than families expect; the jump in independence and in what counts as a complete answer is larger. The summer before the Diploma is the efficient time to do it.

faqs.question: Which subjects are hardest to pick up after a mid-year move into the Eastern Province?
faqs.answer: Anything sequential. Higher Level mathematics is the hardest, because each topic rests on the one before and a missed unit keeps resurfacing. Higher Level physics is close behind for the same reason. Languages are difficult mid-course because the assessed oral work has already been partly built. The easiest to join late are the subjects assessed in discrete blocks, such as geography or business management, where a missed case study can be learned independently without undermining what follows.

faqs.question: What happens to coursework a student already completed at a previous school?
faqs.answer: It depends on the board and the component, and the new school's examinations officer is the only authority on it. Some internally assessed work can transfer with the candidate when the board and syllabus match; often it cannot, and the student repeats the component under the new school's supervision. Ask that question in writing during admission rather than after enrolment, because the answer changes the workload for the whole first term and sometimes changes which subjects are viable at all.

faqs.question: Is it better to finish IGCSE at the previous school or restart after moving to Ras Tanura?
faqs.answer: If the move happens in the final IGCSE year and the boards differ, finishing where the candidate is entered is usually less damaging, even if that means a term of remote schooling or a delayed family move. Changing board mid-course means new syllabus codes, possibly a different tier and a practical component prepared differently. If the move is earlier, in Year 10, switching is manageable with an audit and a term of targeted support. The entry, not the teaching, is the constraint.

faqs.question: What does the diagnostic session cover for a student with two weak subjects at once?
faqs.answer: It covers one of them properly rather than both badly. We ask which subject has the nearer deadline or the bigger weighting and diagnose that one, using marked work from it. Most students with two weak subjects have one underlying cause — technique, pace, or a gap in mathematics feeding into both sciences — and finding it in one subject usually explains the other. If they turn out to be genuinely separate problems, that is the finding, and we schedule a second diagnostic rather than guessing.

faqs.question: How is progress reported to a parent working a shift rotation at the refinery?
faqs.answer: In writing after every session, short enough to read on a phone in two minutes: what was covered, what the student got wrong, one thing to do before next week. The written record is the primary channel rather than a phone call, precisely because a parent on rotation cannot be relied on to be available at a tutor's convenient hour. Monthly reviews are also written first, with a call only if you want one. Nothing important is communicated verbally through the student.

faqs.question: What happens if the first month shows no movement at all?
faqs.answer: We say so, and we change something rather than selling a second month to see what happens. Usually one of three things is wrong: the diagnosis was incomplete, the tutor is not the right fit for this student, or the problem is not academic at all — sleep, a timetable with no gaps in it, or a subject choice that was wrong from the start. We name which one we think it is, reassign at no cost if it is the second, and tell you plainly if it is the third even though that means fewer billable hours.

ras-tanura.closingHeading: Find the component first, then buy the hours
ras-tanura.closingBody: If you are looking for IB and IGCSE tutors in Ras Tanura, start by adding up where the marks went on the last two marked papers. Send us that, the board, the level and the earliest hour that works once the coach is back, and we will match a specialist to the component rather than to the subject. The first hour is a free diagnostic and the written view that follows it is yours whether you continue or not. Lessons are one-to-one and delivered live online, Sunday to Thursday, pinned to Arabia Standard Time. Online IB tuition on the Gulf coast is what makes a Higher Level Physics tutor in the Eastern Province reachable at all.

riyadh.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach the Riyadh cases that come up most often: a Diploma student in Al Malqa who needs Mathematics AA HL, an IGCSE candidate in Al Olaya rebuilding Chemistry 0620 before the June series, an MYP 5 student in Hittin facing the Personal Project. Each teaches one or two subjects, at one or two levels.

intro.heading: Riyadh is one city with a dozen different school runs
paragraphs: Riyadh holds the largest international-school enrolment in the Kingdom, and most of it sits north of the Northern Ring Road, around Al Malqa, Hittin, Al Narjis and Al Yasmin. The rest is split between Al Olaya and the Diplomatic Quarter in the centre and west, and Ar Rimal, Al Rawdah and Al Hamra out east. A family chooses a school, and then discovers that the school run is the thing that decides their week. Two students who share a desk can live forty minutes apart, and the one who gets home at a quarter past four has a completely different evening from the one who gets home at twenty to six.

That is the practical reason this page exists. Finding an IB Chemistry HL specialist in Riyadh is rarely the hard part. The hard part is finding one who is free at the only hour your child is at a desk, awake, and not still in a car on King Abdullah Road. In-home tuition narrows the search twice over: first to tutors who know the syllabus properly, then to tutors willing to drive across the city to your district on a school night. The second filter removes far more people than the first, and it removes them on grounds that have nothing to do with teaching.

One-to-one online lessons remove that second filter. Delivery for Saudi families is online, over live video, with tutor and student working on the same screen and the same past paper. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Riyadh address, and home visits are a service we offer only in India. What that buys a family in Al Narjis is the same tutor pool a family in Al Olaya has, and a slot that holds through the autumn term and through the eight weeks before the June series without renegotiation.

The second constraint is the clock. The school week runs Sunday to Thursday, with Friday and Saturday as the weekend, so a Monday-and-Wednesday pattern copied from a British or Indian provider misses the point entirely. The Kingdom keeps Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, and does not change its clocks at all, so a slot agreed with a tutor in a country that does will drift by an hour twice a year unless it is pinned to Riyadh local time from the first lesson. Both problems are fixable. Neither fixes itself.

The rest of this page is written for the parent who has already chosen the school and now has to make the week work: what the north Riyadh school run leaves of an evening, which evenings are realistically usable, what the Riyadh market charges and why, which subjects a school cluster here tends not to staff, and what changes when a family arrives mid-course from a national-curriculum, British or American school.

riyadh.programmesIntro: Riyadh schools run both routes to university, and a few run them in the same building: the IB continuum from the Primary Years Programme through the Middle Years Programme to the Diploma, and the British route of Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel IGCSE followed by A Levels. Support looks different inside each one. Here is what each asks of a student, and where Riyadh families most often need an outside specialist.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: Six transdisciplinary themes, inquiry-led units and no external examinations, finishing with the PYP Exhibition in the final year. Assessment is continuous and teacher-designed, which means a parent sees portfolios and reports rather than paper marks. The skills being built are reading stamina, number fluency, and the habit of explaining a method rather than only producing an answer.
programmes.countryNote: Several northern Riyadh schools run PYP and then hand students either into their own Middle Years Programme or into a British Year 7. The handover is where gaps surface: a student who has never sat a timed written paper meets one in the first term. Primary support in Riyadh is usually about arithmetic fluency and written explanation, not content coverage.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: Five years across eight subject groups, assessed against four published criteria per subject, each marked out of eight. Marks are converted to a one-to-seven grade using boundaries the school applies. MYP 5 carries the Personal Project, and Service as Action runs throughout. There are no public examinations unless the school opts into MYP eAssessment.
programmes.countryNote: Riyadh families move in and out of the MYP constantly, usually from a national-curriculum school into MYP 4 or from MYP 3 into a British Year 9. The criterion language is the part nobody briefs them on: a student who writes a good essay can still score poorly on Criterion D because the question wanted evaluation, not description.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus the core: Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and CAS. Subject grades run one to seven, and the core contributes up to three further points through the TOK and Extended Essay matrix. Internal assessment sits inside almost every subject and is marked at school, then moderated externally.
programmes.countryNote: DP students are the Riyadh group the school run hurts most, because DP2 evening work collides with the longest commutes in the city. A Diploma student in Al Narjis attending a central school has perhaps two usable weekday evenings. Deciding which two, and what goes in them, matters more than adding a third.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: A two-year, examination-heavy course taken subject by subject. Cambridge reports grades on an A*-G scale and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE on a 9-1 scale. Several Cambridge subjects are tiered, so a student sits either Core or Extended papers, and the sciences split their practical assessment between a practical test and an alternative written paper.
programmes.countryNote: Riyadh has more British-curriculum places than IB ones, so most families here meet IGCSE before they meet the Diploma. The two decisions that matter are tier and practical route, and both are made by the school rather than the family. Ask which papers your child is entered for before buying any support.

riyadh.subjectsIntro: Scarcity, not popularity, drives who is hard to find in Riyadh. A Mathematics SL tutor is available at almost any hour; a Physics HL specialist who has marked for the board is not. The subjects below are the ones Riyadh families ask for most, with what each is actually assessed on and where the marks tend to go missing.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Two papers at Standard Level, three at Higher Level, with Paper 3 at HL carrying extended problem-solving in an unfamiliar context. The HL course adds proof, complex numbers and far heavier calculus. Marks go missing on method lines that are never written down: an answer with no working earns almost nothing on a long question.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: The modelling and statistics route, assumed to be the easier choice and frequently not. The graphical calculator is central, and students lose marks by quoting a calculator output without naming the model or the parameters behind it. Paper 3 at Higher Level is an extended investigation that rewards structured commentary.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Three papers plus the internal investigation. Paper 1 mixes multiple choice with data analysis, Paper 2 is extended response, and Paper 3 draws on experimental work and options. The recurring failure is unit and significant-figure discipline, closely followed by explanations that describe a graph instead of accounting for its shape.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Structure and reactivity across both levels, with the data booklet allowed in the examination and routinely under-used. Organic mechanisms and equilibrium carry the heaviest Higher Level extension. Students lose marks by giving an observation where the command term asked for an explanation, and by skipping state symbols in equations.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: Content-dense, with command terms that separate outline, describe, explain and evaluate far more sharply than most students expect. The internal investigation needs a measurable, controlled variable and a sample size a student can defend. Diagram-based questions are the cheapest marks on the paper and the most often rushed.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagram, definition, explanation and evaluation in a fixed order, with Paper 1 essays and Paper 2 data response. Higher Level adds quantitative questions and a policy paper. The internal assessment is three commentaries on published news articles, and the usual mistake is choosing an article with no clear diagram in it.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tools, techniques and theories applied to real organisations, with a pre-released case study for Paper 1. Higher Level adds a further paper and extra toolkit content. Marks are lost when answers explain a concept correctly but never apply it to the stimulus, which is where the application and evaluation criteria actually live.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: Textual analysis across literary and non-literary works, assessed through Paper 1 guided analysis, Paper 2 comparative essay, the individual oral and, at Higher Level, the HL essay. Students lose marks by summarising content rather than analysing how meaning is constructed through a writer's choices.

subjects.name: English B
subjects.description: Receptive, productive and interactive skills across five prescribed themes. Paper 1 is a writing task in a chosen text type, Paper 2 covers listening and reading, and the oral is internally assessed. Text-type conventions carry real marks: a blog written as an essay loses them before the language is even judged.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: System fundamentals, computational thinking and a solution developed for a real client. Higher Level adds abstract data structures and resource management. The internal solution fails most often on documentation rather than code, because the criteria reward evidence of design decisions and testing against client criteria.

riyadh.igcseSubjectsIntro: Most Riyadh families meet Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel before they meet the IB, and the two boards differ enough on the same subject that a tutor needs to know which one your child is entered for. The codes below are the ones Riyadh schools enter candidates for most often.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Edexcel 4MA1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Foundation and Higher
igcseSubjects.description: The revised Cambridge syllabus splits each tier into a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper, which catches out students who have practised entirely with a calculator in hand. Edexcel 4MA1 keeps two equally weighted calculator papers. Tier choice caps the grade, so confirm the entry with the school before planning any support.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Edexcel 4PH1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Cambridge Extended candidates sit a multiple-choice paper, an extended theory paper and then either the practical test or the alternative-to-practical paper. The alternative paper is where marks vanish: it asks for apparatus, precautions and sources of error that a student who has watched demonstrations cannot describe.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620, Edexcel 4CH1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and organic chemistry dominate the grade boundary conversations. Students lose marks writing equations without balancing or without state symbols, and on qualitative analysis questions that need a named reagent, the observation and the conclusion in the right order.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610, Edexcel 4BI1)
igcseSubjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
igcseSubjects.description: Definitions are examined strictly: osmosis, diffusion and active transport are marked against wording, not approximation. The paper rewards labelled diagrams and penalises vague causal language. Extended candidates meet genetics and transport in depth, and these are the topics most often taught too quickly at the end of Year 11.

igcseSubjects.name: First Language English (Cambridge 0500)
igcseSubjects.description: Reading and directed writing in one paper, composition in the other, with a coursework route at some schools. Marks are lost on the directed-writing task when a student answers the passage instead of the audience and purpose named in the question. Timing is the other recurring failure.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510 and 0511)
igcseSubjects.description: Reading and writing, listening, and speaking, with the difference between the two codes sitting in how speaking is reported. Students who speak English all day at a Riyadh international school still lose marks here, because the examination tests exercise technique and register as much as fluency.

riyadh.regionsTitle: Riyadh districts, and what the commute does to a lesson slot
riyadh.regionsIntro: These are the districts Riyadh families most often name when they describe their week. The detail that matters for tutoring is not distance but the time a child gets back to a desk, because that is what sets the earliest hour a lesson can start and how much of the evening is left afterwards.

regions.name: Al Olaya
regions.note: Central, dense, and well served by schools in walking or short-driving distance along Olaya Street and the Metro line that runs under it. Families here usually get home earliest, which makes two separate lesson evenings realistic rather than one long session. An IGCSE tutor in Al Olaya is competing with the shortest commute in the city.

regions.name: Al Malqa
regions.note: North Riyadh, heavily populated by families whose children attend either a nearby international school or one back towards the centre. The split matters: a local school means a five o'clock start works, while a central school pushes the first usable slot half an hour later. Most requests for an IB tutor in Al Malqa are for Diploma subjects.

regions.name: Hittin
regions.note: West of Al Malqa and similar in profile, with a lot of Diploma and British-curriculum enrolment. The run back from a central or Diplomatic Quarter school lands in the worst of the afternoon traffic, so Sunday evenings tend to be the most reliable slot of the week for a long or demanding subject.

regions.name: Al Narjis
regions.note: Further north again, and the district where the commute bites hardest. Families attending schools in Al Olaya or the Diplomatic Quarter are regularly not home before half past four, and a second subject squeezed into the same evening usually collapses within a fortnight. One lesson, two separate evenings, works better here.

regions.name: Al Yasmin
regions.note: Northern residential with a mix of international and private national-curriculum schools. The pattern here is one weekday lesson plus weekend work, because Friday and Saturday mornings are genuinely free and are the best time in the week for Internal Assessment or Personal Project drafting.

regions.name: Diplomatic Quarter
regions.note: Self-contained in western Riyadh, with schools inside or close to the quarter and short internal journeys. Students here often finish the run before four, which leaves room for a shorter review session alongside a main weekly lesson. Entry and exit routes, rather than distance, shape the timings.

regions.name: Ar Rimal
regions.note: East Riyadh, out towards the eastern ring road, and the longest regular run in this list for a family attending a northern or central school. A six o'clock start is often the first realistic one, which rules out two subjects in one evening and makes Thursday a useful catch-up day.

regions.name: Al Rawdah and Al Hamra
regions.note: Established eastern districts with their own school options and a shorter run than Ar Rimal. Families here tend to hold a mid-evening weekday slot plus a Thursday session, and are the group most likely to ask for support in a subject their school teaches with a non-specialist.

schoolClusters.city: North Riyadh: Al Malqa, Hittin, Al Narjis and Al Yasmin
schoolClusters.note: The heaviest concentration of IB and British-curriculum enrolment in the Kingdom, and the districts where most Diploma requests originate. Families here commonly drive south or west to school and back north again, which is why the usable lesson window starts late and why a fixed slot matters more than a flexible one.

schoolClusters.city: Central and west Riyadh: Al Olaya, the Diplomatic Quarter and Irqah
schoolClusters.note: Older, denser and closer to the schools that have been in the city longest. Students here get the shortest commute, and the Diploma cohorts are the ones most likely to be following subject choices made across two schools. Term dates differ school by school, even within a single district.

schoolClusters.city: East and south Riyadh: Ar Rimal, Al Rawdah and Al Hamra
schoolClusters.note: Mixed provision, with private national-curriculum schools alongside international ones and more families following the Cambridge route than the IB one. The practical consequence is a higher proportion of IGCSE requests, and a greater chance that a Higher Level subject simply is not offered at the local school.

riyadh.modesIntro: Four patterns cover almost every Riyadh family who gets in touch. The right one depends less on the subject than on the commute: how late the student gets to a desk, how many evenings are genuinely free, and whether the family is working towards a series or recovering from a mid-year move into the city.

modes.title: One weekly lesson on a fixed evening
modes.description: The default, and the one that survives a Riyadh school year. A single named slot each week, held for the term, on the evening the commute actually allows. Pinned to Arabia Standard Time so it does not move when a tutor's own country changes its clocks, and reviewed at the end of each term rather than renegotiated weekly.

modes.title: Two subjects across two separate evenings
modes.description: For the Diploma student carrying two weak subjects. Splitting them across different evenings almost always beats stacking them back to back, particularly for families in Al Narjis or Ar Rimal where the second hour would start after half past seven. Two tutors, two slots, one shared view of what the week looks like.

modes.title: An intensive block before a series
modes.description: A short, heavier run of lessons in the weeks before a June or November series, built around past papers and mark schemes rather than new content. It works when the content is mostly there and the marks are being lost on technique, timing and command terms. It does not work as a substitute for a year of teaching.

modes.title: Mid-course arrival in Riyadh
modes.description: For families relocating into the city part-way through a course, which happens constantly here. The first job is a diagnostic against the new school's scheme of work, not a general assessment: what has been covered, what the previous school never taught, and which internal assessment deadlines have already passed.

sections.heading: What the north Riyadh school run leaves of a weekday evening
paragraphs: Start with the hour, not the subject. A tutoring plan that ignores the commute fails in the third week, when the student arrives at the screen having been in a car since half past three. Riyadh is roughly an hour across in traffic from the northern districts to the southern ones, and the afternoon school run coincides with the general late-afternoon load on King Fahd Road, the Northern Ring Road and the eastern ring. The result is that two families at the same school have different usable evenings.

The table below sets out the pattern families describe to us, district by district. It is illustrative rather than school data: your own school's finishing time, the direction of travel and whether a sibling is collected from a second campus will move every figure in it. Use it to work out how many lessons an evening can really hold, which is almost always fewer than a parent assumes at the start of a term.

Two conclusions come out of it consistently. The first is that one well-placed lesson beats two badly placed ones, because a session that starts half an hour late and finishes near bedtime teaches very little. The second is that the weekend is underused: Friday and Saturday are free here, and a Saturday morning is the best hour in the week for Internal Assessment work, Extended Essay drafting or a Personal Project review, where a student needs to think rather than react.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week, and which two evenings actually work
paragraphs: The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday. Friday and Saturday are the weekend. That single fact invalidates most of the scheduling advice a Riyadh family will find online, because the providers writing it are working from a Monday-to-Friday assumption inherited from British or Indian copy. A Tuesday-and-Thursday pattern is a mid-week and an end-of-week lesson here, not two evenly spaced ones.

Sunday is the first school day, and it behaves like one: students arrive at a Sunday evening lesson with a full week ahead, no accumulated homework and reasonable energy. It is the best evening of the week for a demanding subject such as Mathematics AA HL or Physics HL. Monday and Tuesday are workable. Wednesday is the point at which homework from three school days has piled up, and Thursday evening is the start of the weekend, which makes it useful for review, marking feedback and drafting, and poor for new content.

For a student carrying two subjects, the pairing that holds longest is Sunday plus Tuesday, or Sunday plus Wednesday. Back-to-back hours on one evening look efficient on a calendar and are the first thing a family drops in the eighth week of a term. If the commute means the first lesson cannot start before six, treat the second hour as unavailable and use a weekend morning instead. The aim is a pattern the family can still keep in the term before a series, when everything else has become heavier.

sections.heading: Arabia Standard Time against the clock your tutor keeps
paragraphs: The Kingdom sits on Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, and does not observe daylight saving. Riyadh's clocks never move. That makes scheduling simple inside the country and awkward across borders, because a slot agreed in a tutor's local time with a tutor in a country that does change its clocks will quietly shift by an hour twice a year. Families discover this in the spring, when a six o'clock lesson starts appearing at five or seven.

The fix is to agree every slot in Riyadh local time and let the tutor absorb the change on their side. That is a small administrative point with a large practical effect, because a drifting slot collides with the school run and then with bedtime, and the lesson is quietly abandoned rather than rescheduled. It is worth asking a prospective tutor directly which time zone they will hold the slot in.

The second question is the tutor's own working week. A tutor in India or the United Kingdom works Monday to Friday, so a Sunday evening slot in Riyadh is their weekend. Plenty of tutors are happy to teach then, but it has to be agreed rather than assumed, and it is the single most common reason a promising match falls apart in the first fortnight. A tutor in Jordan or Egypt already works a Sunday-to-Thursday week, which removes the problem entirely. Ask where the tutor is based and what their own weekend is before the first lesson is booked, because the answer decides whether the slot you want exists at all for them, and a tutor who is teaching on their day off is a tutor who eventually asks to move it.

sections.heading: What Riyadh families are quoted, and what the number is paying for
paragraphs: Rates in this market are published inconsistently and often hidden behind a contact form, which is why parents cannot calibrate a quote. The figures below are advertised rates taken from tutoring platforms, tutor marketplaces and tutoring companies serving Riyadh. They are what providers say they charge, not a market average, and none of them is IB Gram's price. Treat them as a band to judge a quote against, not as a benchmark to pay.

What moves the number, in rough order of weight: subject scarcity first, then examiner or marking experience, then level, then whether the tutor travels, then package length. A Mathematics AA HL or Physics HL specialist costs more than a Mathematics SL one in every market on earth, because there are fewer of them and their hours are already full. A tutor who has marked for a board charges for knowing what the scheme pays for, which is a different thing from knowing the subject.

The travel loading is the part Riyadh families consistently underestimate. An in-home tutor crossing the city for a six o'clock lesson in Al Narjis is paid for the journey as well as the hour, either explicitly or through a higher rate, and the advertised senior-subject figures in this market reflect that. Removing the journey does not make teaching cheaper on its own, but it does mean the rate is paying for teaching rather than for a car on the Northern Ring Road.

sections.heading: Online against an in-home tutor in a city an hour across
paragraphs: This is the comparison most Riyadh parents are actually making, and it deserves a straight answer rather than a sales one. An in-home tutor has real advantages: a teenager cannot close a laptop on a person sitting at the table, and some students concentrate better with someone physically beside them. For a younger child, or a student who genuinely cannot work without supervision, that matters.

The cost of it in Riyadh is the size of the pool you are choosing from. In-home tuition means a specialist who lives within a workable drive of your district and is free in the narrow window after your school run. For Mathematics SL, that pool is large enough. For Physics HL, Mathematics AA HL, Economics HL, Arabic A or Design Technology, it may contain nobody at all in your part of the city, and a family then quietly settles for a generalist who is available. That is the trade that costs grades.

Online delivery removes the geography and keeps the subject specialism. The lesson runs on a shared screen, with the past paper annotated as it is worked through and saved afterwards, which is better revision material than a page of handwriting the student cannot read back. It also holds on a bad traffic day, when an in-home lesson would be lost. The honest summary is that online tuition is not better than in-home teaching in principle; it is better at finding the right teacher for one named paper in a city this size.

sections.heading: Which subjects a Riyadh school cluster tends not to staff
paragraphs: No school in any country staffs every subject at every level equally well. The pattern in Riyadh is recognisable because the city has a large number of international schools competing for the same small group of specialist teachers, and because teacher turnover in the Gulf runs on a two-to-three-year cycle. A school can run an excellent Higher Level Biology course for several years and then lose the only person who taught it.

The subjects families here ask for most are the ones that are structurally scarce rather than unpopular: Physics at Higher Level, Mathematics AA at Higher Level, Economics at Higher Level, Computer Science, Design Technology, Psychology, Music, and Arabic A for students who speak Arabic at home but have been schooled in English. Several of these appear on a school's option sheet and then run with a single small class, or do not run at all if too few students choose them.

The consequence for a parent is practical. Ask the school two questions before the option sheet is signed: who teaches this subject at this level, and what happens if that person leaves mid-course. Where a school cannot run a subject, some families take it with an outside teacher alongside school study, and that works best when the school knows about it and the outside teaching follows the same scheme of work rather than a parallel one. The question to put to the coordinator is who remains responsible for the internal assessment in that subject, because that answer tells you whether the arrangement is supported by the school or merely tolerated by it.
