sections.heading: Arriving mid-course: national-curriculum, British and American transfers
paragraphs: Riyadh takes in students mid-course constantly, and the transfer is where most of the academic damage happens. The content gap is usually smaller than the assessment gap. A student arriving from a national-curriculum school into IGCSE Year 10 often knows the mathematics perfectly well and has never written an extended answer to a command term, never drawn a labelled scientific diagram for marks, and never sat a paper where the method is worth more than the answer.

From a British school into the Diploma, the subject content maps reasonably well, but three things are new: the internal assessment in every subject, Theory of Knowledge, and the requirement to carry six subjects rather than three or four. Students who thrived on narrow specialisation feel that immediately. From an American curriculum, the gap tends to be depth in Higher Level sciences and mathematics, where the Diploma assumes more content and far more unfamiliar-context problem solving than a typical honours course.

The sequencing of recovery matters more than its intensity. Work out what is assessed first, not what is weakest: an internal assessment deadline six weeks away outranks a topic examined at the end of the following year. Then establish the new school's scheme of work and follow it, because a student being taught two different orderings of the same syllabus at once learns less than one being taught either of them properly. Transfers also need a longer settling period than parents expect: the first month is spent learning how the new school assesses, and judging progress before that month is out produces a false reading in both directions.
bullets: The assessment gap after a transfer is usually larger than the content gap
Order recovery by what is assessed first, not by what feels weakest
Ask the receiving school which internal deadlines have already passed
Follow the new school's scheme of work rather than running a parallel course

sections.heading: What a tutor may do with assessed work, and what they may not
paragraphs: Internal assessment is a large share of an IB grade, and the Personal Project and Extended Essay carry their own rules, so the boundary between help and malpractice is worth stating plainly. A tutor may teach the underlying skills, explain the criteria, discuss a research question, work through the statistics, question a conclusion, and give general feedback on a draft the student has written. A tutor does not write the Internal Assessment, does not draft the Extended Essay, and does not produce coursework of any kind.

The practical test a parent can apply is authorship. If a sentence in the submitted work was composed by anyone other than the student, the work is no longer the student's own, and the school is required to treat that as malpractice. Schools also limit how much formal feedback a supervisor may give on a draft, which is a rule set by the programme and the school, not by the tutor; ask the coordinator what the limit is before any outside help starts on an assessed piece.

Several providers in this market advertise what amounts to a writing service, sometimes in careful language. It is worth knowing what the consequence of using one is: the student loses the component, and in serious cases the Diploma. Honest feedback on a weak draft is more useful anyway, because the examiner is marking the student's reasoning, and reasoning that was inserted by someone else falls apart at the first follow-up question in an oral or an interview.
bullets: A tutor teaches the skill and the criteria, and leaves the writing to the student
Ask the coordinator how much draft feedback the programme allows
Keep dated drafts, so authorship is demonstrable if it is ever questioned
Treat any offer to produce assessed work as a reason to walk away

process.title: Tell us the hour, not just the subject
process.description: The first question is which district you are in, which school the run is from, and what time your child is genuinely at a desk. That decides more about whether tutoring works than the choice of tutor does. Subject, level, board and the paper your child is entered for come next.

process.title: A diagnostic against the real syllabus
process.description: A short first session on the actual syllabus and papers your child is sitting, not a generic assessment. It produces a written list of gaps ordered by what is assessed first, so the plan starts from evidence rather than from a parent's impression of which topic is the problem.

process.title: A free trial lesson with the tutor you would keep
process.description: Not a sales call and not a different teacher. The trial is with the specialist proposed for the slot, so you see how they explain something your child has already failed to understand once. If the match is wrong, say so and we propose another rather than asking you to persist with it.

process.title: A fixed weekly slot, pinned to Riyadh time
process.description: One named hour each week, agreed in Arabia Standard Time so it does not move when the tutor's own country changes its clocks. The slot is held for the term. Work is set between lessons and marked before the next one, so the hour is spent teaching rather than reading.

process.title: Review at the end of the term, against papers
process.description: Progress is judged on marked work under timed conditions, not on how the lessons felt. At the end of each term you get a plain statement of what has moved, what has not, and whether the weekly hour is still the right purchase. Sometimes the honest answer is to stop.

whyPoints.title: The commute is treated as the constraint it is
whyPoints.description: Lesson planning starts from when the student is actually home, which in Al Narjis or Ar Rimal is later than most providers assume. A plan built on an hour that does not exist is abandoned by the third week, and that failure is usually blamed on the student.

whyPoints.title: A tutor pool that is not limited by district
whyPoints.description: Online delivery means your choice of Physics HL specialist is not restricted to people who will drive to your part of Riyadh on a school night. The match is made on the subject, the level and the paper your child sits, which is the only basis that affects a grade.

whyPoints.title: Slots pinned to Arabia Standard Time
whyPoints.description: Every slot is agreed in Riyadh local time, so it survives the clock changes that other countries make twice a year. A drifting lesson time collides with the school run and bedtime, and a family stops it rather than rescheduling it. Pinning the hour prevents a problem that looks like a motivation problem.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted as what they are
whyPoints.description: The SAR figures on this page are other providers' advertised rates, named as such, so a parent can judge a quote. We do not present a vendor's marketing number as a market average, and we do not publish a success statistic we cannot evidence with a sample size and a method.

whyPoints.title: A clear line on assessed work
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches the criteria, questions the reasoning and gives feedback on the student's own draft. Nobody here writes an Internal Assessment, an Extended Essay or a Personal Project. That line is stated before the first lesson, because the consequence of crossing it falls on the student, not on the tutor.

faqs.question: Our child is moving from a Saudi national-curriculum school into IGCSE Year 10 in Riyadh — what actually transfers?
faqs.answer: Content transfers better than most families fear, particularly in mathematics and the sciences, where the topics overlap substantially. What does not transfer is assessment technique. IGCSE papers pay for method, labelled diagrams, named reagents, units and command-term discipline, and a student who has been assessed mainly through recall has never practised any of it. Expect the first term to be about how answers are written rather than what is known. Ask the receiving school which tier your child is entered for in each subject, because that caps the available grade and changes what support is worth buying.

faqs.question: What should a British-curriculum Year 11 student in Al Malqa cover before starting DP1?
faqs.answer: Three things, in this order. First, algebraic fluency, because both Mathematics AA and AI assume manipulation a GCSE student may have done with a calculator. Second, extended writing with evaluation rather than description, since the Diploma rewards judgement in almost every subject. Third, familiarity with what internal assessment is: a student who has only met controlled assessment is surprised by the independence required. The summer before DP1 is better spent on those than on pre-reading content the school will teach anyway. One weekly session across that period is usually enough.

faqs.question: Our American-curriculum child joins a Riyadh IB school in DP1 — where will the Higher Level science gap be?
faqs.answer: Usually in depth and in unfamiliar-context problem solving rather than in topic coverage. A strong honours or advanced course covers much of the content, but the Diploma examines it with questions that combine two topics and ask for an explanation of a mechanism rather than a recalled fact. The practical requirement is the second gap: the internal investigation demands a defensible variable, a sample a student can justify and real uncertainty analysis. Starting that conversation in the first term of DP1, rather than in DP2, is what makes the difference.

faqs.question: Is it realistic to join the Diploma in Riyadh a term late after a relocation?
faqs.answer: It is done regularly, and whether it works depends almost entirely on which term. Joining a few weeks into DP1 is recoverable with intensive support in the first two months. Joining in the second half of DP1 is harder because internal assessment work and the Extended Essay process are already under way. Joining in DP2 is possible but unforgiving, and the honest conversation is about which subjects to protect rather than all six. Ask the receiving school for the schemes of work and the internal deadlines already passed before agreeing anything.

faqs.question: Which subjects do Riyadh school clusters most often leave to a non-specialist?
faqs.answer: The recurring ones are Physics and Mathematics AA at Higher Level, Computer Science, Design Technology, Psychology, Music, and Arabic A for students who speak Arabic at home but are schooled in English. These are structurally scarce rather than unpopular: there are few specialists, their hours fill early, and Gulf teacher turnover runs on a short cycle. A subject can be taught well for years and then lose its only specialist. Ask who teaches it at the level your child will take, and what the school does if that person leaves mid-course.

faqs.question: What happens when a Riyadh school cannot run a Higher Level subject my child needs?
faqs.answer: Schools handle it in three ways: the subject is dropped from the option sheet, it runs at Standard Level only, or it is taught through a supervised online arrangement the school organises. Some families add outside teaching alongside school study. That last route works when the school knows about it and the outside teaching follows the school's scheme of work rather than a parallel syllabus. It fails when a student is taught two different orderings of the same course at once. Confirm with the coordinator who is responsible for internal assessment in that subject.

faqs.question: How do Riyadh international-school calendars differ from the Ministry of Education school year?
faqs.answer: Public schools run a two-semester year that starts in late August and finishes in late June, with an autumn break, a midyear break and an Eid Al Fitr break. International and British-curriculum schools set their own calendars and most run three terms, so term dates differ school by school inside the same district. Two children in neighbouring villas can be on holiday in different weeks. Never plan tutoring from a published city-wide calendar; take the dates from your own school, and expect them to be confirmed term by term.

faqs.question: Why do families in Al Narjis and Al Yasmin commute to a school in Al Olaya or the Diplomatic Quarter?
faqs.answer: Because programme availability is not evenly spread across the city. Some of the longest-established international schools, and some of the only ones offering a particular Diploma subject combination or a particular curriculum, sit in central and western Riyadh, while much of the newer family housing is in the north. Families choose the programme and absorb the drive. The practical consequence is a late return home on school days, which is why a single well-placed weekly lesson works better for these households than a stacked double session.

faqs.question: How late can a lesson start for a student travelling home to Ar Rimal after school?
faqs.answer: Six in the evening is a realistic first slot for a family on the eastern ring returning from a northern or central school, and half past five is optimistic. That matters because a lesson starting at six finishes at seven, which still leaves time for homework but not for a second subject. Families in this position do better with one weekday lesson plus a Thursday or weekend session than with two weekday hours. Tell us the actual arrival time rather than the school's finishing time; the gap between them is the whole problem.

faqs.question: Can a DP2 student in Hittin take two subjects in one evening?
faqs.answer: Occasionally, and rarely for long. A double session that begins at half past five can work for a student who gets home early and is studying two related subjects. Starting at six, the second hour lands when concentration has gone, and it is the first thing a family cancels in a heavy term. Separate evenings, usually Sunday and Tuesday, hold far better. If only one evening is available, use it for the harder subject and put the second on a Friday or Saturday morning, when there is no school day behind it.

faqs.question: Our tutor is based in the United Kingdom — what happens to our six o'clock Riyadh slot when their clocks change?
faqs.answer: Nothing, provided the slot was agreed in Riyadh local time rather than in theirs. The Kingdom keeps Arabia Standard Time, UTC+3, all year and never moves its clocks, so when the United Kingdom shifts, the gap between the two changes from three hours to two. If the lesson was booked as a fixed hour in British time, it arrives an hour early or an hour late for you. Agree the slot in Riyadh time, ask the tutor to confirm it that way in writing, and the problem disappears.

faqs.question: What does the time difference to India mean for an evening lesson in Riyadh?
faqs.answer: India is two and a half hours ahead, so a six o'clock lesson in Riyadh is half past eight in the evening for the tutor. That is workable for many India-based teachers and impossible for some, so it has to be agreed rather than assumed. India does not change its clocks either, which means the gap is stable all year, with no seasonal drift to manage. The other consideration is the working week: an Indian tutor's Sunday is a day off, so a Sunday evening Riyadh slot needs their explicit agreement.

faqs.question: Do lessons for Riyadh families ever run on a Friday or a Saturday?
faqs.answer: Yes, and they are among the most productive hours in the week. Friday and Saturday are the weekend here, so there is no school day behind the lesson and no homework waiting after it. Weekend mornings suit work that needs thinking time: Internal Assessment drafting, an Extended Essay plan, a Personal Project review, or a full past paper under timed conditions. Weekday evenings suit shorter, sharper sessions on a single topic. Many Riyadh families end up with one of each rather than two weekday hours.

faqs.question: What happens to a Riyadh family's weekly slot during the long summer break?
faqs.answer: It can be paused or kept, and the choice depends on where the student is in the course. A student moving into DP2 or into a final IGCSE year usually benefits from keeping a reduced pattern through part of the summer, because the alternative is returning in the autumn term having lost technique. A student who has just finished a series should stop. If the slot is paused, say so in advance so the tutor holds the hour; an unannounced pause is how a good slot is lost to someone else.

faqs.question: How do shortened school days during Ramadan change a weekly lesson in Riyadh?
faqs.answer: School days shorten, which brings the school run forward, and evening study patterns shift later in the day. For most Riyadh families the practical answer is to move the slot rather than to cancel it: an earlier afternoon lesson or a later evening one, agreed for the whole period rather than week by week. Ramadan moves earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, so it lands in a different part of the academic year over time, and it is worth asking the school early how its timetable will change.

riyadh.closingHeading: Start with the hour your child is actually free
riyadh.closingBody: Tell us the district, the school the run is from, the subject and the level, and what time your child is genuinely at a desk. We will say whether a specialist is free in that window, and if nobody suitable is available we will tell you that rather than offering a generalist. The trial lesson is free and is taught by the tutor proposed for the slot, so you can judge the teaching rather than the pitch. Lessons are one-to-one and delivered online over live video, pinned to Arabia Standard Time, and timed to the Sunday-to-Thursday week.

tabuk.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach IB Diploma and Cambridge or Edexcel IGCSE subjects to students across Tabuk Province. Each one is matched to a specific syllabus and component rather than to a subject in general, because a Physics Higher Level teacher and a Combined Science teacher are not interchangeable.

intro.heading: Start with the calendar, not with the tutor search
paragraphs: The first question worth answering in Tabuk is not which tutor, but where the school year already is. A student in the autumn term of a first Diploma year has two years of movable ground: subject levels, Higher Level choices, the Internal Assessment topic, the study habits that decide everything after. A student in the spring term of a final year has technique and paper-by-paper mark recovery, and almost nothing else. Same family, same subject, same budget, two completely different pieces of work. Most pages in this market open with a list of subjects. That is the wrong order, because the calendar decides what is still possible, and in a city where the nearest alternative school is most of a day's drive away, a wasted term is expensive.

Tabuk's school market is moving faster than its teaching capacity. The city is the administrative anchor for the NEOM and Red Sea development zones, and the staff those projects bring in arrive with children already part-way through a Cambridge or an IB course. Private and international schools in the Kingdom are licensed by the Ministry of Education, with school evaluation running through the Education and Training Evaluation Commission. A licence says a school may operate. It does not say the school can field a Physics Higher Level specialist for a cohort of nine, or a Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches teacher who has marked Paper 3. In the north-west that gap is the single most common reason a family ends up looking outside the school.

Delivery matters more here than it does in Riyadh. Lessons are delivered online, one-to-one, over live video. IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the Kingdom; home visits are a service we offer only in India. In a city this far from the Kingdom's large international-school clusters, that is not a compromise. The number of adults within driving distance of a Tabuk address who have taught Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level and marked for a board is close to zero, and an agency promising otherwise is promising a generalist with a car. Online, the question changes from who lives nearby to who knows this syllabus and this paper.

What follows is the north-west in detail: which subjects local schools struggle to staff and why, the academic year counted backwards from the June series, what a workable evening slot looks like against a tutor's own working week, what other providers advertise in SAR and who publishes those numbers, and the Ministry of Education equivalency step that turns an international certificate into something a Saudi university will read. None of it is a price list. Every SAR figure on this page is somebody else's advertised rate, reproduced so you can judge a quote when you receive one.

tabuk.programmesIntro: Tabuk families meet four programmes in practice: the three IB programmes and the Cambridge or Edexcel IGCSE route that most British-curriculum schools in the province follow. The useful distinction is not prestige but assessment shape, because that decides what outside teaching can and cannot change once a student is inside the course.

programmes.name: Primary Years Programme
programmes.description: The PYP is inquiry-led and has no external examinations. Progress is judged on teacher assessment and on the exhibition in the final year. Support at this stage is about arithmetic fluency, reading stamina and writing in English for a child who may be using it as a second or third language. The work that pays off later is number sense and the habit of explaining reasoning aloud, because both are examined indirectly for the next ten years.
programmes.countryNote: In Tabuk the PYP is mostly a transition issue. Children who start in a national-curriculum primary and move into an inquiry-led classroom often read well but freeze when asked to justify an answer. A short block of online one-to-one work on explaining reasoning in English usually does more for a Year 5 or 6 child here than extra worksheets.

programmes.name: Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The MYP runs five years and assesses against four criteria per subject, each marked out of eight and reported as a one-to-seven grade. The Personal Project sits in the final year. Mathematics splits into standard and extended pathways, and the extended pathway is what a future Analysis and Approaches Higher Level student needs. Criterion-referenced marking is the thing parents find hardest to read, because a strong answer can still score low against the criterion actually being assessed.
programmes.countryNote: Tabuk schools running the MYP often have small year groups, which means one teacher covers several subjects and the extended mathematics pathway can be taught alongside the standard one in a single room. That is where outside support earns its place: an extended-pathway student needs the harder work set deliberately, not handed out as an extension sheet.

programmes.name: Diploma Programme
programmes.description: Six subjects, three at Higher Level and three at Standard Level, plus Theory of Knowledge, the Extended Essay and Creativity, Activity, Service. Subject grades run one to seven, giving 42 points, with up to three more from the Theory of Knowledge and Extended Essay matrix. Internal assessment carries roughly a fifth to a quarter of most subject grades, and written papers carry the rest. Almost every Saudi IB school sits the May session.
programmes.countryNote: The Diploma is where Tabuk's staffing gap bites hardest. Higher Level Physics, Chemistry and Analysis and Approaches are the three courses a small school most often cannot staff with a specialist, and they are also the three that university engineering and medicine routes care about most. Families here usually discover this in the first term of DP1, not before choosing.

programmes.name: Cambridge and Edexcel IGCSE
programmes.description: A two-year course examined by written papers at the end, with a small amount of coursework in some subjects. Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended, and Edexcel offers Foundation and Higher papers in mathematics. The tier decides the grade ceiling, so it is a decision with consequences rather than an administrative detail. Candidates in the Kingdom sit the June and November series.
programmes.countryNote: British-curriculum schools in Tabuk Province use IGCSE as the bridge into A Levels or into the Diploma. The practical problem is tiering: a borderline student placed on Core mathematics cannot reach the top grades however well they perform, and a Tabuk parent is rarely told that in those words. Ask the school which tier your child is entered for, in writing.

tabuk.subjectsIntro: These are the IB Diploma subjects Tabuk families ask about most. The description says what the subject actually assesses and where the marks go, because a tutor who knows the content but not the paper structure will teach the wrong thing well.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches
subjects.description: Algebraic fluency carries this course. At Higher Level, Paper 3 is a long investigation-style problem where students lose marks for abandoning an unfamiliar context rather than for not knowing the method. Calculus and proof are where the gap between a 5 and a 7 opens, and the Toolkit exploration needs a mathematical idea, not a survey.

subjects.name: Mathematics: Applications and Interpretation
subjects.description: Modelling, statistics and technology-led work. Students arrive expecting an easier course and are surprised by the graphical-calculator demands and by how precisely the mark scheme wants a model interpreted in context. Higher Level adds matrices, graph theory and more statistical inference than most students expect.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: The content is not the problem; the extended-response marks are. Paper 2 asks students to explain mechanisms in full sentences, and partially correct physics scores nothing if a step is missing. Higher Level adds fields, induction and quantum topics with no Standard Level equivalent, which is why a late switch down is harder than it looks.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Organic mechanisms and energetics generate most of the lost marks, along with the data booklet, which students either use fluently or ignore. The Internal Assessment needs a genuinely measurable variable and enough repeats to say something about uncertainty. Higher Level extends every topic rather than adding separate ones.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The volume of terminology makes this look like a memory subject, and then the paper asks students to apply a concept to an unfamiliar organism or data set. Command terms decide the mark here more than in any other science: 'outline', 'explain' and 'evaluate' want different lengths and different structures.

subjects.name: Economics
subjects.description: Diagrams earn marks and most students draw them too fast. The paper wants labelled axes, correct shifts and a written link between the diagram and the question. Higher Level adds quantitative questions and the policy paper. Real-world examples must be specific; a general reference to a market earns nothing.

subjects.name: Business Management
subjects.description: Tools such as SWOT and Ansoff are the easy part. Marks come from applying them to the stimulus in front of the student rather than describing them. Higher Level adds extension topics and a longer pre-released case study that rewards preparation months ahead of the paper.

subjects.name: English A: Language and Literature
subjects.description: The individual oral and Paper 1 unseen analysis are where most of the grade is won. Students who read widely still lose marks for describing a text instead of analysing how it produces an effect. Higher Level adds the essay on studied works, which needs a defensible line of argument rather than coverage.

subjects.name: Computer Science
subjects.description: Pseudocode, data structures and the written papers matter more than coding ability. Higher Level adds abstract data structures, resource management and the case study. Students who are confident programmers frequently underperform because the paper wants formal reasoning about algorithms, not working code.

subjects.name: Theory of Knowledge and the Extended Essay
subjects.description: Together these contribute up to three points through the matrix, which is often the difference between an offer and a near miss. The Extended Essay needs a narrow, answerable research question; the Theory of Knowledge essay needs real-world examples analysed against the prescribed title, not summarised.

tabuk.igcseSubjectsIntro: The IGCSE side of the Tabuk market is dominated by a handful of Cambridge syllabuses. Codes are worth knowing: they tell a tutor exactly which papers a student sits, and they are the fastest way to check that a prospective tutor has taught the right course rather than a similar one.

igcseSubjects.name: Mathematics (0580) and International Mathematics (0607)
igcseSubjects.description: Two different syllabuses that parents routinely confuse. 0607 is written for international schools and is the usual feeder into Analysis and Approaches. Extended tier is the only route to the top grades, and a Core entry caps the grade regardless of performance.

igcseSubjects.name: Additional Mathematics (0606)
igcseSubjects.description: Taken alongside 0580 by students heading for Higher Level mathematics or A Level. It front-loads calculus and trigonometry, and it is the single best preparation for the first term of the Diploma. Small schools often cannot timetable it.

igcseSubjects.name: Physics (0625)
igcseSubjects.description: Six-mark explanation questions and the practical paper decide the grade. Students lose marks for describing an observation rather than explaining a cause, and for graph work: scale choice, best-fit lines and gradient calculations are examined every series.

igcseSubjects.name: Chemistry (0620)
igcseSubjects.description: Moles, electrolysis and organic chemistry are where the Extended paper separates candidates. The alternative-to-practical paper rewards precise experimental language, which is exactly what a student taught from a textbook rather than a laboratory tends to lack.

igcseSubjects.name: Biology (0610)
igcseSubjects.description: Definitions are marked strictly and the syllabus wording is what earns the mark. Transport in plants, genetics and the human systems carry most of the content. The data questions ask for interpretation, and students who have only revised notes find them unfamiliar.

igcseSubjects.name: Co-ordinated and Combined Sciences (0654, 0653)
igcseSubjects.description: The common compromise where a school cannot staff three separate sciences. Co-ordinated Sciences is a double award, Combined Science a single one. Either can feed into the Diploma, but a Higher Level science from a Combined background needs a deliberate bridging block.

igcseSubjects.name: First Language English (0500)
igcseSubjects.description: Directed writing and the reading passages dominate. Marks go on selecting and using evidence, not on retelling. Students who write fluently but do not answer the specific prompt plateau around the middle grades until that is corrected.

igcseSubjects.name: English as a Second Language (0510, 0511)
igcseSubjects.description: 0510 carries a separately reported speaking endorsement; in 0511 the speaking mark counts towards the grade. Which one a school enters matters for a student applying abroad, and it is worth asking the examinations officer directly.

igcseSubjects.name: Economics (0455) and Business Studies (0450)
igcseSubjects.description: Both reward applied answers and punish definitions offered as answers. Economics wants diagrams drawn properly; Business Studies wants recommendations justified against the case material. These are the subjects most often taught in Tabuk by a non-specialist.

tabuk.regionsIntro: Tabuk Province covers the whole north-west corner of the Kingdom, from the Gulf of Aqaba to the Red Sea coast and inland to the oases. Distance, not district choice, is the organising fact: several of these towns have no international school at all, and the drive to the nearest one is measured in hours.

regions.name: Tabuk city
regions.note: The provincial capital and the only place in the north-west with a real cluster of private schools. Sits at altitude, so evenings are cooler and study time tends to start earlier than on the coast. Most online slots for the province are booked from here.

regions.name: NEOM and Sharma
regions.note: Project housing on the Gulf of Aqaba coast, with staff arriving mid-course from the United Kingdom, Europe, India and North America. Children frequently join a school part-way through DP1 or Year 10, which makes diagnostic work before the first lesson more useful than a syllabus plan.

regions.name: Haql
regions.note: The northern tip of the province on the Gulf of Aqaba, closer to Jordan than to Tabuk city. Families here are a long drive from any international school, and online one-to-one teaching is usually the only way to reach a Higher Level specialist at all.

regions.name: Duba
regions.note: A Red Sea port town west of Tabuk city and one of the staging points for the Red Sea development. School choice is limited, so families either board, commute long distances or supplement a local school with outside subject teaching.

regions.name: Al Wajh
regions.note: Further south along the coast, serving the Red Sea project's southern end. The practical constraint is the working day: parents on project rosters are often unavailable at the exact hour their child is free, so evening slots after the school run matter here.

regions.name: Umluj
regions.note: The southern coastal edge of the province, nearer to Yanbu than to Tabuk city. Families routinely look south rather than north for schooling, which means a student may be following a different school calendar from their neighbours.

regions.name: Tayma
regions.note: An inland oasis town south-east of Tabuk city with a long agricultural history and a small school market. Students here are typically in national-curriculum schools and come to IGCSE as a deliberate switch rather than as a continuation.

regions.name: Al Bad'
regions.note: North-west of Tabuk city towards the coast, small and remote. For a family here, a specialist within driving distance does not exist in any meaningful sense, and the only practical question is whether the connection supports a stable live video lesson.

schoolClusters.city: Riyadh, the nearest large Diploma cluster
schoolClusters.note: When a Tabuk family needs to compare what their school offers against what is normal, Riyadh is the reference point, and it is also where many relocating families transferred from. Several schools there appear in IB directories across the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma programmes.

schoolClusters.city: Jeddah and the Red Sea coast
schoolClusters.note: The closer of the two big clusters by road and the one Tabuk families on the coast tend to know. The mix here is wider: IB World Schools, Cambridge schools, and long-established national international schools following German, American and Indian curricula.

schoolClusters.city: Dhahran, Dammam and Jubail

The International Schools Group runs several campuses and the Diploma is offered at some but not all of them, which is exactly the question to ask before enrolling anywhere.

tabuk.modesIntro: Four ways families in Tabuk Province actually use outside teaching. The right one depends on where the year is, which is why the diagnostic comes before any plan. All four are delivered one-to-one over live video on Arabia Standard Time.

modes.title: Weekly one-to-one through the term
modes.description: A fixed slot, usually one or two a week per subject, running alongside the school's scheme of work. The tutor keeps pace with what the class is covering and spends the hour on the parts the class moved past too quickly. This is the mode that changes a grade over two or three terms rather than two or three weeks.
bullets: Same tutor, same slot, pinned to Tabuk local time
Work set between lessons and marked against the published mark scheme
A short written note to the parent after each session
Pace follows the school's order of topics, not a generic syllabus march

modes.title: Catch-up for a mid-course arrival
modes.description: For a student who has joined a Tabuk or NEOM school part-way through IGCSE or the Diploma. The first job is finding out precisely which topics the class has already covered and which of those the student has never seen. That audit takes a session or two and saves a term of teaching the wrong material.
bullets: Topic-by-topic audit against the school's scheme of work
Priority order agreed with the family before teaching starts
Separate attention to assessment style, which is often the real gap
Honest advice on whether a Higher Level choice is still realistic

modes.title: Intensive block before a series
modes.description: A short, heavier run of sessions in the weeks before the June or November series, built entirely around past papers under timed conditions. Content teaching stops; the work becomes reading the question, choosing what to attempt first, and writing answers a mark scheme can reward. Rates for intensive work are typically higher per hour across this market.
bullets: Full papers under time, then marked line by line
Paper-by-paper analysis of where the marks are actually going
Exam-day decisions rehearsed: order, timing, what to abandon
Works best when content coverage is already broadly complete

modes.title: Internal assessment and coursework feedback
modes.description: Structured feedback on the student's own draft: whether the research question is answerable, whether the method produces data that supports a conclusion, whether the criteria are being addressed at all. The tutor comments, questions and teaches. The student writes every word, and the school's own supervision process stays in charge.
bullets: Feedback against the published criteria, criterion by criterion
Early attention to the research question, where most drafts fail
No part of the work is written, drafted or edited for the student
Records kept so the school's academic honesty process is straightforward

sections.heading: Where the year already is, and what that leaves you
paragraphs: Every useful decision about tutoring in Tabuk follows from one fact: how much of the course is already behind the student. Families often phrase the question as a budget problem when it is really a timing problem. A term of weekly work in the first year of a two-year course changes which grade is reachable. The same spend eight weeks before the papers changes how many of the available marks the student collects from the knowledge they already hold. Both are worth doing. They are not the same purchase, and a provider who sells them identically is not paying attention.

The second thing the calendar decides is whether a structural choice is still open. Subject level, tier, and in some cases the subject itself can be changed early and cannot be changed late. A Tabuk student struggling with Physics Higher Level in the autumn of DP1 has a real option to move to Standard Level. The same student in the spring of DP2 does not, because the Higher Level content has no Standard Level equivalent and the entry is already made. Knowing which door is still open is often more valuable than the teaching itself.

Third, the calendar sets what evidence exists. Predicted grades rest on mock papers and classwork, and universities see those predictions long before any final result. A student who improves after the mocks has improved after the evidence was collected. In a small Tabuk cohort, where one teacher may set and mark everything, this matters more than in a large school with a department moderating each other. Work the table below backwards from your own child's position rather than forwards from today.

sections.heading: What Tabuk schools cannot staff, and why it is not their fault
paragraphs: A school needs roughly a full class to justify a specialist teacher. In Tabuk, international-stream cohorts are small, so one teacher covers a department. That teacher may be excellent and still be teaching three sciences, or both mathematics pathways, or Years 7 to 13 in one subject. The consequence is predictable: the hardest courses get the least specialist attention, because the generalist's time is spread across everything else.

The subjects this hits hardest are consistent across the north-west. Higher Level Physics and Chemistry come first, because they demand both laboratory work and extended-response teaching. Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level comes next, particularly Paper 3, which almost no non-specialist has taught. Then the subjects a small school simply cannot timetable: Additional Mathematics at IGCSE, Computer Science, a second science at Higher Level, Economics taught by someone who has marked it. Families usually discover the gap in the first reporting cycle, when a confident student comes back with a 4.

This is also why the honest argument for online teaching in Tabuk is not convenience. It is supply. A family in Haql or Duba is not choosing between an online tutor and a local specialist; there is no local specialist to choose. A family in Tabuk city has slightly more choice and still faces a pool of adults who happen to live nearby rather than a pool of people who have taught this syllabus. Matching by syllabus removes geography from the decision, which in this province is the only way to make the decision at all.
bullets: Ask the school which subjects are taught by a specialist in that subject, and which are covered
Ask how many students are in the Higher Level set; a set of four is taught differently from a set of fourteen
Ask whether Additional Mathematics or a second Higher Level science can actually be timetabled
Ask who marks the mocks, and whether anyone else moderates that marking

sections.heading: The academic year, counted backwards from the June series
paragraphs: Nobody in this market writes the year out properly, so families plan forwards from today and arrive at the papers with work unfinished. Counting backwards is more useful. The June series is the main sitting for Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel candidates in the Kingdom, and the November series exists for resits and November-entry candidates. Cambridge also runs a February and March series, but that is an India-only series and a Tabuk candidate will not be entered for it, whatever an Indian tutoring site says.

Almost every IB school in the Kingdom sits the May session. Specific examination and results dates are published by the boards and by your school, and they move, so the only reliable source is your school's examinations officer or Diploma Programme coordinator. What does not move is the order: entries close months before the papers, internally assessed work is submitted well before that, and mocks sit earlier still because they are the evidence a predicted grade uses.

The two dates that catch Tabuk families out are both internal rather than external. The school's own internal assessment deadline is normally weeks ahead of the board's submission date, and the entry confirmation, including which tier a student is entered for, happens quietly. Both are worth asking about in writing. The November option is the other thing to understand early: the gap between results and the November entry deadline is short, so a resit decision made calmly in advance beats one made in a panic.

sections.heading: The Sunday-to-Thursday week and a tutor's own clock
paragraphs: The school week in the Kingdom runs Sunday to Thursday, and Friday and Saturday are the weekend. Most tutoring copy aimed at this market is recycled from the United Kingdom or India and quietly assumes a Monday-to-Friday week, which is how families end up offered a Saturday slot that collides with the only free family day and a Thursday evening slot the night before the weekend starts. The workable slots in Tabuk are Sunday to Wednesday evenings, after the school run and before a teenager stops functioning, plus Friday or Saturday mornings for longer intensive work.

The second half of the problem is the clock. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change it. Most of the countries tutors live in do change theirs, twice a year, which means any slot agreed as the tutor's local time will silently drift by an hour and land either in the middle of dinner or on top of homework. The fix is simple and worth insisting on: agree the slot in Tabuk time and let the tutor's own clock move around it.

The third constraint is the tutor's working week, not the student's. A tutor in the United Kingdom teaching a 7pm Tabuk slot is working at 4pm or 5pm, which is comfortable. A tutor in India is working at 9.30pm, which is possible but tiring if it is their fourth lesson. A tutor on the eastern seaboard of North America is working late morning, which suits a Friday session in Tabuk and almost nothing on a school night. None of this is about quality; it decides whether the arrangement survives a full term.

sections.heading: Where the marks are actually lost
paragraphs: Parents in Tabuk usually describe the problem as content: my child does not understand electromagnetism, or cannot do calculus. Sometimes that is true. More often the student knows a good deal and is not being paid for it, because the answer they write is not the answer the mark scheme buys. This gap is invisible from a report card, which records the grade rather than the reason, and it is the single most common finding in a first diagnostic session.

Command terms are where it starts. 'State' wants a sentence. 'Outline' wants the shape of an idea. 'Explain' wants a causal chain, and a chain missing a link scores nothing even when every other link is right. 'Evaluate' and 'discuss' want both sides and a judgement. Students who answer every question at the same length, usually too short for the long ones and too long for the short ones, lose marks evenly across every paper and cannot see where.

The second source is working. In the sciences and in both mathematics courses, method marks exist independently of the answer, so a student who writes only a final figure throws away marks they had earned. The third is graph and diagram work: axes, scales, best-fit lines, labelled shifts in an economics diagram. These are mechanical skills, examined every series, and they respond to practice faster than anything else on this page. A tutor marking a student's own work against the published mark scheme, line by line, finds all three in a session or two.
bullets: Ask for one marked past-paper question back with the mark scheme beside it, not a grade
Count how many marks were lost to method and presentation rather than to not knowing
Check whether answer length tracks the mark allocation at all
Rehearse the long-answer structure separately from the content; they are different skills

sections.heading: Predicted grades, grade boundaries and the small-cohort problem
paragraphs: A predicted grade is a professional judgement by the school about what a student is likely to achieve. It is not a promise, it is not negotiable in the way families sometimes hope, and universities treat it as the school's view rather than as a result. It rests on evidence: mocks, classwork, internally assessed drafts. That is why the timing of improvement matters as much as the improvement. A student who starts working seriously after the mocks may finish with a strong final grade and a modest prediction, and the prediction is what the application carried.

Grade boundaries move between series because the boards adjust for how hard a particular paper turned out to be. A raw mark that earned a 6 in one series might earn a 5 or a 7 in another. This is the reason a tutor who quotes a fixed percentage as a grade threshold is guessing, and the reason past-paper marking is more useful as a diagnosis of which marks are being missed than as a prediction of the final grade.

In a small Tabuk cohort there is a particular wrinkle. Where one teacher sets, marks and moderates the mocks, the prediction rests on a single professional judgement with little internal comparison. That is not a criticism of the teacher; it is a structural fact of a small school. It makes an independent read of the student's work more useful here than it would be in a large department, and it makes it worth asking the school how predictions are arrived at and what evidence they draw on.

sections.heading: What the market advertises, in SAR
paragraphs: Rates in this market are published inconsistently, so parents compare numbers that are not comparable. The table below collects what other providers advertise, with the kind of source each figure comes from. None of these are IB Gram's prices, and none of them is a market average: they are advertised rates, which means they are the opening position of a company that wants the enquiry.

What moves the number, roughly in order of weight: scarcity of the subject and level first, because a Higher Level Physics or Analysis and Approaches specialist is scarce everywhere and a Standard Level mathematics tutor is not; then marking or examiner experience; then level, where Higher Level sits above Standard Level, which sits above Middle Years and IGCSE work; then whether the tutor travels, which loads an in-home rate with time nobody teaches during; and finally package length. In-home rates quoted in the large Saudi cities carry that travel loading, which is a real cost to the family and buys no extra teaching.

Two warnings about the bottom of the range. A rate advertised from about SAR 35 an hour for IGCSE is usually a group rate, a large-roster platform rate, or an introductory offer that moves once a specialist is assigned, so ask who will actually teach the lessons and what their subject background is. And a figure quoted in dollars is a currency decision as well as an academic one; providers quoting around USD 60 an hour are often in time zones that do not fit a Tabuk school evening.

sections.heading: Equivalency, Qudurat and Tahsili: the part nobody explains
paragraphs: A Tabuk family planning for a Saudi university has a step that families planning for the United Kingdom or Canada do not. A foreign or international school certificate needs an equivalency decision, mu'adalah, from the Ministry of Education before a Saudi university treats it as equivalent to the Saudi secondary certificate. This applies to an IB Diploma, to A Levels and to an American high school diploma alike. It is paperwork, it takes time, and it is nobody's job inside the school unless the family asks.

Alongside it sit the Qiyas tests. Qudurat, the General Aptitude Test, is run by the Education and Training Evaluation Commission through its National Center for Assessment. It tests verbal and quantitative reasoning rather than syllabus content, and it is available in Arabic or in English. Tahsili, the Achievement Test, covers the science-stream subjects: mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology and English. The point most international-curriculum families miss is that Tahsili content follows the Saudi national curriculum.

That last sentence is the whole problem. An IB or IGCSE student has studied material that overlaps heavily with Tahsili and has met it in a different order, with different notation and a different framing of what counts as an answer. Strong Diploma students can find Tahsili harder than their own examinations, not because they know less but because the questions are shaped by a syllabus they never sat. Preparation is therefore a mapping exercise before it is a revision exercise. Universities publish their own admission formulas combining school grades with these tests, weightings differ by university and by programme, and competitive engineering, medicine and science routes lean hardest on Tahsili. Read the university's own published criteria; do not trust a third-party summary, and treat any quoted cut-off score with scepticism.

sections.heading: Academic honesty on the exploration, the Extended Essay and the Personal Project
paragraphs: This market contains providers who will write assessed work, and some of them advertise it in language designed not to look like that. It is worth being blunt about where the line sits, because a family can cross it without intending to and the consequence falls on the student, not the tutor.

A tutor may teach the skills the task needs. They may discuss whether a research question is narrow enough to answer, challenge a method that will not produce usable data, explain what a criterion is actually asking for, show a worked example of a different investigation, and give feedback on a draft the student wrote. That is teaching, and it is the most valuable hour a Diploma student can buy, because the exploration or the Extended Essay is where a motivated student can still move a grade late in the course.

A tutor may not write, draft, rewrite or edit any part of the work, choose the topic for the student, supply data, or produce text the student then submits. The student's school owns the supervision process, including how many drafts may be formally reviewed, and the school's deadlines and its academic honesty policy are the ones that apply. Keep the student's own notes, drafts and version history; if a question is ever raised, a clear record of the student's own working is the answer. If a provider offers to produce the work, that is not a shortcut, it is malpractice with the student's name on it.
bullets: A tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback; the student writes every word
The school's supervision rules and draft limits take precedence over anything a tutor suggests
Keep drafts and notes; a version history is the simplest defence of authorship
Treat any offer to produce assessed work as a reason to walk away

sections.heading: Starting, when you are a long way from everything
paragraphs: The practical sequence is short. Tell us the subject, the board, the level and where the student is in the course. We arrange a free trial lesson with a specialist in that syllabus, which doubles as a diagnostic: the tutor works through recent material and a past-paper question with the student and reports back on what is actually missing. Then a plan, a weekly slot on Tabuk time, work between sessions, and a short note to the parent after each lesson.

Two honest caveats, because the north-west makes both more likely. First, availability: the scarcer the specialism, the fewer people teach it, so a request for Higher Level Physics with examiner experience in a 6pm Tabuk slot may take longer to fill than a request for Standard Level mathematics. When no specialist is free at the hour you want, we say so and offer the nearest workable alternative rather than putting a generalist in the room and hoping.

Second, the connection. A live video lesson needs enough bandwidth for a shared whiteboard and a clear voice, and in the smaller towns of the province that is worth testing in the trial rather than discovering in week three. A tablet works; a laptop with a separate notebook for working out is better, because the student should be writing by hand in a mathematics or science lesson. If the fit is wrong after two or three sessions, say so and we change the tutor. That is a normal part of matching, not a complaint.

process.title: Tell us where the student actually is
process.description: Subject, board, level, the school, and how far through the course the student is. The last one matters most, because it decides whether we are changing what is reachable or collecting marks from knowledge already in place. A recent report or a marked paper is more useful than a description of the problem.

process.title: A free trial lesson that works as a diagnostic
process.description: A specialist in that syllabus teaches a real session and works through a past-paper question. You get a written summary of what is missing: content gaps, command-term problems, method and presentation marks, or exam timing. That summary is yours whether or not you continue, and it is usually the most useful hour of the process.

process.title: Matched by syllabus and component
process.description: Not by subject in general. A Cambridge 0580 Extended student and a 0607 student need different teaching, and Physics Paper 3 needs someone who has taught Paper 3. We also match for the slot: a tutor whose own working day fits a Tabuk evening will still be there in the final term.

process.title: A weekly slot pinned to Tabuk time
process.description: The slot is agreed in Arabia Standard Time, so a clock change in the tutor's country moves their hour and not your child's. Sunday to Wednesday evenings after the school run work best in term time, with Friday or Saturday mornings kept for longer intensive sessions before a series.

process.title: Work between lessons, marked properly
process.description: Questions set, attempted and then marked against the published mark scheme rather than ticked. The marking is where the diagnosis lives: it shows whether a lost mark was a content gap, a command-term miss or a presentation problem, and it tells the next lesson what to do.

process.title: Review at the end of the term, honestly
process.description: What has moved, what has not, and whether continuing is the right call. Sometimes the answer is fewer sessions, a different subject, or stopping because the student has what they need. A provider who never recommends stopping is selling hours rather than teaching.

whyPoints.title: Supply, not convenience, is the argument here
whyPoints.description: In Tabuk Province the choice is rarely between an online specialist and a local one. Outside Tabuk city there is often no local specialist in a Higher Level science or in Analysis and Approaches at all. Matching by syllabus rather than by distance is the only way a family in Haql or Al Wajh reaches that teaching.

whyPoints.title: The slot survives a clock change
whyPoints.description: Arabia Standard Time does not shift and most tutors' home countries do. Agreeing the lesson in Tabuk local time means the arrangement does not quietly collapse twice a year into a slot that lands on dinner or homework. It sounds administrative until it has happened to you in the middle of a final year.

whyPoints.title: Matched to the paper, not the subject
whyPoints.description: A tutor who has taught Chemistry is not automatically a tutor who has taught the Higher Level organic mechanisms or the alternative-to-practical paper. We match on the syllabus code and the component, which is also the easiest thing for a parent to verify: ask which papers the student sits and watch whether the answer is specific.

whyPoints.title: Marks diagnosed from the student's own work
whyPoints.description: The first session reads real marked work against the published mark scheme instead of starting from a syllabus checklist. In most cases a share of the lost marks is method, command terms or presentation rather than missing knowledge, and those respond faster than anything else in the final terms.

whyPoints.title: Clear lines on assessed work
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches the skills, questions the research question and gives feedback on the student's own draft. They do not write, redraft or edit any part of it, and the school's supervision process stays in charge. That boundary protects the student, and it is stated here because not every provider in this market states it.

whyPoints.title: No claims we cannot show you
whyPoints.description: No success percentages, no star ratings, no counts of families served. Every SAR figure on this page is somebody else's advertised rate, labelled as such. What we will give you before any commitment is a free trial lesson and a written read on where the marks are going.

faqs.question: What does a first diagnostic session look like for a student who has just joined a Tabuk school mid-term?
faqs.answer: The tutor spends the hour finding the boundary between what the class has covered and what the student has actually met. That usually means working through the most recent topic, then a past-paper question on something from earlier in the course, and asking the student to narrate their reasoning aloud. The output is a topic-by-topic list in three groups: never taught, taught elsewhere in a different form, and taught but not secure. For a mid-course arrival the middle group is the surprise, because material covered in a previous school often used different notation or a different order, and that reads as a gap when it is really a translation problem.

faqs.question: How soon after starting should a Tabuk family expect to see something measurable change?
faqs.answer: Presentation and method marks move first, often within three or four sessions, because they are mechanical: showing working, matching answer length to the mark allocation, labelling a graph properly. A whole grade is slower and depends on where the year is. In the first year of a two-year course, a term of weekly work is a fair point to judge. In the final spring term, judge it on past-paper marks for the specific papers being targeted rather than on an overall grade, because the overall grade also carries internally assessed work that is already submitted.

faqs.question: What should a tutor's first written report on a Tabuk student actually contain?
faqs.answer: Specifics, not encouragement. It should name the topics covered, the questions attempted, and where the marks were lost, separating content gaps from command-term misses and from presentation. It should say what was set for the week and whether the previous week's work was done. It should name one thing the student should do differently in the next assessment. If a report says the student is engaged and making good progress without naming a single topic, paper or mark, ask for the version with the detail in it.

faqs.question: What happens if the tutor we are matched with in Tabuk turns out to be the wrong fit?
faqs.answer: Say so and we change the tutor. Two or three sessions is usually enough to tell, and the signals are concrete: the student is not talking, the work set is the wrong difficulty, or the tutor is teaching a syllabus the student is not sitting. Mismatch is not unusual and it is not a complaint about the teaching; a tutor who suits a quiet, methodical student may not suit one who needs to argue their way to an answer. The diagnostic notes from the first match carry across, so a new tutor does not start from nothing.

faqs.question: What time do evening lessons usually start for a Tabuk family once the school run is finished?
faqs.answer: Most families settle between 5pm and 8pm Arabia Standard Time on Sunday to Wednesday. Earlier than 5pm collides with the end of the school day and travel; later than 8pm costs more in concentration than it buys in content, particularly for a Year 10 or 11 student. Tabuk city sits at altitude and evenings are cooler than on the coast, which in practice means families here often start earlier than those in Duba or Al Wajh. A Thursday evening slot works on paper and rarely survives, because it is the start of the weekend.

faqs.question: Our tutor works from the United Kingdom, so how is a Tabuk slot kept stable when their clocks change?
faqs.answer: The slot is agreed in Tabuk local time and the tutor absorbs the change. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not adjust its clocks, while the United Kingdom moves twice a year. A 7pm Tabuk lesson is 4pm for a tutor on Greenwich Mean Time and 5pm for the same tutor in British Summer Time, which is comfortable either way. The failure mode is agreeing the lesson as the tutor's 5pm, because that becomes 8pm in Tabuk half the year, which is a different lesson with a tired teenager in it.

faqs.question: Does a tutor based in India suit an evening slot in Tabuk, given the two-and-a-half-hour difference?
faqs.answer: It works, with a caveat about their end of the day. India is two and a half hours ahead of Arabia Standard Time, so a 7pm Tabuk lesson is 9.30pm for the tutor. One such lesson is fine; being the fourth consecutive evening session is not, and that shows up as lower energy in the room by the middle of a term. If you want an Indian-based specialist, aim for a 5pm or 6pm Tabuk slot, which lands at a more sustainable hour for them. Ask directly how many lessons they teach before yours.

faqs.question: How do the shorter school days during Ramadan change a Tabuk student's lesson pattern?
faqs.answer: School days shorten and the whole family's rhythm shifts, so the afternoon slot that worked all term stops working. Most families move lessons later in the evening or into the earlier part of the day, and some reduce to one session a week and pick the pace back up afterwards. Because the month drifts earlier against the Gregorian calendar each year, it falls at a different point in the academic year each time, which is why it is worth agreeing the change a few weeks ahead rather than improvising. Plan around your own school's published timetable, not a general rule.

faqs.question: Can a Tabuk student keep the same tutor through the long summer break without losing the slot?
faqs.answer: Yes, and families use the break in two different ways. One is to hold the slot with a reduced frequency, which keeps the relationship and the habit alive without filling a holiday with schoolwork. The other is a deliberate bridging block: a student moving from IGCSE into the Diploma, or from the first Diploma year into the second, uses the weeks to front-load the topics the new year assumes they already have. For a student heading into Higher Level mathematics, that second option is the most productive few weeks available all year.

faqs.question: How much of a Higher Level science grade is decided by the internally assessed work rather than the papers?
faqs.answer: In most IB sciences internal assessment carries roughly a fifth of the subject grade, with the written papers carrying the rest, and your subject teacher can confirm the exact split for the current syllabus. The practical consequence is that it is the one component a student can still improve deliberately and calmly, months before any paper. It is also submitted long before the examinations, so a student who leaves it late trades a controllable fifth of the grade for a rushed draft. Start it early and treat the deadline as the school's, not the board's.

faqs.question: Why does a student who knows the content still lose marks on an explain question?
faqs.answer: Because explain wants a causal chain and marks are awarded for the links, not for the conclusion. A student who writes the right final statement but skips two steps has written a correct sentence that earns part of the available marks or none. The same student handles state and outline questions well, which is why the problem hides: the grade dips without any obvious topic to blame. The fix is mechanical. Practise the long questions separately from the content, with the mark scheme visible, until the student can see where each mark sat.

faqs.question: How do grade boundaries move between series, and what does that mean for a mock result?
faqs.answer: Boards set boundaries after each series to account for how demanding that particular paper turned out to be, so the raw mark needed for a grade is not fixed. A mock marked against last series' boundaries gives a useful ranking and an unreliable grade. Read the mock as a map of which marks were missed and why, not as a prediction. Anyone quoting a fixed percentage as a permanent threshold for a 7 or an A is guessing, and a tutor who talks that way is the wrong tutor for the final terms.

faqs.question: Who decides a predicted grade for a Tabuk student, and can a tutor change it?
faqs.answer: The school decides it, based on mocks, classwork and internally assessed drafts, and a tutor has no part in setting it. What outside teaching can do is improve the evidence the school is looking at, which means the timing matters: improvement that arrives after the mocks arrives after the prediction was formed. If you think a prediction is out of line with the student's work, ask the school what evidence it rests on and what would change it. That is a reasonable question and it is better asked early than argued late.

faqs.question: How is internally assessed work moderated, and what does that mean in a small Tabuk cohort?
faqs.answer: The school marks internally assessed work against the published criteria and the board samples it to check that the school's marking is in line with the standard, adjusting the whole cohort if it is not. In a large department several teachers compare marking before anything is submitted. In a small cohort where one teacher teaches and marks the subject, there is less internal comparison, so an external read of the draft against the criteria is more useful here than it would be in a bigger school. It also makes the criteria worth reading yourself.

faqs.question: What do the last eight weeks before the June series look like for a final-year student in Tabuk?
faqs.answer: Content teaching mostly stops. The work becomes full papers under timed conditions, marked line by line, then targeted repair of whatever those papers expose. Sessions often get longer and less frequent, because a full paper plus a proper review does not fit in an hour. Friday and Saturday mornings carry the long sessions and midweek evenings carry the repair work. The single most valuable thing in those weeks is rehearsing exam-day decisions: which question to start with, how long to spend, and when to leave something and come back.

faqs.question: My child moved into a Tabuk international school from a national-curriculum school, so where do we start?
faqs.answer: With assessment style before content. A student arriving from a national-curriculum classroom usually knows more mathematics and science than their new grades suggest and has never been asked to explain, evaluate or justify in the way these papers demand. Start with command terms, written-answer structure and the specific vocabulary the mark scheme rewards, then audit content gaps topic by topic against the school's scheme of work. Doing it the other way round produces a student who knows the syllabus and still writes answers the mark scheme cannot pay for.

tabuk.closingHeading: Where to start if you are in Tabuk Province
tabuk.closingBody: Work out where your child is in the course first, because that decides what outside teaching can still change. Then ask your school two questions in writing: which subjects are taught by a specialist in that subject, and which tier or level your child is entered for. If the answers leave a gap, a free trial lesson with a specialist in that exact syllabus will tell you what is actually missing, and you keep the written summary either way. Lessons are one-to-one over live video, on Arabia Standard Time, timed around the Sunday-to-Thursday week. No tutor travels to a Saudi address, and in the north-west that is the point: your child gets the right specialist rather than the nearest one.

taif.tutorsIntro: The tutors below teach Diploma and Cambridge subjects to Taif students over live video, one student in the room at a time. Each one works to a named syllabus and a named paper, so a Chemistry HL request is answered by someone who has taught Chemistry HL, not by a generalist with a free evening.

intro.heading: Start with the paper, then work outwards to the week
paragraphs: Most tutoring decisions are made backwards. A family notices a grade slipping, asks around for a tutor, and only later finds out which paper the marks were lost on. The order that works is the other one. Find out how the subject is assessed, find out which component the marks went missing in, then find a tutor who teaches that component. A student losing marks on the Diploma internal assessment and a student losing them on the long-answer paper need two different kinds of help, and in some subjects two different tutors.

That is a harder thing to arrange in Taif than on the coast. The city's private schools are largely national-curriculum, which is a strength in its own right, but it means an international-curriculum student here is frequently the only one in their year group sitting what they are sitting. There is no corridor of classmates comparing mark schemes, no teacher next door who taught the same option last year, and often no local tutor who has read the subject guide. The pool of people within driving distance who have taught Mathematics: Analysis and Approaches at Higher Level is, realistically, very small.

This is the honest argument for teaching Taif students online, and it is an argument about supply rather than convenience. IB Gram does not send a tutor to a Taif address: home visits are a service we offer only in India, and every lesson for a family in the Kingdom runs live over video. What that buys a Taif family is not a saved car journey. It is access to a named subject specialist who may be teaching from another city or another country entirely, matched to the syllabus your child is actually entered for.

The second thing Taif changes is the clock. The school week runs Sunday to Thursday, so Thursday evening behaves like a Friday night and Sunday morning behaves like a Monday. Arabia Standard Time is UTC+3 and the Kingdom does not change its clocks, which means a slot agreed with a tutor in a country that does will quietly drift twice a year unless it is pinned to Saudi local time. Add the school run, which in Taif varies a great deal between a central district and the escarpment villages above the city, and the set of workable evening slots narrows fast.

So this page is ordered the way a planning conversation should be. First the assessment structure, paper by paper, because that is what a grade is made of. Then the command terms and the places marks go missing. Then the school run and the hours it leaves. Then what tuition is advertised at in this market in SAR, what Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel do differently with the same subject, how the year counts back from the June and November series, what a tutor may and may not touch on assessed work, and finally the equivalency and Qiyas steps that sit between a good grade and a Saudi university place.
