sections.heading: Academic honesty on the internal assessment, the Extended Essay and the Personal Project
paragraphs: This matters more than anything else on this page, because getting it wrong ends a Diploma rather than lowering a grade. A tutor may teach the skills an assessed piece of work needs, explain the criteria, discuss a research question, read a draft the student wrote and say where it falls short of a descriptor. A tutor may not write, part-write, redraft or supply text for any assessed piece. There is no version of that which is acceptable, and no framing that makes it acceptable.

The distinction is clear in practice even when it sounds fine in theory. Showing a student what a criterion descriptor asks for and letting them find the gap in their own paragraph is teaching. Handing back a paragraph rewritten in better prose is not, however it is labelled. We give written feedback on the student's own work, the student does the revising, and the record of drafts stays with the student. Several of the providers competing for this search are plainly selling the other thing, and a Yanbu school's coordinator will recognise it.

Schools have their own internal supervision structure and their own number of permitted formal draft reviews. An outside tutor works inside that structure rather than around it, which means knowing what the school's deadlines are and what the supervisor has already said. The family should tell the school that outside subject support is in place; there is nothing to hide and a coordinator who knows is a coordinator who can help.

For the Middle Years Programme Personal Project the same rule applies with one extra wrinkle: the process journal is itself assessed, so the record of how the work developed matters as much as the product. A student who is coached into a polished outcome with no honest trail of its development is in a worse position than one whose project is rougher and genuinely theirs.

sections.heading: Starting from Yanbu: the honest version
paragraphs: The first conversation is about diagnosis rather than scheduling. We want the subject, the board or programme, the level, the syllabus code if you have it, the school's term structure, and ideally a marked piece of recent work. A mock script with the examiner's marks on it is worth more than any description a parent or a student can give, because it shows where marks were actually lost rather than where everyone thinks they were.

A trial lesson comes before any commitment, and it is a diagnostic rather than a sales call. The tutor works through a problem with your child and then says what the issue looks like from inside the subject. Sometimes the answer is that weekly support is not what is needed: a student who understands the content and is losing marks on command terms needs a short, specific block, and a student two topics behind needs those two topics, not a term of general help.

Sometimes there is no specialist free at the hour your evening falls. That happens, particularly for scarce subjects at Higher Level and particularly in the weeks before a series when everybody wants the same slot. We will say so rather than offering a generalist and calling it a match, and we will say what alternatives exist: a different hour, a different day inside the Sunday-to-Thursday week, or a start date after the current block clears. A match you were talked into is not worth having.

After that, the rhythm is simple. A fixed weekly slot in Arabia Standard Time, work between lessons, written feedback to you after each session, and a review at the end of the first month where either side can say this is not working. A relocation inside the Kingdom or out of it does not interrupt anything, which for an industrial-city family is more than an administrative convenience.

process.title: Tell us the syllabus, not just the subject
process.description: Chemistry is not a request; Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry at Extended tier, or Diploma Chemistry at Higher Level with the internal assessment due this term, is. The board, the level, the paper causing trouble and the school's term structure let us shortlist by syllabus rather than by subject label, which is the whole point of matching.

process.title: Send something marked
process.description: A mock script, a returned internal assessment draft with the supervisor's comments, a test paper with the marks visible. One marked script tells a subject specialist more than a long conversation, because it shows which marks were lost and to what: content, technique, timing or command-term reading. Guesswork at this stage costs lessons later.

process.title: Settle the slot before the tutor
process.description: Fix the hour that works against your district's school run and your household's week, in Arabia Standard Time. Then we match inside the pool that is genuinely working at that hour. Doing it the other way round produces a tutor who suits on paper and cannot sustain the time, which is a change of tutor two months in.

process.title: Use the trial as a diagnostic
process.description: The trial lesson exists to produce an opinion, not a signature. Your child works through a real problem and the tutor says what the difficulty actually is and what the first four weeks should do about it. If the honest answer is that a short block beats a term of weekly lessons, that is what we will tell you.

process.title: Review at the end of the first month
process.description: Four sessions in, there is enough evidence to judge. We look at what the written feedback has said each week, whether the same errors are still appearing, and what the school has observed. Either side can stop or change tutor at that point without an argument, and continuing should be a decision rather than a default.

whyPoints.title: Matched by syllabus, not by postcode
whyPoints.description: A Yanbu family's local pool is short before any constraint is added. Matching on the syllabus code, the level and the specific paper draws on everyone working at your hour instead, which is the only version of this search that gets a scarce Higher Level specialist in front of a student on the Red Sea coast.

whyPoints.title: Built for the Sunday-to-Thursday week
whyPoints.description: Slots are set in Arabia Standard Time and judged against the tutor's own working week, so a Sunday school night is not quietly somebody's weekend. The arrangements that survive a full year are the ones where both sides' weeks were checked before the first lesson rather than discovered in the third month.

whyPoints.title: Rates quoted per subject and level, with the market shown
whyPoints.description: The advertised figures on this page are other providers' published rates, with the source type named, so you can see the range before anyone quotes you. We price the specific thing: this subject, this level, this many sessions, with a clear answer on what happens to sessions you do not use.

whyPoints.title: Feedback on the student's own work, never a rewrite
whyPoints.description: A tutor teaches the criteria, reads what the student wrote and says where it misses a descriptor. No assessed work is written, part-written or redrafted for a student, on any subject, at any level. That is a rule rather than a preference, and it is the line several providers competing for this search do not hold.

whyPoints.title: Continuity through a relocation
whyPoints.description: Industrial-city postings move families mid-course between Yanbu, Jubail, Jeddah and out of the Kingdom. Because teaching is delivered over live video, a move changes the address and nothing else: the same tutor, the same slot translated into the new local time, and no restart in the middle of a Diploma year.

whyPoints.title: Honest about what is not available
whyPoints.description: When no specialist is free at your hour, we say so and offer the alternatives rather than substituting a generalist and calling it a match. The same applies to outcomes: no grade, score, place or admission is ever promised, because nobody in a position to promise those things is telling you the truth.

faqs.question: What should a Yanbu parent look for in a tutor when the local school could not staff the subject at all?
faqs.answer: Look for somebody who has taught that exact syllabus at that exact level, repeatedly. Where the school has no specialist, the tutor is carrying the assessment literacy on their own: the command terms, the mark scheme, the internal assessment criteria and the paper timings. A degree in the subject is not the same qualification. Ask how many cohorts they have taken through this specification, what the last three questions they marked on it looked like, and what a typical student gets wrong in the extended response. Vague answers to those questions are informative. A tutor who answers them in detail is telling you they have sat in the room.

faqs.question: How do I check an examiner-experience claim before committing a term of lessons?
faqs.answer: Ask three narrow questions. Which board, which component, and over roughly how many series. Someone who has marked will answer specifically and will usually talk about standardisation, the point where markers are calibrated against sample scripts, because that is the part examiners remember. Then ask what the mark scheme rewards in a particular question type that a textbook answer misses. Marking experience shows up as fluency about how marks are awarded rather than as a certificate, and a tutor who cannot discuss that fluently has probably taught the subject without ever marking it, which is a different and lesser qualification for examination technique.

faqs.question: Does it matter whether our tutor has taught in the Kingdom before, or is the syllabus the only thing that counts?
faqs.answer: The syllabus is the larger part, but Kingdom experience earns its place in two specific ways. A tutor who has worked with Saudi families already understands the Sunday-to-Thursday week without being reminded, and understands that school calendars differ between international schools in the same city. They also know the university endgame exists: the Ministry of Education equivalency decision and the Qiyas tests. A tutor unfamiliar with that will give good subject teaching and miss the context of why a subject choice matters. Syllabus first, Kingdom familiarity second, and never Kingdom familiarity instead of syllabus depth.

faqs.question: What happens if we decide after three lessons that the Yanbu time slot is working but the tutor is not?
faqs.answer: The slot and the tutor are separable, and that is deliberate. If the hour suits your district's school run and your household, we keep it and change the person inside it. You tell us what is not working, which is usually pace, explanation style or the balance between content and technique rather than subject knowledge. The next tutor is briefed with what the first one found, so your child does not repeat a diagnostic. There is no argument about it and no penalty for saying so; a match that is wrong in week three is wrong in week twenty.

faqs.question: Should a Yanbu student taking a Higher Level subject their school teaches at Standard Level have a specialist in both?
faqs.answer: One specialist in the Higher Level version, working on the gap. The Higher Level content that has no Standard Level equivalent is the part the school will not cover, and it is usually the part the final paper weights heavily. A tutor teaching the Higher Level specification can hold both in view: they know what school has done and what remains. Two tutors covering overlapping ground is how a student ends up with two sets of notation for the same topic and no confidence in either. One person, one specification, with the school's scheme of work visible to them.

faqs.question: What does an online lesson actually look like from a Yanbu student's side of the screen?
faqs.answer: A video call with a shared whiteboard the tutor and the student both write on. The tutor works a problem in real time rather than presenting slides, and the student writes too, because watching somebody else solve something teaches very little. Past paper questions are shared on screen and annotated as they go. The student needs headphones, a laptop and a surface to write on, and ideally a way to photograph handwritten working so the tutor can see the method rather than just the answer. The session ends with something specific to do before the next one.

faqs.question: How does a tutor teach a diagram-heavy subject like Physics or Economics over video?
faqs.answer: On a shared digital whiteboard, drawn live, with the student drawing their own version alongside. For Economics the diagram is the mark, so the tutor watches the student label axes and shift a curve rather than showing a finished one. For Physics, free-body diagrams and circuits are built step by step and the student redraws them. Finished diagrams are saved from the session so the student has their own version afterwards. This works better than a classroom whiteboard in one respect: the student's attempt is visible to the tutor at full size, immediately, with nothing hidden behind a shoulder.

faqs.question: Are sessions recorded, and who can see a recording afterwards?
faqs.answer: Recording is arranged with the family rather than assumed, and when it happens the recording is for the student's revision. The practical value is real: a worked Chemistry calculation watched again a week later is worth more than a note about it. The practical caution is also real, because a teenager who knows a session is recorded sometimes stops asking the questions that make a lesson useful. Many families record the first few sessions, then stop once the student is comfortable. Written feedback after each session is sent regardless, and that is usually the more useful record.

faqs.question: What happens to a lesson when the connection drops part-way through in an industrial-city district?
faqs.answer: The tutor waits, then reconnects, and the time lost is made up rather than charged. If a session cannot be recovered it is rescheduled inside the same week where the Sunday-to-Thursday timetable allows it. Practically, a dropped connection is survivable if the work was already shared: a student who has the question on paper in front of them can keep working through a reconnection. Tutors are asked to share the session's material at the start for exactly that reason. A persistent problem is worth solving at the household level, and a wired connection for the study corner fixes most of them.

faqs.question: Can a parent in Yanbu sit in on sessions, and is that a good idea?
faqs.answer: You can, and for the first session it often helps, particularly with a younger student who needs to see that this is sanctioned. After that it usually works against you. A teenager with a parent in the room asks fewer questions, and the questions a student does not ask are precisely the ones a one-to-one lesson exists to answer. The better substitute is the written feedback after each session, which tells you what was covered, what was set and what is still wrong. If you want to observe, say so in advance rather than appearing.

faqs.question: Which IB topics do Yanbu families most often need taught from outside the school?
faqs.answer: The Higher Level extensions with no Standard Level counterpart, because those are the parts a school running mostly Standard Level groups covers last and thinnest. In Mathematics Analysis and Approaches that means proof and the additional calculus. In Physics it is the extension topics and the extended-response technique that carries them. In Chemistry, organic mechanisms and energetics. Across all three, internal assessment design is the other recurring request: a question narrow enough to generate real data is harder to write than the analysis that follows it, and a cohort with one supervisor spread thin gets less help with it.

faqs.question: Where do IGCSE students on this coast lose the most marks, subject by subject?
faqs.answer: In Mathematics, in visible working: a right answer with no method is worth less than an honest flawed method. In the sciences, in explanation questions answered with description, and in units. In Biology, in definitions marked strictly and in six-mark answers given two lines. In Business Studies and Economics, in generic answers that never use the figures printed in the case. The pattern across all of them is the same, and it is not knowledge. Students lose marks because they answer the question they expected rather than the one the command term actually asked for.

faqs.question: My child understands the content but the marks do not move. What is actually wrong?
faqs.answer: Almost always technique, and technique is diagnosable from a marked script. Four things account for most of it: misreading the command term, so an explain question gets a describe answer; answering at the wrong length for the marks available; losing the method marks by not showing working; and running out of time because the early questions were over-answered. None of those improve by covering content again, which is what a worried family usually does. They improve by working past paper questions under time, against the mark scheme, with somebody who can say which of the four happened.

faqs.question: Which subject is most often rushed at the end of the course in a small Yanbu cohort?
faqs.answer: Whichever one the teacher is covering alongside another course, which in a small cohort is usually a Higher Level option with few students in it. The symptom is a syllabus whose last topics were taught in the final weeks or set as reading, and those topics then appear on the paper weighted the same as everything else. Check this in the term before the series by asking your child which topics have been covered and comparing that against the syllabus contents list. A gap found then is teachable. The same gap found after the mocks is a compromise.

faqs.question: Do we need a tutor for the whole Diploma, or for one subject at a time?
faqs.answer: One subject at a time, in almost every case. A student taking outside support in four subjects at once has no evenings left and no capacity to act on any of the feedback, and the Diploma core still needs doing. Pick the subject where the gap is widest or where the stakes are highest, usually a Higher Level subject a destination programme expects, and fix that one. Add a second only once the first has a rhythm. A family doing everything at once is usually solving anxiety rather than a subject problem, and the student pays for it.

yanbu.closingHeading: Start with the subject, the level and one marked script
yanbu.closingBody: If your child's school in Yanbu cannot staff the subject at the level they need, the local pool is not the answer to that problem and no amount of searching makes it one. Tell us the board, the syllabus code if you have it, the level and the paper that is costing marks, and send one recently marked piece of work. A trial lesson follows, and it is a diagnostic rather than a sales call: the tutor will say what the real difficulty is and what the first four weeks should do about it. Lessons run one-to-one over live video, in Arabia Standard Time, inside your Sunday-to-Thursday week. No grade, score or university place is ever promised, and the administrative route through equivalency and the Qiyas tests stays yours and the Ministry's.
